EAWR DICK'S BEAWN A-COOAR-T-IN' TO-NEET. There's twopence bin gi'n to eawr Johnny, For cleynin' a new air o' sham Some 'bacco's bin bowt for ml gronny, For airin' yon breeches o' th' oon ; A:reef hearty kiss to eawr Lizzie, For fixin' a collar on reet. Yo wonder what meks o so busy— Eawr Dick's beawn a-cooartin' to-neet !

For many a week he's bin ninin', An ceawrin' th' nook like a fon ; But neaw t' sun's beginnin' a-shinin'. Ant' sky slows a wee bite' blue. His luck hes bin varra like t' weather, But things are at last geddin breer; - Aw've sin him an' Nelly together, An' Dick's beawn a-cooartin' to-neet! He's just hecl a dust wi' mi fayther O'er nod cornin' in afoor ten; Mi dad tells him straight as he'd rayther Nod see bits o' lads actin' men: "When he wer a lad, there wer never Such pride when a lass wer to meet." Mi granny chimes in, " Well, iv ever! What's up wi' thi memory to-neet ?" Mi mother toyles on—heaven bless her! Hoo hesn'd a deeal to say; Though aw wear feeard th' news would distress her, When hoo heeard id so sudden to-day. For Dick thinks the waurld ov his mother, He's kind, an' his temper's so sweet, Hoo knows 'at hoo'll ne'er see another Like him as goes cooartin' to-neet ! But hoo likes the shy look o' good natur' As shines i' sweet Nelly's blue eon; For t' lass is as daicent a craytur As ever come trippin' o'er t' green. Her bonny face fills mu wi' pleasure Whenever aw happen to see 't. May joy be shared eawt i' full measure To them as goes cooartin' to-neat! Good heavens! o t' drawers are upended; He's left o his rags upo' t' floor; His stockin's hey o to be mended Wel he's swellin' off eawt o' t' door. Neer mind,. aw's be like to excuse him, His heart's mecl his heyd a bit leet ; An' aw know Nelly winnod refuse him, When Dick goes a-cooartin' to-fleet! Higher Walton.
GEORGE HULL.

German professors are proverbially absent-minded, but none of them more so than Professor nese% of Bonn. He noticed one day his wife placin'r a large bouquet on his desk. "What does this mean?" he asked. "Why, this is the anniversary of your marriage," replied Mrs. Buse!. " Ach! is that so? Well, let me know when yours cotnes around. I'll reciprocate." One day a missionary's wife gave a dinner to some of her foreign friends, and, among other things, ordered her native servant, to have cont.,// for dessert. The din- ner proper passed oft' beautifully, but what was her horror at the close of the meal to see her servant enter the dining-room, bearing on a large waiter three pairs of her husband's trousers! The merriment may be imagined. STRANGT4 NINIFF.NTO OF A GRRAT FIRF.—In October, 1871, a terrible fire laid the town of Chicago in ruins. . Nearly 18,000 houses were burned. 230 lives were lost, and property to the vain., of £39,000,000 wasdestroyed. In Booksellers' Row the only relic of more than one million books was te'S charred leaf of a Bible. On it was printed the first chapter of "Lamentations." con- taining these words among others—" How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people, hoev is she become as a widow! She weepeth sore in the night, anl her tears are on her cheeks "—a touching memorial of the dread- ful disaster.—Little Folks' Magazine. ROW Tax COLLIE REACHED HIS ROME.—The following is a true story about a collie who took a hansom. He , was lost in Oxford-street; so after having spent some time in looking for him. his mistress went home, and what was her surprise when she arrived to see him in the hall. The butler told her the story, ani it was this :—After the doe had been lost, he saw an empty hansom, which he got into; and the cabby could not get him out, for he showed his teeth. He called a police- man, who could not move him either, but with some and difficulty they read the unmeand address on his collar, settled it would be best to drive him to his home. They shut the doors, and drove him home. When lie arrived the cabby rang the bell, and asked for his fare (which he, of course, got), and then the butler opened the doors, and the dog jumped out as if nothing had happened.— Little Folk, .Ilaya:ine. Tug REWARD OF PERSEVERANCE.—At one of the mills in the city of Boston, a boy was wanted; and a piece of paper was tacked on one of the posts, so that all the boys could see it as they passed by. The paper read:— "Boy wanted. Call at the office to-morrow morning. At the time named there was a host of boys at the gate, All were admitted; but the overseer was a little per- plexed as to the best way of choosing one from so many, and said he—" Now, boy's, when I only want one of you, how can I choose from eo many ?" After thinking a moment, he invited them all into the yard. and driving ' a nail into one of the large trees, and taking a short stick, told them that the boy who could hit this nail with it st.ck a little distance from the ttee s iuld have the place. The boys all tried hard; and, after; three trials, each failed to hit the nail. The boys were told to come again next morning; and this time, when the gate was opened, there was but one boy, who, after being a lmitted. picked up the stick, and, throwing it at the nail, hit it every time. " How is this ?" said the overseer. "What have you been doing ?" And the boy, looking up with tears in his eyes, said—. You see, sir, I have it mother; and we are vel, poor. I have no father, sir, and I thought I would like to get the place, and so help all I can; and, after going home yesterday. I drove a nail into the barn, and have been trying ever since, and have come down this morning to try again." The boy was admitted to the place. Many years have passed since then, and this boy is now a prosperous and wealthy man; and at the time of an accident at, the mills he was the first to step forward with a gift of seo dollars to relieve the sufferers. His success came by perseverance.

RAMBLES AMONG ROCKS. • B C/BSTRIAN. The place of my habitation is much begrimed with smoke from divers and extensive works. The air, as may be imagined, is. for the same reason, not over salubrious. It is oftener surcharged with chlorides and bi-carbonates than with oxygen. A gentleman passing by in the train once asked your correspondent how people lived in such a neigh- bourhood; and, proceeding to reply to his own query. said " I suppose they do not live; they only exist." To get away, therefore, to the pure atmo- sphere of the mountains, or of the sea shore, is a treat not to be despised. It has rarely been my lot to decide voluntarily o'n the country or locality in which ,I have rusticated for the season. The decision has been made by others, or byeircumstances arhich were beyond my control. And it was the rule, not the exception, which prevailed on this occasion. As the child of Fate, I started off on the 14th July for the North Wales coast. There was no lack of companions, and the number steadily increased as we halted here and there along the line. lino ing a good part of the district through which the iron horse carried us, it was possible to reply to many of the queries of fellow-passengers as to prominent objects on the route. On the left, and almost con- c,ealed by the foliage of huge oaks, and beaches, and chestnuts, we could just , discern the Castle of Hawarden, the country residence of the G.O.M. Then, a few minutes later, on the right hand, we saw the spot where that übiquitous railway company (the Midland) is engaged on its latest great enter- prise. viz., the construction of a viaduct across the Dee' by which it will emir access to the chief mill- ing districts in the north of the Principality. But we must not linger too long en the various points of interest on the line. A run of about forty minutes brought tie to Rhyl.which is pre-eminently the children's watering place. Starting again, we were whirled past station after station, but as it was a fine clear day the high rate of speed did not prevent us seeing in the distance the spire of the famed Bodelwyddan Church, and the famous Gwrych Castle in the defile of Cefu Ogo, where brave Welshmen, under the command of Owen Gwynedd once wrought great havoc on the forces of Henry H. As we had no inclination to spend an eighth or tenth part of our holidays in a railway , carriage, though our companions were most agreeable, we alighted at the village of Llanfair-, fechan. At the back of this picturesque village stands the Penniaenmawr mountain, some 1,700 feet high, and ' which conduces not a little to the geniality of the climate, inasmuch as it cuts off the east wind. /fence, under its shadow, gereeiums,- fuschias. and other delicate plants thrive in the open air all through the winter. The common and orthodox route to the top of this eminence is by a winding path round to the back of it. But being in search ef adventure we determined to make the ascent by a less frequen- ted path. Accordingly, having walked along the Penmaenmawr-road as far as the little chapel bear- ing the name of " Garizina," we struck up the face of the hill. For a considerable distance rough steps had been laid down, and so far the ascent aas easy. But when these had been passed it was a case of clambering over jagged ;Atones and huge boulders which had been tipped from ,t he quarries above. Here the ascent was so steep that in places it seemed like scaling a wall. More than once we wished ourselves down at the bottom again. , But if going up, was difficult going down would have been far worse. So there was nothino. lor it hut to go forward till the summit might be reached. There- fore we crept upward very cautiously, holding on to, a rock now and again for dear life's sake. Each time we turned to view the expanse of ' sea we felt. we were amply rewarded for our trouble. But when, after a climb of about two hours, the summit was attained, there was presented to our gaze a perfect panorama of sea and mountain, islands and bays, creeks and rivulets. The island of Anglesea, with its little sisfer (Puffin Island), lay open before Us like a map, and Beaumaris, Niettai Bridge, and the hills above Holyhead were plainly seon. We ascended this mountain a second time from another side, and we could not but remark the ex- hilarating (we had almost said intoxicating) effect which its air had upon us. Just as a drunken man will sometimes lie down on the brink of a precipice, so we were inclined to venture where angels would perhaps fear to tread. - Our next ramble was to the Aber waterfalls. The approach to the falls is throu.„4l.l a deep glen fully two miles in length. We were reminded at more than one point of the journey up this glen of the Trossachs between loch Katrine and Callander. The scenery is truly romantic. The fall itself was a little disappointing, perhaps because the volume of water was so small. The rock over which it descends in two leaps is about 100 feet high, and at the top of it is a road (sea friend says) which conducts the traveller over the mountains to the Penrhyn quar- ries at Bethesda: The day following we took a return ticket to Bangor, which, as it contains the Normal College,,a University College, and an Independent College. deserves to be called "The Athens of Wales." On leaving the railway station, we were almost over- whelmed with the entreaties of breugliam drivers. ' But as our " understandings " were firm, we pre- ferred to walk to Garth, whence for twopence we were ferried across the Straits. From the ferry-boat we obtained a good view of the Clio training ship, where 2.50 boys are being educated in tliA craft-, of a sailor. Landing on the Anglesea shore, we madu for the highway and walked to Beaumaris. The road which lies between the park of Baron Bill, the resi-1 deuce of the Bulkeley family, and the shore, is beautifully shaded and cemmands extensive views. Beaumaris itself, though the county to we, i 3 a dull little place. Its streets are narrow and its buildings commonplace: We arrived just in time to pintas- bulate one or two streets, have dinner at the Bulkeley Arms Hotel, and catch the Alexandra, one' of the steamers that sail daily from Liverpool for Llandudno, Beaumaris, and Menai Bridge. We got off at the pier of the last-mentioned town, then crossed the Straits via the Suspension Brialge, and walked back to Bangor. At one turn of the road between the Suspension Bridge and Upper Bangor there is to be had a magnificent inew of the Straits. Only once before have we had such a delightful view, and that was from the heights of the larger Cumbrav as we looked down on the broad stream of the Clyde, with ships of every nation sailing on its bosom. Subsequently we had rambles to Conway and Llandudno. The former we reached after a walk of about seven miles, along what is known as "The old road," on one side of which are towering rocks, and on the other the Irish channel stretching away to ,the horizon. Conway, is renowned for its castle, so ancient and so strong. But latterly another at- traction has been added in the shape of the Cam- brian Art Gallery, which is located in Plas Mawr, a building which bears the date of 1585. The six- pence charged for admission is not too much, for many of the paintings, both of scenery and persons, are really great works of art. Llandudno was reached by train. Here we soon scrambled over rocks and hedges to the top ef the Great Orme's Head. where we had a view of Tudno's Church. The Same day we reached the heights of the Little Orme, whence we saw a most glorious sunset. The great orb of day disappeared in,a deep crimson sea,which gradually changed as the eye followed the horizon towards the north, into a reost lovely purple. Llan- dudno is without doubt the queen of Weld!) water-

PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY Hi)Ort,iferyz. X X I I.—T H E P ,0 T E. The pote continues to edge his way to the front with a pertinacity worthy of a dozen Csesars, and it seems nothing short of studied cruelty that nobody takes any notice of him. I ought to say that nobody appears to take any notice of him, because no man can have his mind unhinged repeatedly without hazarding some con- jecture as to the cause. It appears to me, therefore, that the pote has been treated to a very large amount of that abstract commodity, silent contempt. He rises on the horizon now here, now there, and before he Can diffuse his light as a settled star he splutters and goes out like a ,wet candle. If you were to ask me to tell you tersely what a pote is I should reply that I don't profess to be a genius, but I would endeavour to enlighten you at some length. The pote is a member of the vertebrata, and is sup- posed by a few naturalists to have some clam to be classed with the genus man. He dots not seem to have been brought forward as a living argument to help' to elucidate the Darwin theory as much as he might successfully have been, but this may be owing to naturalists taking the same view of him that is taken by nearly the whole of the civilised world. The pote resembles in one respect the untutored African. The latter reaches the height of enjoyment I when engaged in stringing glass beads of various colours together; whilst the former has developed the blissful mania for stringing words and sometimes meanings together upon much the same principle. lam not aware that I am much above the average in love for the untutored African, but viewing his characteristics side by tide with those of the pote, I feel for the African a love that is more than brotherly. In using the word "pote' to distinguish a particular member of the 'animal kingdom from a vegetable,,l hut anticipate the dictionaries of -the next generation, whose definitions will doubtless be nearly as follows 1 Pote. n. (corruption of poet) a mutilator of high thoughts and pure emotions by a measured jangle in verse; a human being under the hallucination that he is inspired; ' an individual who has persuaded himself that lie is a 1 poet, hut who cannot convince anybody else of the same ' thing." I think we can settle the point that potes are-a species of humanity. The typical pote has long hair and a wad face. The melancnoly expression on his face may be owing to debt, or dirt, or abuse, according to what degree of a pote he is. The eye of the pote is the most conspicuous part of his physiological structure; it, shines forth the watery expression of his soul, so to speak; and this extreme peculiarity sometimes conveys to the mind of the base and ignorant observer the impression that the plate is an imbecile; but we who know him better would not wrong him, or see him wronged to such an extent, for we know that his eye simply mirrors the Prnmethean fire that is burning his vitals. Tne pote can create imaginative glens and woodlands with his immaculate eye rioting, on a whitewashed wall, and at the same time he will borrow five shillings from you with perfect grace; that is supposing you carry two lialfcrowns about with the intention of having them borrowed. I don't imply that the pote will so far degrade himself as to descend from ethereal heights to dwell long bn such sordid subjects as money; on the contrary, he will farget the transaction as soon as com- pleted, in a song of the rippling brook. There is one feature in the history of the pote that to me is rather knotty. Reasonably assuming that there is an analogy between the present time and every par- ticular epoch since the time of Homer, it is a dead certainty that there would be some thousands of notes in every epoch. Consequently the following is a riddle. What has become of the millions of verses rolled out by notes in the ages when there were no hewspapar editors? can only suggest that the verseswere too much inflated with gas and floated heavenward, or that the Muses made them the subjects of their special vengeance. At the present era there exists a very powerful factor that prevents the pote from being immortalised. There is an antidote to every poison if you can only discover it, and as rats and mice have their natural enemies in the shape of dog and cats, so the pote finds, his natural enemy in the form of the newspaper editor. You will probably have noticed the deep furrows on the face of any newspaper editor you may happen to have seen, hut perhaps you never reflected as to what might be the cause of them; if not, I will tell you something that may be called putting you up to the wrinkle. Make the acquaintance of some pote (understand, I don't advise this out of enmity, but a man will some- times go to dangerous lengths to learn something) who is about to make his debvt, especially if lie has a maiden aunt supporting him behind the scenes. Arrange to go with him when he submits what we call (for want of a better name) a "vome" to some newspaper editor. If you can persuade the editor to read the copy while you wait—which is next door to an utter imposs?bility— watch his features closely, and if 'you are not struck with the adaptability of the said furrows for the taking of a plaster cast, I should say you either know nothing of cause and effect or that you have made a mistake, and the submitter is no pote. I orieinally intended to give a few specimen effusions of some undoubted notes, but they are omitted for two reasons. In the first place, when I made application to the editor of this paper to rummage through his waste paper basket he refused me point blank, saying that it was against the rules; besides which, he didn't want to have a lot of work to do over again. I daren t even think of the awful insinuation contained in that latter remark of his. In the second place, I reflected that I had no special license for inflicting mental torture, so after all the specimens are perhaps better left out. From what has been said it may be concluded that there is a slight similarity between the poet and the prate. just as there is a similarity between a diamond and a piece of ice; there is no danger of confounding the two in either case To write of the poet, my finest quill were far too heavy; but to scribble of the poto, a worse writer than myself could do ample justice, if it were possible to find him.

LEGGE.

-- --- The remains of the late Mr. Legge, whose death we recorded in our last issue, were on Saturday in- terred in the Warrington- Cemetery, and the large attendance of mourners abundantly testified to the great respect in which the deceased Was held. The funeral procession started from Arpley-st. about half-past two in the midst of a heavy fall of rain. Nearly 200 workmen from Whitecross, Dallam, Bewsey, and Messrs Monks, Hall, and Company's works, walked 1 in front of the hearse, and following these came the car- riage of the late Mr Leg,ge's medical attendant—Dr Fox —who was accompanied by Mr Ziba Armitage and the, Rev John Yonge. Walking by the side of the car were the bearers—eight of the workmen who had had the longest connection with Mr Legge—Messrs John Saun- ders, Thomas Williams, Frederick Jones, John Casswell, James Barlow, Daniel Poole, James Allen, and David Hill. Following came a string of no fewer than sixteen • carriages. In the first were Mr George Legge (son). Mr: Isaac Hayward and Mr John Morris (sons-in-law), and ..so Mr David Budge (brother-in-law). The second contained the grandchildren. The third, Mr Kirkham, Mr Mossley, Mr Iligginson, and Mr John Hayward. The fourth, Mr Thomas Birdiell, Mr A. Rathbone, Mr John Peers, and Mr Charles Allen. The fifth, Mr T. Evans, Mr J. T. Perry, Mr C. Glover, and Mr R. Whitfield. The sixth, Messrs Hertford, Darker, Perris, and Perry. Subsequent carriages were occupied by, amongst others, the Rev F. Roberts, Messrs Thomas Burton (Monks Hall and Co.), W. Charnock, R. Wehster, W. Richardson. J. Richard- son, Councillor Barker, H. Rathbone, W.. Roberts, and John Westgarth. The Whitecross Wire and Iron Com- pany was represented by Mr W. Carson, managing director; the Liberal Association by Mr McMinnies, Conneillor Henry Roberts, and the xecutive Committee; the British Workman Company, by Mr Thomas Morris and Alderman Holmes; the Starr-Bowkett Buildino, cloy'

by the following: Messrs T. Burton, R. &Atoll, . D. Sumner (directors), J. Titchett (sec.), and J. P. Jones; and the Cricket and Bowling Club by several members. Floral wreaths er crosses were sent by the workmen at Whitecross, Mr. Walter Milner, Mr.. Z. Armitag,e, Councillor Barker, Mr. J. Richardson, Mr. W. Richard- son' Mr. and Mrs. Uolford, Councillor" Henry Roberts, the Directors of the British -Workmen Company, Mr. John Hayward, Mr. Birtles, Mr. Smethurst, Mrs. Clay, Mr. Mainwaring, Mr. W. Roberts, Mr. and Mrs. Ferns, and Mr. W. Hayward. The service, both in the chapel and at the grave. was conducted by the Rev. John Yonge, who had returned to Warrington' having been away on ,his holiday at the time of Mr. Legge's death, expressly for the purpose. Upon the breast-plate of the coffin, which was of brown polished oak, With bra.ss mountings, Was the simple inscription :—" Noah Legge, died August 2nd, 1888, aged 56." The funeral arrangements -had been entrusted to Mr. E. Connor, Sankey-street; It may he mentioned that Mrs. Legge has been the re- cipient of the following letter, which has been sent to her by Mr. William Brown, on behalf of the workmen at Whitecross, viz :—" Bear Madam,—We, the• work:nen employed at the,wOrks of the Whiteeross Wire and Iron Company, Limited, desire to express our sympathy with you in the great loss you _have sustained in the death of our much,respected late manager, Mr. Legge. We can only share with you in a small degree the sadness which his death mttst cause, but having known him, a.s many Of us have, for nearly 20 years, and having had daily evidence of his great kindness of ' heart, and seen the almost ffitherly interest which he has constantly shown towards those with whom he was brought in contact, we cab understand to some degree what must be the toss to you and your family. We can only assure you that our heartfelt sympathy is with you, and we pray that TM, may receive consolation from the only source whence true consolation can come. And for ourselves, we trust I that the evidence of practical Christianity—of sterling

TFIE SINGULAR PARTNERSHIP
PUTE.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, an Saturday, before Aldermen J. Harrison and T. Cook, Joseph. Hewitt, a partner in the firm of Messrs. Hugh McCarron and Co., provision dealers, was charged with embezzling £6. the money of the firm. The prosecutor alleged that defendant drew £6 from the bank, unknown 'to his partner, Mr. McCarron, and that he was at the railway station, going away when apprehended. Mr. 'Mearns said he was in hope the time of the court would have been saved, as the prosecution had offered what they considered an easy compromise. He and Mr. Swift, who defended, were within an ace of agreeing, and the only question was whether the case should be adjourned or withdrawn. He felt he could not in justice to his client withdraw: He had ' offered to take an ad:- joumment so as to go-into the accounts of the firm.— The Deputy. Clerk (Mr.:-Davidson) : If you take an ad- journment and go into the accounts, you cannot then come and ask. the magistrates to compromise this. It would practically be-asking them to compound a felony. —Mrs Swift : We say we only want what is right.. This firm isundoubtedly insolvent, and there is £BO or £9O due to the creditors. My client says he is anxious to the utmost of his ability to meet the creditors and pay as much as he possibly can ; that he is ready and willing to go into the accounts so as to meet the creditors ; and that fie had no intention of running away from it. He is charged with getting the sum of £6 from the bank, and he had obtained that sum from his father, and he has paid it to me for the bene- fit of his/ creditors, and he says he will add any other sum he may be able to raise. My objection is that he should not go into figures with his partner with a rope'round his neck.— Mr. Mearns How my friend can say that I don'tknow., Defendant had his luggage bOoked at the railway station and was clearing off. Now, when he finds he has a rope round his neck, and is in the hands of .the police, he says it is his intention to help to compromise with his creditors. But if he had got safely away, nothing more would have' been seen or heard of him.—Some little Con- versation between the solicitors resulted in Mr. Mearns saying that a way out of the difficulty was to leave the £6 with the prosecutor for the creditors.—The Clerk: You should not mention the terms of a compromise. The proceedings must either be withdrawn or go on.—Mr. Mearns On terms that are agreeable to both of us the proceedings for the present will be withdrawn, and I hope the creditors will benefit by it.—Mr. Swift : I don't know so much abok* it. We don't believe in compound- ing a felony any int/re-than you do, and we sav—The Clerk (interrupting) ; The proceeding are withdrawn; settle the terms between you.

BY Mils. J. K. SPENDER,
• Author of "Mr. Nobody," .7," Parted Lives,' "Both in the Wrong," Recollections 4,1 Country Doctor," " Trust &e.

- CHAPTER -IV. • " A PoSTUUMOUS LETTER. The invalid had probably made too great an 'err. Ort for her strength.- Dr. Bayard perhaps knew it; but, if so,he was also aware that it would have been a pity to cross her, and that it could not make much difference one way or the other. • , .She was light-headed after he left .her, babbling to herself, not as Falstaff did, of green fields, but of balls and Pretty dresses. - "Do you remember inv wedding day ?" she startled Peggy by saying suchlenly, for her marriage was generally the last subject to which she would allude, " I walked to the church in that plain grey cash• Mere, with grey feathers td my hat, and yet I heard the people saying how pretty I was ! " ' Then her mind wandered to something else, for ,Peggy was fanning her with a handsome relic of the days of her girlhood. It was painted with. eoses and a butterfly in the corner. " My- partners always asked inc if the butterfly was going alter the flowers; but- there were few flowers in my lice," she said, pitying herself. As the night wore on, the old woman' was more surprised.. For it was in the . darke4 and dreariest part of it. that Agnes Campion sat, 'With • sudden strength, upright, asking her; as she had asked the middle-aged doctor, for a kiss. . "You have been good to me," she said, with a flicker of her usual intelligence, pressing ths; old hand in hers, "taking care of me ever slime- I was a baby—and that, Was not quite thirty years ago—l wonder if, we ithall meet once more.. bo you know it is so odd? They said it would be dark when I cape to die—but a dawn is breaking—it is bright." I• Peggy .burst into tears, which seemed out of keep- ing with her buxom old age, as they rolled down her rough cheeks. . "Do not weep," said the sick woman as she took her hand again and stroked it. "We Live neither of us been too happy. You gave up a • good deal to follow my brokea fortunes—bat—l think---" Again a strange smile lit up her Pain& face. She let go Peggy's hand, and sank back gently on the pillows. ' There' was an interval of silence, but 'no sign of 'suffering: "She is asleep," Whispered the old nurse to her- self. But suddenly the dark blue ~•eyes opened widely, again. "My faithful friend," she muttered in a broken voice, `God's Messily, be with. you. Be good to my children. I would.:l cannot ruse myself---lift me up- a-little." Peggy lifted her up„ and her/young 'mistress tried to make a movement, 'which she afterwards recogs mused to be the sign of the Cross. • " Do you remember," she gasped out, with that same .strange smile, " how I once told you there was no life to conic?. I told you wreng—Peggy—forget my wild words—l—l feel—so strange—just as ilmy body—is—no longer niine—as if—as • if—l am-L-put- ting.on—a new shape." ' • • They were the last Words she spoke. Her hands fell idly on the counterpane, and she ceased to'breathe. It was a little while before Peggy recognised that. life was extinct, and then she rocked herself to and fro with wild lamentations. She was no • more heathenish in her wild bewailings than a large majority of Christians; who; when the souls of their brothers and 'sisters pass into the world of spirits pity them for their loss in missing the blessings ot this life, call them by half-compassionate names, and after a while cease to mention them. " ' But she had not much time to lament. For the whims of the. dead had to be carried out, and one of her young mistress's directions was that directly the breath had left her body a telegram was to be sent, to her husband, Leonard Campion. He was not all bad. Perhaps a Man who is all bad dries not actually exist. He had neglected his wife in her life time, ever since they had had passionate altercations on the. ambjeet of nimey But he still loved her in a selfish fashion, and had ' seriouslybelieved that if she took a cottage, as he ad- vised her, in tbe neighbourhood of St. Agatha's, Mrs. ' Maclurchaa for very shame would provide for her daughter. He had not counted on a pride of which hel had no comprehension, and which, inherited by the daughter from the mother, was equally great on both sides—preventing the .one from asking, and the other from inquiring. In justice to Mrs. Maclurchan, it must be ad- mitted that she never. knew the terrible Straits-to Wrich Agnes had been reduced, and though she did not offer to come to minister to the dying woman, she had lately anticipated all her wants, and now gave directions for her funeral. Thus it was that Leonard Campion, travelling at once from Paris, was ushered into a rgOM resplendent with wax tapers and decorated with white lace, in which the beautiful body of his wife—sublimated by death into a grandeur oi supreme heavenly beauty, of which all earthly beauty is but a type—reposed like time figure of Elaine in the well-known illustra- tion of Gustave Dore. But .Dore's study was in black and white; this was in colour. For the pink dressing-gown al delicately trimmed had been put on by Mrs. Campion's own

directions for the lirsi time. "My 'mother shall not say I scorned that Which, though it was not the love .I craved from her, Was at' least a sign of relenting," Agnes Campion had remarked to Peggy when she gave that direc- tion. • "It was the queer fancy of a sick lady," as Peggy said when she dressed her in it. It was terrible to the old woman, as it is in most cases to the poor to go against the tradition which connects blackness and ghastliness with death. There was nothing ghastly in the -picture which Leonard Campion was summoned to see. All his artistic instincts rose in admiration of this feat accom- plished by his wife—this triumph ova the horrors .we are accustomed to connect with death. , notoriginal—women are so rarely original," as lie even now said to himself with one of the detract- ing sneers, which he in common with many men ate ! accustomed to fling at the sex, "They cannot , originate but they can follow." At any rate it was beautiful, and he succumbed, at. be always did, to the master instinct of wor- ' shipping beauty. The dead lips did not reproach him. They had • flung bitter taunts at him the last time they had met. . " If you were a poor man," was one of the things she had said, "you would be summoned before a magistrate, to shew cause why you could not support. your own children." He had sent her instalments 'from tune to time— such a bare pittance for the necessaries of life—as suffieed, as he told him scornfully in one of her lotters, "just to keep them out of the workhouse." The luxuries which she needed had been sent to ' her owing to a little child's unexpected interven- tion, but her mother had sent her .thee luxuries too late. It was no reproach now, but a hopeful, encourag7 InL-, Smile which those dead lips gave him. • Yet the hope in the Man's heart had so lone been extinguished that he said to liints?lf, weepmgly, as be kissed her, _" They always smile—good and bad alike—the same 'thing happens to them all. He had been an unusually handsome man, and women admired him extremely even now. If the forehead was wanting in phrenological development —being neither broad nor high—that was a defect which was hidden by the masses of chestnut hair which curled over hls brow, whilst the lips--which were too thick, suggesting an absence of , finer feeling were efrectually hidden by the , golden moustache. , The laSt time, he had kissed her she had shrunk ,nack?cOmplaining," Oh, Leonard,that terrible drink, how it always taints your breath !" But she did not shrink now. She continued to smile en as Elaine smiled at Launcelot. • Her magnilicent brown hair hum,l on either side .7 below her waist ; Peggy had combed It out according to her directions. Her hands were folded so meekly, and yet she had not been a meek woman. It eceined fit that they should hold a lily—a the-tight 'crossed his ninel that he would go and see if it were possible to purchase some—the lilies of. the Annun- ciation, as they called them abroad. - But instead of that there was-a good-sized letter sealed and directed to himself, placed beneath one of the folded hands. " She told me to put it there—her blessed' self —and she was that busy a-writin' of it for weeks afore her death," explained the tearful Peggy. " Often and often I asked her, but she wouldn't let me send for yer. - No, Peggy, it would ts, .too much for me,' was all as I could got out o' • iut.. will sp.ouk to him when I have gone. ' • Mr. Leonard -CamPion, like many people who grudge their love to the warm .beating hearts of the living, was ready to give it without stint now that a heart was cold and still. Thave protestations were

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. JERRY'S MISHAP. lieaw, young Jerry wur allus a swell, As thowt a gret deol ov hissel, But one day misfortun' befel. As knocked off d lump ov his pride. It happened, at one Darrun Fair, sed he'd inek trippers stare, Ate i'th' height ov his folly. He took red-haired Molly A cooartin', away to th' seaside. Moll wur known as a bit ov a jide, As snubbed them as warked at her trade, For hoo wur a weyver tle shade Wheer Jerry looked o'er an' booked cuts. Her yore wur just like copper wire, An' id heot set his dry heart afire, When he clapt his een on her, Th' vraylr lad wur a " goner,"— Mixt up th' top sto4rey—deod nuts ' Off to Blackpool they seet, an' on t' sands. Watched t' niggers, an' heeard German hands, Then, wearied wi' time o' ther hands, They went to stert spoonin'—alooan ! Wod they slaver'd o'er—nobry con tell, But at last Molly gi'e Bitch a yell. For th' tide bed surroavrnded 'En neer ; summat seawnded, Fro' Jerry's chest, like a long grooan ! Hey, Molly, ! Wod nion we do ?" "Tha mon god me off here soon, tha foo ! Wod a smert mess aw've gotten into, Thro' hevin' a gawpy like thee !" Jerry blabber'd an' cried. " Aw korn'd swim !" An' big tears med his een red an' dim. "If t' watter keeps swellin', di lass, there's no tellin'— Hey, dear !—lv we booath hey to dee 1" A creawd watched o' t' gam,—id wur rich! An' wi' laffif ther ribs ached so rnitch, One chap bawled eawt at a heigh pitch, "lie sharp, lad, an' carry her o'er, Or else t' lifebooat 'll ha' to be launcht !" Jerry's teeth gr un an' chattered an' crancht, An' snapt, "Iv thall tarry A bit, Moll, aw'll carry The thro' o that ocean to I.' shore !" Then deawn be set plump o' t' wet sand, llooave his stocking an' shoon off so grand, Then give 'em to Moll in her hand, An' sed, " Here, mi luv, carry these!" Deawn he diked, an' soon t' check breeches slop Up his legs he rolled reight up to t' top, Then he sheawted, " Aw'm ready! Come on, clip me steady, That's id—easier; Molly—dornd squeezer' Wod a weight Molly felt in his arms, While his, heart frittered fast alarms, He'd no time to look on her charms, But, whackerin', in t' wetter he went. 'Twur th' middle, six inch deep or sooa, Wheer a crab-fish uipt howd ov his tooa ; An' der, wi' a splatter, Flip flop, reight t' wetter, They splashed to ther sad discontent! • MolFstood up, wi' her temper hot, theer, An' hit Jerry a cleawt upo' th' ear Wi' his idiom, an: Oiled fair med him sweear, • As shiverin' he crawled cawt on t' beach. His shoon an' booath stockin's wur lost, 0' th' creawd, nobry knew who lafft t' wost, For Molly hed derted ; An' Jerry, sad hefted, Watched his hat, till id cooin to his reych. * * Thad neet, varra late, while th' owd moon Pept at th' stars as wur winkin' aboon. A poor wrung-eawt thing, witheawt shoon, Thee' back streets slunk ditherin' wi' cowd. His pride wur kilt quite wi' thad fo', For Molly leet o her pals know, • An' then, actin' shabby, Hoe nicknamed him "Crabby !" Hee's ne'er cooarteil sin', aw've bin towd ! JACK 0' ANN'S.

„ . . Possibly ho believed these protestations himself. The one person ,who knew their worthlessna,s,s would -never 'itgain be attic ,to- contradict them. • 1 It was with an tethete's sense of the lusicury of superficial'. sorrow combined with the perfection Of beauty that Leonard Champion .dismissed Peggy,' telling he,r that he would see her klgain and make ar- rangements about the children in a little while, but that for the present he must be alone'and read his
Letter. • . . , He was a little astonished when he broke the aeal. . . . ..
The letter was a recapitulation of mach of his past life and in it he did not appear in the most amiable

You were the first nitifi,islie wrote," Who touched my -.heart. You.. know , how I. had grieved my mother by refusing all the plans. she Made for my future happiness. I preferred my independence. was happy and fancy-free. Then you Came into my life; you made an impression on my imagination. You spoke to inw of the stars, and of the flowers and the trees—in a word, of all the attractions of that Nature which I had loacd as you had with passionate enthusiasm.' Yo 7:. preached eloquently te me-of this new . worship of Nature— in which we were agreed. I ..did • not believe the reports which even then were circulated against you.: .You-seemed to me to be 'generous; sensible; • hertiic, devoted. I" credited you with the nosseSsion of a heart vowed not only to Me, bat to the painting which we both loved—a heart easily stirred by emo- tional impulses, easily melted by the attractions of• amsic. You aceined to have capability, and, if_ not a moral power, at least an artistic capacity for sway- ing your fellowmen. It was the sort of empire which pleased me. - " You know what came mixt. I pass over my own heartless treatment of my mother,- for which. I deserved to .suffer, and for which I have suffered. keenly, being without -an hope that ' such suffenng may expiate We both' took life and. marriage gaily. From one end of the year to another at first, it was a constant round of .waltz- ing, sketching, singing, riding, driving; going- from opera to theatre-7-or from balls to suppers—in‘ that amusing Bohemian life which-suited us sO thoroughly. And then our baby arrived. You—had spent all your money, and expected me to apply. for more to my- mother. I knew that it-would be useless for me to. do so, and for the first time I suspected that you had married Inc for my money. "The whole of your stock-in-trade was the power of wielding a paint brash skilfully. . You had painted one picture before -our marriage which had succeeded. It had made a little stir in the artistic world, been coininented on kindly by the 'newspapers, and had raised expectations. as to the great things you were to accomplish. But you never followed your success up by another picture which might have brought y6u• tame, or at least have enabled you to support , your family. The few luxuries which your first success 'ensured for us but served to enervate you: You took to drinking, to borrowing money from people whom you afterwards hated because yen could not repay the obligation. kneari little of the world', but I foresaw that a man with such vices would be always adrift. It Was my first experience of evil. A man with such good qualities, and such bad ones, considered admirable by a let ge number of the people Whe constituted our little world, and spoken of by others as vile—so infatuated to his own ruin, and yet with •redeeming qualities, could yet retain the love of a woman such, as I was. In,truns I pleaded with you and blamed you. Even had I been less devoted to you I could -not have helped admiring you. And yet—hard as it is for me to say it—you made the misery of your family.' And in the mine which ,I had thonglit so .rich—your heart--I had to .dig and dig and could find no metal. What I had taken to be treasures of gold proved merely scorke, flung, as it • were, from a burning volcano. • When I came to ex- amine them I found them to be nothing bat rubbish, after all. I tried tears, I tried entreaties —they Are of no avail. You dragged me about on the Continent where we could live cheaply—l and my little children. I was exposed not only to foul odours but to foul associations. I remember as. if it Were yesterday the wretched little salle d man- gers, reeking with had tobacco and ill-cooked food, Into Which you would stagger, drunken. For, 0 my husband, one thing dogged us about in all Our wanderings, whether in the rumbling- diligences or -in the •crowded cities, where we were exposed. to pestilence, making you -forget your • hive to me and your duty to the little ones. It was ;so small at first, so tempting to you, making you forget all your griefs and disappointments. So small, and creeping on -so slowly with its fatal fascinations =like that lovely little coral snake,braided with red and white, one reads of in the tropics—its head so tiny that even little children have been tempted to play with it, not. knowing that aim scratch is eertair death. • . . "Then people looked at me pitythgly. 'Did yon not know it ? His father 'died a victim to alcohol ; there is seldom any hope of them when the tendency is inherited.' "Let me not dwell on the time that followed—our mutual recriminations,•of my despairing grief, with the ill-health that naturally fellowed. " Whenever yon were angry you coald find fresh fuel for our destruction; whenever you were repentant you knew whereto seek forgetfulness. In short, while graved sympatliyartnil was breaking my heart in solitude, you had ever the means of keeping reflection at arm's length. "Then, indeed, my, courage as well as my health gave way. There came a day when Dr. Havard, who attended ice without 'charge, found me with my head resting on my arm, and my arm on the table, sobbing as I had not allowed myself to sob for months. He was shown in accidentally or he would not have witnessed my loss of self-control. He offered to lend me ruoneya hut I I cannot take anything -from you, or from any other man without the know-. ledge of .iny husband.' He respected my 'decision, :tad told lime that he thought I was gaining more by • experience of sorrow than I could have been taught by happiness. Other men would haVe helped me— men ,who had not the delicacy of feeling always • shown by Dr. Havard. -But I answered them in-the same way. I could not allow even an act of kindness to come between me and my natural protector—the rnan I had married. " All would' be well in the end,' Dr. Havard had • said, if I would have patience, and put my trust in Cod.' But I wore myself out with fretting. I could have endured the semi-starvation for my• self, but not for my growing children. It begar to prey. upon my mind that they,—easpecially th boy—might inherit the terrible curse which da scent's from the fathers upon the children ; that they —forgive inc for saying this--might grow up dipso- mauiace, and suffer—as I had seen you suffer— horrors of delirium. I thought of doing all that lay in my power teavert thus enrse, knowing that my best hope fay in doing all I could to strengthen their bodice. ' '.".l"herefore, when I bad no hope—when I found that we were on the road to real and final poverty; that my boy could not be sena to a school where he would associate with other boys of his own stand- ing, and be strengthened with wady sports; and that my daughter Was picking up vulgar way, I humbled may pride at last to beg help , from my mother. ' • " I will confess that long before, -when you , asked me to do so, I WM revolted at the thought, not only from the redollectiou of bow Vesely I had de- ceired alai, mother and trampled on her heart, . but 1- because you urged me. It seemed like the last drop of bitterness added. to my cup. I was quick to think that when you pretended to admire rrie ex- travagantly, with an admiration that bordered On worship, you were an avaricious man, who, in persuading -me to make a runaway marriage with you, had -tried to make a crafty and advantageous bargain. If I wronged you, forgive me again; but thinking that, I also thought then I would rather ,die than apply to .my mother.. But when I once (humiliated inYself to it down and write to her, I felt that the ties of blood were stronger than 'I had imagined. I poured mit my 'heart to her ; the flood- ..i4ates of my grief were open indeed. . ".1 never told you this before. • I tell it to you now that You may know how futile it will be for you to apply twher again. How well I remember the day when I wrote that long letter, and closed it with a beating heart, thinking, ' Why was I so long ir hunibling myself before ? Now at least my troubles . are over, my mother will conic to my assistance for. the sake of the chi f" Alas, I calculated too soon on forgiveness for such an error as mine! - When my tender and en- treating words were returned 0 meaaa when I opened the big envelope amid sheet alter sect Of my own - handwriting looked mockingly at me, falling on the floor from my nerveless hands •, and when my, strained eyeballs could see nothing but a few cold and formal words dictated by my motherthen in- deed I. had death in my heart. ' The message was a cruel one. Proud aa she is, I call scarcely think. how she could brine herself to give it. It told me that I had played with a false die, but that, having thrown it, I must remember I had cast it against her advice, and Must abide the aonsequenees of my own -reckless act. Her words, so far as I can recall them) were something like this: The young lady

FRANCE, ITALY, AND MASSOWAH. %., CON3TANTINOtLIi, Starnay.—Tlhe controversy which is Tfteeediag between France and Italy on the Massowati llttestion having attracted the attention of the Porte, at the last Cabinet Council it was decided to address a note to the Powers protesting against the continued pre- eeace of Italian troops in that place, and giving expres- 810a to the Turkish fears of further Italian aims on Tri- ton and Barbary. Turkish statesmen are convinced that ,telY is preparing to filch these rich African possessions ?um their present owners, notwithstanding that the 4l4lian journals make out that France has designs in 1 that quarter. The Turkish Minister, alluding to the . I?Pach taunts that Turkey looked on helplessly while eq.:lnes to her detriment were taking place all round, remarked that this charge was particularly unjust, for ,averY time the Porte showed a disposition to take action , Powers at once stepped in to prevent the carrying eta of hes intention. DEATH OF GENERAL SHERIDAN. NIM Your., MONDAY.—General Sheridan died at his residence at Nouquitt, yesterday evening. , General Philip Henry Sheridan was born in Somerset, '-'hio, March 6th, 1831. He graduated at the Military Academy at West Point in 1853, and served on frontier duty in 'Texas for nearly two years, and in Oregon from 1855 to 1861. At the commencement of the civil war he 'WM.,. appointed Quartermaster of the Army of the rsouth-Western Mission. and in April, 1862, Chief 1 . Quartermaster of the Western Department. In May, 1862, he was r-ppointed Colonel of the 2nd ' Michigan Volunteer Cavalry, was commissioned ' ti3rig.-General of Volunteers, July 1, 1862. and after a brief period was put in command of the 11th division ', • 'lt the Army of Ohio. He commanded a division in the Army of the Cumberland; and at the battie of Stone ,fiver„ December 31, 1862, saved the army from rout by Rig stubborn resistance. For his gallant conduct he was Promoted to be Major-General of Volunteers. In April, 1 ' 1864, he was called to the Army of the Potomac by J General Grant,'plit in command of the Cavalry Corps. and within the months of Mac, Thne, and July, besides Protecting the flanks of the army and reconnoitring the ' enemy's position, was successfully engaged in eighteen distinct actions. On the 4th of August, 1664, he was put in command of the Army of •Shenarkdoali, and soon after of the. Middle Military Division, where Ile gained several successes over General Early, for Which he was made a Brigadier-General of the United States army, and in November following was made lifajor-General. He joined General Grant's army at City point. from whence he started, March 25th, 1865. to strike the final blow for the overthrow of General Lee's army of Northern Virginia. He fought the battle Of Dinwiddie Courthouse, March 31, and that of Five ?arks, which necessitated Lee's evacuation of Richmond and Petersburg. April 1, and as the Army of Northern Vir- ginia fled he constantly attacked and harrassed them, end compelled their surrender at Appomattox Court Rouse April 9, 1365. He was assigned to the command Of the Military Division of the Smith-West, June 3, and Of that of the Gulf June 17. 1865. Under a new reorganisation of the Military Districts and Depart- raents, he was assigned to the Department of the Gulf. August 15th, 1866, and in March. 1867, In the fifth Military District (Loosiana and Texas). Presi- dent Johnson being displeased with his administration, transferred him, September 12th, 1867, to the Depart. bent of the Missouri, where he continued until March. p: 1869, when, by the promotion of Sherman, he became r Lieutenant-General, and assumed command of Western iiand South-western Military 9ivisions, with his head- 41aarters at Chicago. Sir Lionel Sackville-West, British Minister at Washing- ton, has written to Mr. Bayard stating that Lord Salis- bury has requested him to bring to his notice the case of Brooks, alias Maxwell, who lies under sentence of death tor the murder of Mr. Preller, as it was sought to obtain %respite for the condemned man that further inquiry Might be made. Mr. Bayard has replied that the matter rests entirely in the hands of the Governor of Missouri, to whom he lia.s written. The Secretary of State declares, however, that he finds no international aspect in the case laor am- possibility of federal interference. It is under- stood that the British Minister's request for a respite for Brooks is based on the fact that his victim, Mr. Preller, Vas a British subject, and that Sir Sackville-West's inter- vention was secured through representations made to LOrd Salisbury by the condemned man's father, who claims to have obtained fresh eiudt•nce, which he believes . 'WEI result in saving his son's life. THE PARIS STRIKES. PARIS, SUNDAY meeting of the Strtlers at the Salle Favie was marked by an exciting :Incident. The Communist ex-General Endes, who had been anointed chairman, looked pale, and had just time to appoint a vice-chairman and secretary when he fell insensible upon the table. At first it was only supposed to be a temporary indisposition, hut later on it was sinnounced that the citizen Elides was dead. The meeting dispersed with premises to reven7e the death a General Eudes with the blood of the cowardly bourgeoic whom he had combtaed during his life. An ambulance carriage conveyed the dead body of the ex- General to his house.

IRELAND. The Earl of Mayo has called for payment of his Kil- dare rents, with all arrears due. It is expected the tenants Will demand substantial reductions. News reached Armagh on Saturday evening from the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland that tho• sentence of death passed on William Thompson for the murder of his brother-in-law, Thomas Thompson, in Knocknamuckley .church, near Port.adown, in March last, has been corn- tnuted to penal servitude for life. The Tlev. John Elliott, Inton receipt of the news, at once conveyed the intelli- gence to the culprit. Much satisfaction is felt at the result At the last meeting of the Boyle Board of Guardians, One of the relieving officers applied for outdoor relief for an ex-member of the Board, named Patrick Sharkey, , Who, he said, was evicted from his holding during the Previous week. The man had a wife and no fewer than thirteen children, the eldest of whom was only fifteen Years of age. The man, it is said, was evicted at the suit of his parish priest, who had purchased his farm. The Guardians decided to give £2 per week. An extraordinary case of a Ileeed incendiarism was re- ported on Tuesday from Ballymoney, county Antrim. t appears that the police on proceeding on Monday nig;,, to a public-house where a fire was reported to have 'broken out, and having forced an entrance, found a Young married woman, named McMullen, daughter of the landlady, busily engaged throwing paraffin oil against the ceiling in an upper room and trying to ignite it with a candle. She was immediately arrested for at- tempting to set fire to the premises. An amusing description has been reported from Bally- cotton Bay of an encounter with some 120 small whales or grampuses, which were noticed by the fishermen coming shorewards. A very determined but somewhat ludicrous attempt was mnde to land the monsters by a small fleet Of boats, manned with visitors and natives, armed with guns and other weapons. Several battles took place. and some of the grampuses were injured, but ultimately they all got away, one of them in its flight carrying a small punt containing an elderly gentleman, much to the latter's horror and amazement, some distance sea- on its broad back. There was very great excite- ment in Ballycotton while the grampuses remained in the bay. In the Irish Court of Exchequer, on Monday, before Lord chief Baron and other Judges, the case of Mr. John Dillon, M.P., came up int'. argument on the application Made by Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P., for his release. The court was crowded. It was contended that Mr. Dillon "was not legally in custody; but the Lord Chief Baron. after listening to various armiments, said the Court held that Mr. Dillon was in legal custody, and that the County Court Judge had full jurisdiction in the circum- stances under which the case came before him. Three 'things that were necessary had happened here—a notice Of appeal had been duly given, a recognisance had been ' .entered, and the proper form given to the appellant. It Was held by the Lord Chief Baron, and the other Judges concurred, that the warrant was valid, and toe applica- tion for relief was refused, the conditional order being diselt.arowd

STRIKE IN THE COTTON TRADE,-At most of the mills ki Preston the card and blowing room hands gave in a Week's notice on Wednesday that they intend to cease Work unless the employers concede the advance of 10 Per cent and 5 per cent demanded by the male and female Should the strike take place in Preston, and other East Lancashire towns, some 5,000 operatives will 1)e idle. Limn SALISBURY AT THE MANSION HOUSE —Lord Sails- bur. Mr. Goschen, Mr. Balfour, and other Minisqrs Were present at the Mansion House banquet On Wednes- (lay evening. Lord G. Hamilton, responding for the 11,_ Ivy, said London might within the next twenty-four nours be in the hands of the enemy, which was sup- Posed to be harrying our coasts. He hoped the naval ~,laanceuvres would become an annual institution. Mr. manhope responded for the army. Lord Salisbury, re- Plying to the toast of her Majesty's Ministers, saicl this ..,toast had always been proposed hitherto at the end of L.Qe session, but unfortunately it was not so this year, for eir were only in the middle of the session. There had "es, n`some attempts to throw the responsibility for this to of things on Ministers, but he claimed that the Gov- enitn„,. ent in the course of the session had achieved no ',gilt success. Mr. Ritchie had descended to the earth '.e figure was suggested by Mr. "Punch" on Wednes- -9) bearing a splendid triumph in his hand. If this tittlement were final, which he believed it would be, ...en the difficult problem of the Government of the otropolis had been solved without injury to the valu- rye Privileges vested in the Corporation. In the execu- e duties of the Government Ireland held the first rala. ce, and he claimed that the Government had ob- muled great results. It had diminished the tyranny of •_"•egal associations, and had increased the sanctity of F.ontract. If Ireland was governed with the same judg- pilent and firmness as at present for a few year, then rtY would again have become complete, contracts i'vs:ll,ld be respected, and prosperity would be restored. *d regard to foreign affairs, he said, with more con- -4:1°,11 e than he had ever before expressed, that the oh- -01 all the rulers of the world was to secure =inter- fleece.

div.head: PARLIAMENT.
div.p: PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—SArrmasr. Members had so little relish for a Saturday sitting that a House could not be made until noon. At that time the Speaker counted the members present, but only 38 were in the Chamber. At the critical monient, however, Lord Lewisham and Mr. Akers-Douglas saved the dignity of the chair by a hasty entrance, and the Speaker was able to proceed with business.

DISCLOSING OFFICIAL SECRETS. Sir HENRY jamas, calling attention to a statement purporting to give the sense of the report of the Select Committee on the Hydernbad Deccan Mining Company which had appeared in The Times and other newspapers, assured the House that the information published was insufficient, fallacious and misleading. He had not had an opportunity of consulting with his colleagues on the committee as to what course should be taken, but he seized this opportunity to contradict the information circulated, because there were extensive operations in respect to this particular company on the Stock Ex- change, and he desired to warn the unwary and credu- 16us against putting faith in it. Sir GEO. CAMPBELL suggested that in the Official Secrets Bill provision should be mnde for the punish- ment not only of those who stole official secrets, but of the receivers of them. The incident then terminated. SUPPLY. -

The House went into— .Committee of Supply, Mr. Courtney in the chair, on the Army and Navy Estimates. On the vote for army provisions and forage, Dr. FAR- nunAssox made some remarks in regard to the insuffi- ciency of soldiers rations, and moved for an inquiry. Mr. STANHOPE said he had no objection to the appoint- ment of a departmental inquiry on the subject, and upon that understanding the vote was agreed to. Lord CHARLES BICRESFORD criticised the policy which, by building ships for which no guns could be supplied, led to extravagance, and agreed that the area of supply for guns must be enlarged by the employment of private firms. Mr. STANHOPE attributed the present large expendi- ture for deficiencies to so little money being spent be- tween 1;:2 and 1885. He agreed that it was a scandal that there should be ships nearly completed for which the guns were not ready, and steps were being taken to prevent that. After some very rointed remarks from Mr. ANDERSON and Mr. WALLACE about, the neglect of Scotch business, the House adjourned shortly before six o'clock.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNoAr. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4 p.m.

THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. The House went into Committee on the Local Govern- ment Bill.—An amendment proposed by Lord SALIS- BURY was carried, to the effect that peers owning pro- perty in a county may be elected to sit on the County Council. After further consideration, clause 2 was agreed to, and Clauses 3 to 8 inclusive were agreed to, with slight modifications. On clause 9, which dealt with the appointment of the joint-committee to have the control of the police. The EARL of CARNARVON could not help thinking that the Bill contained a principle which would sooner or later touch the government of Ireland, and he would ask the Government whether they were seriously pre- pared to hand over the police to a body consisting of representatives of the ratepayers and justices. Lord HERSCHRLL advocated the continuance of the powers and duties of the justices as conservators of the The Marquis Of SALISBURY said he thought that was a reasonable proposal, but he had perhaps better consider the matter before reporting. Clauses to 41 were agreed to, several amendments being negatived. On clause 42, the Marquis of SALISBURY moved an amendment to provide that from and after the next I vacancy no recorder of London appointed by the City shall exercise any,judicial functions unless be is appointed by her Majesty to exercise such functions. Clauses to clause 45 were agreed to. , The Marquis of BRISTOL moved an amendmant to divide the county of Suffolk into two council districts. —The Marquis of SALISBURY supported the motion, and after a long discussion their lordships divided, and as- sented to the proposal by 59 to 20. The clauses to clause 48 were agreed to:—On clause 49, Earl GRANVILLE moved an amendment to make a County Council district of the Cinque Ports.—Lord Ilm,voon of Boatman opposed the amendinent.—After a lengthened conversation the amendment was rejected on adivision by 35 to 32. Clauses from 49 to 69 were agreed to. On Clause 70., which related to borrowing powers of the County Coun- cils, an amendment was agreed to, on the motion of Earl BEAUCHABIP, providing that the Local Government. Board, before giving their consent to, the borrowing of money under the bill, should take into consideration any representation made by any ratepayer or owner of property rated to the county fund. Clause 70 was added to the bill.—On Clause 71, Earl Fowls moved an amendment, which was ultimately negatived, the object of which was to give trustees power to invest in county stock created under the bill. —Clause 71 and the remaining clauses were agreed to, and the bill passed through Committee at 1 40. The re- port was fixed for Thursday. Their lordships adjourned at 1 45 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Motnoxr. The Speaker took the, chair at 3 5 p.m. Mr. W. IT. SMITH informed Mr. Frank Hardcastle and Captain Cotton that the Currency Commission would be able to present their report in the course of the next two months.
