In reply to another question, the FIRST LORD of the Taanstnrr said he could not alTord facilities for brimlng on a motion in favour of the release of Mr. John Dillon. —Mr. DILLWYN intimated that hewottld at the earliest possible moment bring the question before the House. —Answering Mr. Herbert Gardner, the right hon. gen- tleman said that he could not give an assurance that the Tithe Bill would be postponed until the Committee on Corn Averages had reported. The Committee was granted with the intention of keeping the principle ot tithe apart from that of corn averages. NSW WRIT.—On the motion of Mr. AxEns-Dorora.4. a new writ was issued for one of the divisions of Liver- pool, in place of Lord Claud Hamilton, resigned. ,

div.head: SUPPLY.-SCOTCH BUSINESS.
div.p: SUPPLY.-SCOTCH BUSINESS.

Dr. WALLACH resumed the debate on the consideration of the report of Supply voted in Committee on August 3rd, and protested against the neglect of Scotch busi- ness, which he described as being not only unjust, but an insult to the, Scottish nation and the common sense 01 mankind. He charged the silence of the Lord Advocate with much of the responsibility in the matter, find hinted that it would have been better if the Solicitor. General for Scotland bad shown more interest in the affairs of his countrymen than in posing on behalf 0! the Government as a ''saucy street boy, cluiffire7 the heavy conscript fathers of the front Opposition bench." If the hon. member's intentions were serious, thc hilarity caused by his remarks indicated that little effect in this direction was created upon the Douse; and the SPEAKER eventually deemed it his duty to check the lieu of the doctor's eloquence by a grave reprimand. Mr. W. H. SMITH replietrthat the Lord Advocate lee. Made incessant representations to the Government to afford opportunities for the discussion of Scotch busi., mess, affd he denied that Scotland had been neglected The Government were anxious to consult the wishes 01 the Scotch members, and they had placed Wednesday at their disposal. Several other questions were debated, including the deaths of Mr. Mandeville and Dr. Ridley and the impri- sonment of Mr, Latchford. Mr. Betporn, in replying, said the order for Mr. Lateli- r ford's release was made by the Court of Exchequer, be- cause of a technical error in the form of the order of imprisonment, and it had no relation to the merits of the case, which were not gone into at all: As to the Milltown Malbay case' he said a more shocking case of boycotting than this lied hardly ever been produced in the annals of Ireland. He believed Mr. Lane was under a delusion,and some of the statements in his letter were absolutely false. Mr. MORLEY said Mr. Latchford suffered nearly a month's imprisonment wrongfully. He also declared that Mr. John Dillon would not have been in prison if he had had an appeal to a jury, as he •woula have had in Eng- land. (Cheers.) The Chief Secretary might employ his recess less profitably than in acquiring some knowledge of the details of the prison discipline of which he avowed kis ignorance. (Cheers.) The Irish members spoke of the Chief Secretary as a tyrannical and despotic Minister. He (Mr. Morley) was not at all sure that the right hon. gentleman's position was not exactly the opposite of that of a tyrant and a despot. It was that. of a Minister, who, from his policy, was compelled in every case, right or wrong, to back up his subordinates. (Loud Opposition cheers.) The debate was continued by Mr. Hooper and several other members. The closure was moved at. intervals by Mr. W. Johnston, Mr. Milvain, and Fir W. Crossman, but it was not put. Eventually the report of Supply was agreed to at 12 25 a.m. :Several bills were advanced a stage, and the House adjourned at 1 35 a.m.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.

The House met at 3 15. THE LOCAL GOFRRNMENT BTLL.—Lord BALFOUR said the report stage of this bill would be taken on Thursday. Ile proposed on the report stage to move an amendment For the appointment of a deputy-chairman to every County Council. As there was no difference of opinion as to the principle of the bill, he should ask their lord- ships to read the bill a third time on Thursday, after its report stage had been gone through. MIAS ADVANCF.D.—The Marriage Validation Bill was read a second time, and the standing Order being dis- pensed with, the bill passed through its remaining stages. The Distress for Rent (Dublin) Bill, the Recorders, Magistrates, and Clerks of the Peace, and the Forest of Dean Turnpike Trust Bills were read a third time. PRNSIONS.—On the motion of Lord MONKSWELL, a return was agreed to showing the names of all present lords in receipt of public money from the National Ex- rhequer, whether in the form of salary, pay, or allow- 'aces of any kind. • The louse adjourned at 5 45.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.--Turisper. The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. Mr. Rrrcnia, in reply to Dr. Parquharaen, seta that the officials of the Local Government Board were making inquiry with reference to the communication of con- sumption to the human subject from the milk of cows suffering from tuberculosis of the udder. The House agreed to the suspension of the Standing Order closing the sitting at midnight. - •

Replying to Mr. W. Corbett, Mr. BALFOUR stated that the Lord Lieutenant had ordered the release of the ten men convicted at Wicklow, on July 28th, by a jury not selected according to law. RAILWAY AND CANAL TRAFFIC BILL.—The Lords amend- ments to this bill were considered, and in the main agreed to.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1888.

letter from Count Hattfelcit, the perm9,n Ambassiulor, ' thanking the House in thd namel of hla SovereigrOfee I their sympathy with the German Royal Family atui. nation on the death of the Emperor Frederick. A num- ber of bills, including the Parnell Commission measure, were read a first time, and Lord BALFOUR of BURLEIGH moved to receive the report of amendments to the Local Government Bill. On this Lord DENHAM fulfilled his threat to move that the measure should I be postponed for six months, but a division was not ' necessary to obtain an expression of the sense of the ifouse on the matter, and after amendments providing , for the election of vice-chairmon and for retaining' the duties and responsibilities of the justices as conservators] of the peace, the bill was read a third time. Their Lord- ships adjourned shortly after six o'clock. ' HOUSE OF COMMONS.-.--Tuummay. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—A large number of questions had to be dis- posed of on Thursday in the House of Commons before the principal business of the sitting was reached. The Latchford case was again the subject of inquiries of a more or leas pointed nature.— A question was addressed to the President of the Local 1 Government Board by Mr. Charming, who was desirous ' of ascertaining the facts with reference to the outbreak of smallpox at St. Joseph's Certified Industrial School, Manchester, and what number of the patients removed to Monsen Hospital from the school had been vaccine- ted.—Mr. RITCHIE gave details as to vacCination among the 67 patients admitted to the hospital from the school, and stated that the whole business would be thoroughly Inquired into. THE OATHS BILL.—The suspension of the 12 o'clock rule was afterwards moved by Mr W. H. Smith and car- ried, though not without a protest. On the motion for the third reading of the Oaths Bill, Mr E. Robertson said the measure carried with it a stigma and a brand, and was in no way one of relief.' Others having spoken, in- cluding Mr Picton, who viewed the taking of oaths as a humiliating and superstitious practice, and contrary to the teaching of the New Testament, Mr De Lisle pro- ceeded in the customary form to endeavour to throw out the bill, but although he had the assistance of Colonel Sandys as seconder, the third reading was carried by a majority of 87. Tux INDIAN Bepostr.—The House then considered the Indian Budget in Committee, and Sir JOHN Ohasr, the Under Secretary, made his financial stateMent. In the course of it he referred to Burmah as having grievously disappointed the expectations 'formed of it when the Burmese war was entered upon. ,He learnt that the late king never got more than a million pounds out of the country, three hundred thousand of which was from him- posts which under the British occupation were abolished. During the first year of that occupation the revenue was £200,000, and in thethird itwas expected to be £700,000. If, as he estimated, it rose in ten years to £1,000,000 there'would still be a deficit of £340,000. Touching upon the fall of silver, he said that its continuance placed enor- mous difficulties upon the finances of India. Every fall of fd meant a very heavy extra charge. Following Sir John, who went at some length into the questions affecting Indian revenue and expenditure, came Mr. BRADLAUGH with a condemnation of the salt tax and a complaint that the grievances of the native races did tot receive proper and wise consideration.— Mr. Maclean and others having contributed to the debate, and Sir W. • Plowden haying moved a resolution in favour •of the carrying out of certain sug- gested economies, Sir R. TEMPLE said there were two dark clouds hanging over the future of Indian finance. One was the fall in value of the rupee, invol- ving a loss of a quarter of a million of money every six months in the payment of interest on our sterling debt; and the other was the probable loss of the opium reve- nue in consequence of extended poppy culture in China: Sir J. GORST replied upon the discussion, contending generally that the policy in India should be to decentra- Use rather than centralise. ,

div.head: PARNELL COMMISSION BILL.
div.p: THE PARNELL COMMISSION BILL.

The consideration of this bill was then proceeded with. On the motion of the HOME SECRETARY, a new clause was added empowering the Commission to issue a war- rant for the arrest of any person failing to obey a sum• moos to appear and give evidence.—Mr. StairoN, The HOME SECRETARY moved the insertion of the fol- lowing new clause. "Any person summoned to attend before the Commissioners who shall refuse, neglect, or fail to attend in pursuance of any summons, shall, not- standing the dissolution of the Commission, be liable to punishment for contempt of the High: Court of Justice in England, on the motion of any person aggrieved by such refusal, neglect, or failure.".-.----Objections to the clause were raised by Mr. Molloy. Mr. Bradlaugh, and Mr. M. Healy.—Mr. 'MATTHEWS replied that hon. members opposite were hard to please. The leader of the Irish party had suggested these two particular amendments, which he stated he considered vital. Accordingly he (Mr. Matthews), finding that they could be introduced without doing anything to diminish the scope of the bill, had adopted them word, fer word, and put then' into the bill in his own name. He had no objection te altering the last sentence so as to make it read "or the motion of any person who has appeared before such Commissioners."—These words having een substi• tuted. Mr. Panxert, proposed as an amendment the insertion. after the word "summons," of the following—' or who shall refuse to make a full and true- disclosure touching all the matters in respect of which he is examined." As the clause stood the G3vernment made no provision for the continuation of the punishment of persons beyond the time of the dissolution of the CommiSsion who at- tended before the Commission and refused to be ex- nmined.

Mr. MATTTraws pointed out that contempt of the Commission by refusing to give evidence was dealt with under Clause 2, whereby the Commissioners had power to send to prison any person guilty ot contempt The second amendment of the hon. member for Cork,provid- ing that punishment should not stop because the Com• mission came to an end, he was willing to accept. Mr. PARNIMT, announced that under those circum- stances he would withdraw the amendment. The second• amendment of the' hon. member, adding the following to the clause, was agreed to, "and any punishment of imprisonment inflicted by the Commission shall not come to an end by reason of. the termination of the Corn' mission until the Fligh Court of Justice shall so order," _ _ . .

A new clause proposed by Sir Geo. CAMPBELL, giving the commissioners power to commit any person for trial on a criminal charge, was negatived without a division.' Mr. LABOUCHERE moved the following proviso Nothing in this Act shall relieve the printers or pub- lishers of any libel or libels published before the passin; of this Act from any civil or criminal liability." As the bill stood, supposing it was proved that the letters were forgeries, yet Mr. Walter would be absolved from all consequences if he went into the box and gave a full and true account of how he received the letters from Mr. A, and published them believing them to he true. The proposed new clause was rejected by 191' to 120. Mr. Ctawcy moved a new clause, empowering the Commission to report from time to time.—This was accepted by the Home Secretary, and added to the bill. Mr. HUNTER submitted a new clause imposing on The Times the obligation of furnishing adequate particulars of the charges before the openirig of the Commission, copies of these particulars to be supplied to the persons whom they accuse. It was only fair that the accused persons should know what they had to meet —The HOME SECRETARY objected to the new clause as entirely inconsistent with precedent. —Sir CHAS. RUSSELL con- demned the utter unfairness of telling the Irish meintrs to search tlie mass of allegations and innuendos contained in The Times articles, and to come before the Commission prepared to meet. it all.—Mr. ANDERSON supported the clause.—Mr. FINLAY contended that the particulars asked for Were unnecessary in proceedings which would probably extend over a long period. After further debate, the Cruxes:Liza of the EXCHE- QUER appealed to the House to deal with the clause without more discussion. and it was then put to the vote, and negatived by 184 to 118. Mr. M. HEALY proposed a new clause giving the Com- missioners power to sit in places most convenient for witnesses, and providing that no Irish wit nesses should he forced to be examined in England, and vice terse.— The HOME SEcrigrany opposed the amendment, which was tejected without a division. Mr. M. HEALY moved that no persons. against whom any of The Times charges were brought should be im- prisoned under the Crimes Act during the sitting of the Commission, but at the suggestion of Sir Chas. Russell, offered so to modify it that the Commissioners might order the temporary release only of persons Ise soned.—ln neither shape, however, was the HOME SECRETARY willing to accept the clause. Mr. Column suggested the adoption of a clause ..which had been put down on the paper by Mr. John Redmond, authorising the Commissioners to order the temporary release of certain persons for the purpose of ' allowing them to attend the inquiry.—Mr. SMITH said the Government were willing Co accede to this, and the amendment was accordingly withdrawn. Mr. SEXTON moved the insertion of a new clause pro- viding that. no person be summoned to answer charges or alle,o,tions until cria.nce in respect thereof has been teneered to the Commis ioners. For the amendment 109, against 178 majority 69. Mr. SEXTON moved another new clause, providing that the Cornmission'ers should hear the evidence of all per- sons produced as witnesses by others on behalf of any persons affected by any of such charges and allegations. At the sumstion of Sir W. Harcourt the amendment was withdrawn. Mr. T. P. O'Comgon proposed a clause providing that the proceedings of the Commission should be conducted as in an action for libel. Sir CHARLES RUSSELL supported the amendment, while Mr. FINLAY opposed•it. The House then divided—For the clause, 93; against, 19; majority against, 76. Mr. SEXTON moved that the Commissioners may, in their discretion, at any stage of the inquiry, order any pbrson appearing before thigh in support of any of the said charges and allegations, to specify the charge or allegation in such manner as the Commissioners might ! deem to be necessary. The SOLICITOR-GENERAL said the Government could not accept the clause, and it was rejected without a divi- sion. .

Mr. T. P. O'Cloxxou moved a new clause' which was adopted by the Government, providing that the com- mittal of a person for contempt of the commissioners should not be affected by the dissolution of .the com- mission. . Immediately afterwards the debate was adjourned, and the House adjourned at 2 45.

HOUSE OF COMMONS, WEDNESDAY. -the Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. Pus MERSEY RAILWAY Birz.—Some discussion took place on the Mersey Railway (No. 1) Bill, Mr. Maclure and the Hon. G. Kenyon protesting against a clause which they alleged would create an undesirable mono- pol. On the suggestion of the Chairman of Committees, the clause was struck out, and the bill, as amended, was read a third time. On the motion of the First Lord of the Treasury, the Standing Orders were suspended so as to allow the House to sit after six o'clock.

div.head: PARNELL COMMISSION BILL.
div.p: THE PARNELL COMMISSION BILL.

In the resumed discussion of the Parnell Commission Bill the House negatived an amendment by Mr. Brad- laugh, then proceeded to deal with a proposal by Mr. T. P. O'Connor to insert words so as to make a clause read "enable and compel the! inspection and production of documents." Both the Home Secretary and the Soli- citor General regarded the power vested in the Com- missioners as being wide enough to render this amend- ment unnecessary, and on the part of the Government they refused to accept it. Ultimately, however, a com- promise was effected on the lines of giving a discretionary power to the Commission in the matters referred to. The amendment was there upon vvithdrawn:and then Mr BRAD- IAIIGH Moved the omission of the sub-section relating to the Commissioners tower to take evidence abroad, but this amendment was also not pressed.—After some dis- cussion, provision was made for bringing up prisoners for examination before the Commission. On Mr. W.' H. Smith moving the third reading of the bill, Sir W. LAW- .* SON stepped in with an Amendment to the effect that the House should decline to appoint a.Commission unless the inquiry was confined to definite charges against specified individuals. He held that the proposed Commission would. not give complete satisfaction to anyone, and its scope had been unduly widened.—Mr. LABOUCIEERE could not • support the amendment because it did not go far enough, and intimated that he would move the ejection of the bill, which he proceeded to do, descrißing the measure as one pro- 'riding a kind of Star Chamber inquiry, and one which had been forced down the throats of the Opposition. In a speech condemnatory of the bill, Mr. SEXTON said that in the first instance the Government had refused the appointment of a Committee of the House on the ground that the presence upon it of a majority of the political opponents of the Irish members would not be fair, and yet they now set up a tribunal composed entirely of ad- herents of the Ministry, and including a judge who had openly manifested his hostility to the Irish party. When the division was called ihe Irish members left the House in a body, and in their absence the third reading was carried by a majority of 116. Several bills having been advanced, and Mr. SMITH having given hopes of Satur- day seeing the present sitting finished, the House ad- journed at 2-43. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TimasnAv.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Before leaving town Mr. Gladstone completed arrange- ments for hie visit to Birmingham, under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation. The proceedings will extend over two daysythe dates provisionally fixed being the 6th and 7th of November.

A Parliamentary return just published gives a classified statement of the boroughs of Ericland. There are 44 boroughs with a population of 60.000 and upwards; 118 with a population between 50,000 and 10,000; and 12J. with a population under 10.000. There are 18 boroughs which are counties of cities or counties of towns; 218 boroughs which have separate commissions of the peace; 19 borough; appointing their own sheriff ; and 121 boroughs not having separate police establishments.

Sir W. Harcourt, in replying on Monday to an address presented by the Coventry Liberal Association, said the Government policy of coercion in Ireland was everyday becoming more and more revolting to the judgment and the' conscience of the country. The imp:isonrnent of Mr. Dillon had done more than anything eke to seti the fate of the present. Administration in Ireland. In Ireland they imprisoned the representatives of the people; in Westminster they gagged them, and their only policy for the government of the country seemed to be to insult, the people they oppressed. Their coercion every day became more bitter, savage, and cruel. Sir William subsequently drove to Stone- Well Park, the seat of Lord Leigh, .near Kenilworth, where he addressed a mass tneetincrin the riding School. Referring to the Local Government Bill, he described it as a very fine child that had been so tightly wrapped in its swaddling clothes as to stint its growth and destroy theectivity of its limb. He had no doubt, however, that under some subsequent Liberal Association it would be converted into a really useful measure. He again adverted to the trish question, declared that the Government had never received a mandate for coercion, and said Ireland could only he governed on the founda- tions ef peace, justice, and truth: THE IRISH SECRETARY ON THE OPPOSITION. The Chief Secretary was present at a demonstration of Sussex and Kentish Conservatives, on Monday, at Eridge Park, the seat of the Marquis of Abergavenny. In re- sponse to a complimentary vote; the right hon. gentle- man referred to the steps which the Opposition had taken in regard to the bill which, he said, "was to in- vestigate Parnellism and Crime." The Opposition no longer carried on the Irish controversy by argument, but by calumny, against those engaged in the arduous but got impossible task of restoring law and order in Ireland. Notwithstanding, the closest scrutiny, they had not shown a single case of any man put in prison except tor some offence against the laws of his country. It was said that the Parnell Commission was intended to crush the Government's political oppo- nents, but how was it to crush them if they were inno- cent? He had never relied upen The Times' accusations of what occurred some years ago; he found sufficient materials for'his political controversies in contemporary facts of Irish history. His case against Irish leaders would not be weakened if all The Times' accusations were proved baseless. The Irish party had made short work of the eighth Commandment, not to talk of the ninth, and he did not see why they should boggle over the sixth. He believed the Unionist party were vindi- cating the eternal principles of lustice and liberty.
WRECK OFF SCARBOROUGH. - NINE LI VES .LOST.

On Saturday night the lugger Seagull, of Lowestoft, went down off Scarborough, and her crew, nine in num- ber, were drowned. The captain of a smack which has arrived in port states that while three miles off he was running alongside the lugger in a terrible gale. There were only 20 to 30 yards of searoom between them, and he noticed what heavy weather the lugger was making. He turned to remark the fact ;to one of the crew, and, looking round again; he found, the Seagull was missing. Four men were swimming o'n'tlie spot where she had gone down. Instantly he ran his vessel round, and She had sufficient way qupon her to almost reach the poor fellows. A line was thrown to the nearest man, but it dropped short by a foot, and •before another could be thrown the smack drifted to lee- ward. Another run was made, hut again the men failed to reach the ropes thrown to them. The skipper shouted to keep up their hearts and he would try again, but be- fore the smack got round they had all sunk. The lugger left the port on Saturday morning, and intended return- ing to Scarborough in time for Monday's market. At the time of the accident there. was a strong gale of wind blowing from the north-west, and a tremendous sea running. Had the skipper of the smack attempted to lower his own boat he would probably have lost some of his own crew.

John Henry, of Chapel-lane, went with an excursion from Wigan to Cleethorpes by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, on Sunday, and returned home about eleven o'clock at night. He was then drunk, and some friends took him to their house in Queen- street. Here he was placed on a sofa and left for the night. On Monday morning he was found dead, the doctor who was called in being of opinion that he had had an epileptic fit. -- • -

- • DEAFNESS DITEED.—A very interesting 132 page Illustrated Book on Deafness. Noises in the head. Now they may be cured at your home. Post free 341.--Address Dr. NICHOLSON, 21, Bedford Square, London. W.C.—Ackt. A Cabinet Council was held on Thursday. The Bank rate of discount was raised on Thursday from 24 to 3 per cent. Lord flartington has promised to address a meeting in Rossendale in October. A tenement house in New York city was destroyed by fire on Wednesday. Four of the inmates perished in the flames. At Barnsley, on Wednesday, four miners employed at the Barrow Pits, Worsborough, were fined £2 each and costs for damaging the underground level. It was proved that they had wilfully removed the props supporting the roof. THE NATAL MANOEUTRNS.—LiverpooI was surprised by the "enemy," on Thursday, and the citizens were treated to a fine spectacle. A turret ship engaged some torpedo boats and a cruiser, and there was a vast expen- diture of powder both in the ships and in the forts at New Brighton and Seaforth. The " enemy " was ultimately captured by the " British " fleet of iron dads.

BOATING FATALITIES. A beet containing four persons was capsized in Car marthen Bay on Sunday, and one man was drowned. Mr. G. J. Lennox Mason, of Cambridge, was drowned at Ely, on Stinday, by the capsizing of a small sailing boat, which was caught by a sudden gust of wind. Two gentlemen and a waterman who went out for a row at Shanklin, Isle of Wight, on Saturday, are still missing, and it is feared they have all perished. One gentleman is unknown, but the other is a German, named Gustav May.

A pleasure boat from Ipswich, while sailing on the 3rwell, on Sunday, was capsized. Two swam to shore, two were Melted up by passing boats, a fifth was re- covered la an unconscious state, and a sixth, named Taylor, was drowned. Altogether there was a loss of nine lives. An accident occurred on Derwentwater on Monday, through which two brothers named Walker, of Scotbv, near Carlisle, lost their lives. 'three brothers had been for a row, and when returning to Keswick it is sup- posed the boat sprang a leak and filled in a very short time. While it was sinking, two brothers. -Ichtl.Kod 28. and Peter, aged 24, attempted to swim ashore, but- sank after having gone about 100 yards. The other brother, William, got hold of the keel of the boat, which had cap- sized, and was afterwards rescued. The bodies were soon afterwards recovered.

On Monday, Mr. Lamb held an inquest at Whitehaven, touching the death of Robert Griffin, seaman, 67, who was found drowned on the beach near Whitehaven, on Saturday. The deceased and Henry Humphrey went out in a small boat on the night of June 21st for the purpose of herring fishing. The weather was wild, and next day the nets and a sail belonging deceased's boat were cast up, and this led to the supposition that the boat had capsized and that the men had been drowned. Subsequently the body of Humphrey was cast up at Parton, and a youth named Hetherington found Griffin's body on Saturday. It was in a shocking state of decom- position. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."

RAILWAY COLLISION: SIX PERSONS KILLED—MANY INJURED. Shortly after Monday midnight a disastrous collision cc- curd on the South-Western Railway. at Hampton Wick Station. by which fear persons lost their lives, and a num- ber of persons, nearly all hMiday-makers, were more or less seriously injured. The train from Waterloo, due at Hampton Wick at 11 50 p.m.. was five minutes late, owing to the heavy traffic of the Bank Holiday. but the line was given clear from the Kingston signal-box, and the passenger train was running at a fair speed, when, as it reached the bridge crossing the Upper Teddington-road, it ran into a train of empties, which, by some unex- plained means, had been allowed to get on to the wrong line. The crash was tremendous, and was heard nearly a quarter of a mile off, in the still midnight air. Most fortunately, the bridge did not give way beneath the shock of the collision: otherwise, the results would have been much more disastrous. They were, as it was, sufficiently terrible. The engines appeared to pant at each other like living monsters, and then one mounted the other, crashing, with the attached guard's van, right to the foremost passenger carriage. The driver of the passenger train (William Facey) was dug out of the ruins in a terrible condition, and died within two hours of the collision. His stoker was dreadfully mangled, and, when extricated, was quite dead. Mrs. Figg, of Norbitoa, who was returning from a day's out- ing with her husband and two daughters, had her legs and her chest crushed, and sustained other injuries, from which she died early this morning. Mrs. Mindhall, of Teddington, was killed on the spot: and her husband, who was sitting next to her, was seriously injured. Almost immediately after the collision occurred, telegrams were sent to Waterloo and Nine Elms for a breakdown gang and other assist- ance; and pending their arrival, the local railway officials set manfully to work. The neighbourhood was scoured for physicians and surgeons, of whom a con- siderable number were soon en the spot, and willing aid was rendered by late revellers, and residents who had been roused from their sleep by the noise of the collision, or who had not yet retired for the night. When the wreckage had been sufficiently cleared, it was possible to obtain something like an accurate idea of the magnitude of the disaster, and a rough list of the casual- ties was drawn up as follows :—Killed: Mrs. Mindhall, Mrs. Figg, William Paces, (driver), and his stoker—a comparative stranger, whose name has not yet been ascertained. Injured: George Peck, labourer, King- ston, both legs fractured, and severe scalp wounds; James Mindhall, labourer, Teddington, foot crushed; W. Muinford, Kingston, leg fractured: J. Figg, Norbiton, badly bruised: Lydia Figg, severe contusions and bruises; Mrs. Sadler, Teddington, leg fractured and shaken: Mrs. Gull, Kingston, severe con- tusions and bruises. Other persons complained of bruises and severe shaking, but few of them would give their names for fear of alarming their friends; and all were able to proceed home. The more seriously injured were taken to taverns and houses adjoining the station, where they received every attention. The official report, after stating the facts af the col- lision, says :—" The signalman on duty in the Kingston Junction box allowed the driver of a light engine to proceed towards Twickenham on the wrong line, mid, by some remarkable oversight, the driver of this light engine proceeded as far as Hampton Wick Station without discovering the fatal mistake, and then dashed into the 10 50 down passenger train as it was entering the station. The two engines were destroyed, and the guard's van and a third-class car- riage, which formed the two foremost vehicles of the passenger train, were telescoped. The signalman is an .experienced man, and was perfectly sober, but was over- whelmed with grief when he found what a terrible mis- take he had made." _ . .

The rail Way disaster, which occurred at midnight on Tuesday just outside Hampton Wick station, near Ted. dington, has resulted in the deaths of six persons, and injuries more or less severe to about 25 others. Two of the injured—Mr. Maddenhall and Mr. Sadler, of Teddin,g- ton—have died since the collision from their injuries. Some of the survivors are very badly hurt. The carriages were thrown off the metals, and but for a good stout iron rail along the bridge on which the collision occurred, they must have fallen over with much more appalling results. The rest of the injured, up to the present time, are progressing favourably, and no more fatal results are anticipated.
HORRIBLE FIRE IN AMERICA.-LOSS
OF 18 LIVES.-APPALLING- SCENES.

NEW YORK, SATURDAY Moe/mkt—By the simple up- setting of some benzine in a tenement house. in the Bowery, yesterday, 18 people have met with their death. and many others are dangerously injured. The tene- ment in question was inhabited by a number of tailors. most of whom were Polish Jews. The primary accident occurred on the basement, and the flames produced by the ignition of the benzine spread to the upper storeys with atnazing:rapidity. Escape by means of the stairway was soon cut off, and almost at the same time the customary fire-escapes,outside the building were rendered useless because of the flames leaping through the windows. Many of the occupants were thus surrounded before they bad time to comprehend what had happened. When the firemen arrived they found that access to the interior of the building was very difficult, so that they had to direct some of their jets from the roofs and windows of the surrounding blocks; and, among others, from the People's Theatre. Theemployes of this place of entertainment threw a ladder across a vacant area, thereby forming a sort of bridge, over which many people clambered from the door of death into perfect safety; but, after a time, the flames became too fierce to permit of the others reaching the ladder. and many who made the, attempt became crazed, as it were, before their purpose adis effected. Others turned in desperation to the windows, and jumped below, only too often to be dashed to death. Not a few tried to save their paltry goods in the brief space during which they might possibly have saved themselves, and as a rple perished in the building. Perhaps the saddest incident recorded from the fire was the death of a Mrs. Gm% with her children Joseph and Celia, and a baby that was born to her during the fire. The poor woman's double agony is described as heart-rending in the extreme. Her husband managed to save himself and one of his children. Eleven bodies which were taken from the building on the extinction of the fire were charred beyond recognition. Those who were killed by jumping from the windows were of course recognisable. Altogether, up to the present, 18 deaths are reported. Two of the victims were females, and all were tailors. Of some dozen personS who survived through descent from the windows, it is feared that two or three willdie ; whilst most of the others will be crippled for life. As to damage -to property, it is comparatively trifling, as frequently happens in these appalling cases. Great excitement naturally prevailed. Crowds of rela- tives and friends of the victims hampered the operations of the police and the firemen, in their anxiety to obtain information. Their alarm was increased a hundredfold by seeing certain of their fellow-countrymen, with their clothing and hair on fire, jumping from windows, screaming and running, when able, through the street, unable to explain what had happened, save that they had been working in the upper storeys and now found themselves in the street. Presently the wail of a Jew- ish dirge was raised over the dead, which lent an addi- tional gloomy effect to a mournful scene.

- - NEW YORK. SONDAT.—The number of victims from the effects of the fire now amounts to 20, including men, women, and children. Many others were injured while effecting their escape. From detailed accounts of the fire, it appears that many of those who perished might have saved their lives had they had sufficient presence of mind to avail themselves of the means of escape. As it was, many lost valuable time in trying to save their property, and were overtaken by the flames. The burnt building was six storeys high, mostly let out in tailors' shops, where 300 hands were employed, few of whom, however, resided on the premises.

An Under-Sheriff and a jury were summoned at Ennis, on Friday, to assess damages in an undefended action for breach of promise, but their services were not re- quired, the parties having arranged their quarrel and got married that morning.
GENERAL NEWS.
The Dean of Chichester died at ten minutes to one o'clock on Saturday afternoon.
The admissions to Glasgow International Exhibition up to and including Saturday last have reachod the total of 2,407,659.

It is understood that Mr. Gladstone will attend the Welsh National Eisteddfod of Wales at Wreztara either on the 4th or sth September. THE NEW BISHOP OF OXFORD.—The Queen has ap- proved of the translation of the Bishop of Chester to the See of Oxford, rendered vacant by the resignation of Dr. Mackarness.

The death is announced of Mr. William Roberts, of Manchester, who built Christ Church. Barlow Moor, at a cost of £15,C00, and who restored Darley Dale Church, Derbyshire, at an outlay of £5,000. FATAL QUATIREL.-DUTin a quarrel at a village wake at Smisby, a village near adiby-de-la-Zouch, on Satur- day, a joiner named Higgins fatally stabbed a com- panion named Bowler. The wound WM inflicted with a pocket knife, the main artery of the thigh being severed. The victim leaves a widow and three young children. The murderer wa.s arrested.

LADY GRADUATES.—Miss Letitia A. Walkington, Master of Arts of the Royal University, Ireland, his the distinc- tion not only of tieing the first lady graduate in arts, but also the first to take a degree in laws, having passed most creditably, after private study, the examination for LL.B., just held at Dublin. About a dozen Irish ladies have passed the recent examinations for the deeree of 11. a. DETERMINED Solemn sr Bourow.—A determined suicide occurred at Bolton on Saturday night. A foundry labourer named' Burnarcl Rang!, aged 38, residing off Charles-street, hanged himself in his bedroom by means of a cord attached to a nail in a beam. When found his feet. were only an fnch from the floor. He had been suffering from rheumatism, but latterly had given way to drink. A Monism Tnivn von Dorms MMIDER.—At the Sussex Assizes, at Lewes, on Tuesday, ti-e trial cf Sabina Tilley for the murder of her twin daughters was con- cluded. Mr. Gill delivered a very forcible address in defence, and Baron Pollock summed up the case some- what in favour of the prisoner. Af tee an hour's absence, the jury returned a verdict of not. guilty. The funeral of Mr. Frank 8011, ILA., took place at Highgate Cemetery, on l'ilesclay afternoon, in the presence of a large concourse of specta.tors. The first part of the service was conducted at St. Peter's, Belsize Park, the Rev. Dr. Tremiett, vicar, officiating both there and at the cemetery. Among these at the graveside were. Lord Wolselev, Sir Frederick Leighton, Sir John Millais, Mr. Frith, Mr. Marks, Mr. Boehm, Mr. Maurier, and others.

ARREST FOR MIIRDER.—On the arrival of the National Line steamship Erin, at Gravesend, on Sunday, she was boarded by Detective-Sergeant White, of the Criminal Investigation Department, and he arrested Patrick Kelly. who is charged with murdering two of his shipmates, John Cilapmaia and John Parry. on July 9th last, while the vessel was on her outward voyage to New York. Detective White conveyed his prisoner to Bow-street. THE RACE TO EDINBURGIT.—The London and North- Western Railway Company on Monday commenced run- ning between London and Edinburgh 7.1 .I<zht, hours. The train ran from Huston to Crewe, .. ranee of 153 miles, without a stoppage. Preston was the next stop- ping place. Carlisle was reached eight minutes before the appointed time, and the train arrived at Edinburgh at 5 52 p.m., or with eight minutes to spare.

SENTENCE OF DHATIT.—An engine-fitter. named Jones, was charged at Birmingham Assizes, on Monday. with the death of a little girl named Florence Mabel Harris, the daughter of people with whom he lodged. Accused had been on familiar terms with Mrs. Harris, but having been required to quit, bought a resolver, and gbing to the house attacked Harris, his wife, and two children, the deceased dying at the hospital a few days after, the prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to death.

SAD DEATH OF AN EXCURSION/ST NEAR BOLTON.— On Sunday morning, the dead body of Robert Woifen• dale, aged 55, of New Bury, Farnworth, was found in some old foundations at great Lever, near Bolton. The deceased left home early on Saturday morning for Southport, and on returning late at night must have missed his way home, and fallen down the foundations. The fall had evidently stunned him, and as his head was in a small puddle of water, he was smothered.

LORD WILTON AND HIS BATLEY ESTATE.—Lord Wilton offered some time ago to give twenty acres of land at Carlinghow Shays for a public park for Batley. The ratepayers orpressed)themselves in favour of a park, and recommended the Council to accept his lordship's offer. The Council have held a meeting to discuss the question, and after some exciting argument, in the course of which Councillor Lobley declined "to kneel at Alderman Brooke's feet," a vote was given in favour of the public park, which is to be maintained out of the rates.

AN INTFRESTING HISTORICAL FACT.—It IS pointed out as an interesting historical fact that for the first time in English history there are four cardinals of the Holy Roman Church resident in this country at the present moment, viz., Cardinal Manning. Archbishop of West- minster Cardinal Howard, who is lying, ill at Norfolk House, St. James's; Cardinal Newman, the Oratory. Edgbaston, Birmingham; and Cardinal Lavigerie, Arch- bishop of Carthage and Primate of All Africa. To these may be added a fifth, who is expected in a few days, namely. Cardinal Moran, Archbishop of Sydney and Metropolitan of Australasia.

THE MURDER OP A SWEETHEATIT AT BIRMINGHAM.— Mr. Justice Wills at Birmingham Assizes. on Saturday, passed sentence of death on George Nathaniel Daniels, for the murder of his sweetheart, Emma Hastings, daughter of a Birmingham licensed victualler, in Castle. street, Birmingham. The case proved a very pathetic one in connection with the production of several highly Intelligent letters written by the young woman to the prisoner endeavouring to reclaim him from habits of in- temperance and gambling. The accused's habits had brought him to a morbid state of mind with reference to her, and one evening he went to her father's house with a pistol, kissed her, ani fired at her twice, with a fatal result. ACCIDENT ON A CIRCULAR SWITCHBACK RAILWAY.-- On Monday evening there was great excitement caused in the fair ground at Dewsbury through the breakdown of a switchback roundabout railway, belonging to Mr. Waddington, of Leeds. About 70 persons, men, women, and children, were on the machine at the time, and all was going well, when suddenly a link connecting two carriages broke, other parts snapped, and a carriage was overturned, :the oecupants beinz thrown out amongst some ironwork. ThreZ peons were injured, one a litile boy, whose name was not ascertained ; Mary* Ann Bland, 20, of Park Farm, Liveisedge, who was injured on the temple, and who, after receiving surgical aid, was con- veyed home in a cab; and Frederick Heywood, 30, of Dewsbury, who received a severe wound on the fore- head, as well as some bruises, and was taken to the Dewsbury and District General infirmary. . THE REGENT'S PARK MORDER.—William Elvis, Francis Cole, Peter Lee, William Joseph Gra.efe, William Renshaw, Chas. Henry Govier, and Michael Darling, labourers, who were acquitted of the murder of Joseph Rumbold, in Regent's Park, but pleaded guilty to illegal combination and conspiracy to commit a breach of the peace, were, on Saturday, brought up at the Old Bailey for sentence. Mr. Justice Hawkins commented on the cowardly nature of their conduct in attacking an innocent and defenceless men, and said that anything more cruel than that had not come before him. Such lawless acts as theirs must be suppressed, and prisoners and their companions must be taught that the law was too strong for them, and would not permit such turbu- lent and disgraceful outrages in the public streets or elsewhere. Lee and Govier he looked upon as the worst of the gang, and sentenced them each to fifteen months' hard labour, Henshaw to nine months, Cole to eight months, Grade to seven months, and Elvis and Dialing to six months. In the case of Duling, Elvis, and Grade the sentence was without hard labour.

A DYING MAN'S HATRED.—A strange life story with a remarkable climax has just, ended at Chicago, with the death of James Hutchins, a well-to-do resident of that city. Mr. Ilutchin's death occurred just as..the night was closing on Saturday. The deathbed scene in his comfortable home, was an extraordinary one. The dying man had not spoken a word to his wife in twelve years, and for that time they had occupied separate rooms. He was a singular and obstinate man. Dr. Parsons told him he had. only a few hours to live. Mrs. Hutchins was crying.. and the dying man. with open eyes, watched her. With a sudden impulse of a love that had survived the years of cruel treatment. Mrs. Hutchins threw her arms round her husband's neck. kissed him fondly, and begged him to speak to her once, to break, before he died, the silence of a dozen years There was a struggle apparently in his countenance. His lips opened as if to speak, but only an inarticulate sound came from them. His face grew set and stern again. He silently repulsed her, and he was taken with a spasm of coughing. He asked the doctor for a drink of water. Mrs. Hutchins made no further attempt at reconciliation, and in half-an-hour her husband died. How A WEDDING CAME ABOUT.— KISSING BY A SHKRIFF'S ,ORDER.—An interesting case has just been closed in the Airdrie district. A local solicitor presented in Airdrie Sheriff Court on the 14th June last. a medita- tione fbryre warrant, at the instance of a young woman of 18, against a miner, age 25, both of them Catholics re- siding at Clarkston. At the examination before Sheriff Mair the defender stated, in answer to the Sheriff, that _

he was willing to marry the girl, but was not yet in circumstances to do so. The Sheriff : Will you marry the girl ?—Defender Yes; I am quite willing to marry her.—The Sheriff: Will you acknowledge her now to be your wile?— Defender Yes.— The Sheriff: Then, in order to show your good faith. kiss your future wife by order of the court —The defender proceeded cautiously to execute this order, not being very sure as to how he would be receiited. He, however, put his arms round her and gave her a good "smack." the case was then continued for the couple to get mar- ried. On Sunday, the ceremony was to have been cele- brated by Father Wlntosh at the chapel, but as the happy pair had not yet been Ahrived, the marriage was put off a day. On appearing as candidates for matri- monial honours the second time another hitch took place, the "best man" being absent. The ceremony was again postponed, but it is now stated that the two loving hearts have been made one.

div.head: EXECUTION OF JACKSON, THE MANCHESTER MURDERER.
div.p: EXECUTION OF JACKSON, THE MANCHESTER MURDERER.

CONFESSION OF THE CULPRIT. It would be difficult even among our modern criminal records to discover a more distressing example of the headlong pursuit. of a downward career to its bitter end than that furnished by the unhappy culprit who was executed on Tuesday within the walls of Strangeways Prison. Many of those who come to suffer death upon the scaffold are men of mere brutish instinct with whom people in general can have but little sympathy. John Jackson, such is the name under which this young man has chosen to im down to a dishonoured grave, is not of this chess. On the contrary, he had from youth been well and carefully trained, and it was only after he had attained to man's estate that he hosed into those evil courses which eventuated in his ruin. Probably, if the truth were known, drink has had a good share M bring- ing about his downfall. The unfortunate criminal, who was only 33 years of age, and whose real name was Charles Wood Firth, Was a native of Bine-all, in the West Riding of Yorkshire. His parents were respectable people of the working class, the father having for some years oc- cupied a responsible position as caretaker at aeleading county bank. They made considerable sacrifices to give their children a good education, and the lad who has thus finally plunges] them into overwhelming distress seems to have possessed more than ordinary receptive faculties. He was, in fact, a very promising youth, of good dispo- sition, with cultivated tastes, and the parents had great hopes of his future. NVhett the time came for him to give up schooling, he was apprenticed to the trade of a • plumber. In learning this handicraft., he displayed re- markable aptitude. and before many years had passed he became quite a skilled artisan. Thus he started life with every advantage. Educated beyond the ordinary run of working men, wit' i goad trade in his fingers, he had the possibilities of at, least a respectable competency before him. But unhappily lie had got associated with loose companions, who soon led him astray- Berry, the executioner, arrived at the Straneewaya Gaol on Monday afternoon, and in accordance with the prison regulatihne, he was not permitted to come out until after the execution. John Jackson was hanged exactly at, eight o'clock on Tuesday morning. A crowd, numbering several hun- drees, ‘ominierl the whole length of Southall-street ad- joining tip S.rang.eways prisom from seven o'clock up to the time of the execution. Mr. Wright., acting under. sheriff, arrived about 7 30, and at once proceeded to the gaol. Just as the prison clock struck eight, the black flag was hoieted, denoting that the first and chief portion of the law's sentence had been duly carried out At recent executions members of some religious frater- nity have been in the habit, of imorovine the occasion to the large crowds which assembled, much as was the case in the days of public exectit ions, but there was a striking absence of such demonstrations this morning. The crowds seemed to be composed to a great extent of artisans. but there was a sprinkling of loafers and blacklegs about. The people were very silent, contenting them- selves with gazing fixedly at the flagstaff. round the lower portion of which the black flag was entwined. Just as the prison bell struck eight a man's head appeared above the building on the roof of which the flagstaff is fixed, and the crowd broke into.a low murmur as the sombre emblem was unfurled. The condemned man was visited the night before by Major Preston, the governor of the gaol, who said it Was his unpleasant duty to inform him that the, Home Secretary could not see his way to interfere with the due carrying out o: the sentence. The prisoner, who, we ere informed, has all along maintained a quiet and cairn demeanour, and has entertained no hope of any reprieve, received the 11^WA calmly and quietly. Dropping this head upon his hands, he wept for some time, and appeared brokort-hearted. said he wished to take that opportunity of theeking the governor and all the officials of the prison for their extreme kindness to him during the time that he had been in custody. Ile thought that, it was due to him lie should say this, and the Governor assured him that all his wishes had been anticipated. Jackson went to bed about eight o'cl Kik, and he slept for about two hours. Ile then began to he very restless, and was at parently tossing about in his little prison bed until shortly before he was visited by the Rev. Mr. Dreaper, the chaplain. Mr. Dreeper saw the prisoner three times on Monday, and Jackson ex- pressed himself resigned to his fate, and paid the most devout attention to the rev, gentleman's ministrations. Some considerable time was spent with the prisoner in prayer on the morning of the execution. About a quarter to eight the whole of the prison staff of warders was drawn up near to the entrance cf the wing in which the condemned cell is situated. At three minutes to eight Berry, the executioner, entered the condemned cell with his pinioningapparattts, and said that he had come to prepare the prisoner for execution. Jackson was very resigned, but. appeared exceedingly pale. He quietly submitted himself to the pinioning process. The condemned cell is about six paces from the en- trance to the chapel, and from the chapel to the:drop:is about ten paces. The procession was preceded hy four wardeoe then came the chaplain of the gaol. reading the solemn burial service of the Church. Jackson followed, escorted by a warner on each side, with bent head and firm step. He was very pale, bet wanted without assistance. He made no response audible to those in the precession, hut those in the prison yard state that, when near the chapel, he murmured "Lord, help me." Following Jackson Came iserry, and then Mr. Wright, the acting Under-Sheriff. After that gentleman came the gaol surgeon, Dr. Braddon, and Assistant-Surgeon Paton brought up the rear of the procession, which was visible to the whole prison staff. Three re- presentatives of the press were admitted at five minutes to eight o'clock. In the prison yard were assembled a few members of the prison staff and patrols of warders. Jackson mine on the scaffold exactly at one minute to eight. Ile was quite firm; took a hasty glance round, and then closed his eyes. Berry shook hands with him, then quickly completed the pinioning process, placed the white cap on his head, steeped back, milled the lever, and Jackson fell a depth of sft. 61n. The rope was seen to twitch about twice, and then all was quiet. The execution seemed to be rapidly and efficiently conducted. Itnmediately after the execution the doctor examined the pulse of the culprit, and declared life to be extinct. Death appeared to have been almost instantaneous, the neck being dislocated. Jackson's weight was dOst. 11b., and he was given a drop of sft. tin. Interviewing the Governor of the gaol immediately after the execution, eur reures;,ntativo was in- formed by . Major Preston that Jackson had been depressed ever since his removal from the dock. As a rule he slept fairly well and took his food regularly. When the Governor visited Jackson last night, shortly before lie retired to rest,* he found him rather weak, and he gave way for a short time to tears. Otherwise there was no change in his demeanour. lie has been continually watched. He has never at any time denied that he had emmuitted the crime for which he was condemned, and he appeared to, admit the justice of the sentence, lie had informed the Chaplain that he struck Wirier Webh 9. blow with the hammer, not when kneeling as was generally believed, but when he was standing with his hack towards him. Be, however, did not admit that he intended to murder him. On this point he made no statement. THE INQUEST. The inquest on the body of John Jackson. who was described as a house painter, aged 33, was held on Tuesday morning, in the officers' library at Strangeways Gaol, before :Mr. F. Price, county coroner. Previous to the evidence regarding Jackson's death being given, there was an inquiry into the death of a prisoner who haul been committed to the 'gaol for vagrancy and who had had an apoplectic fit. The jury then inquired into the cause of Jackson's death. Major Preston, governor of the gaol, was the first wit- ness called. He gave the usual evidence as to identifica- tion, and said that he was present when the sentence of the law was carried out. After the drawing of the bolt the body was left hanging for an hour. There was no • deviation in this case a•orn the usual method of hang- ing. He fell about 51t. 6in. when the bolt was with- drawn. A Juryman: Did he make any confession? Witness: He made no confession. He said he had done it.

The Coroner: He had never denied it. Another Juror: Did he give way at all on the scaffold Major Preston: He went very firmly. A Juror: Did he gain or lose weight? Witness: He had gained 31bs. since his committal for murder. He has had good health, and he slept well up to last night. His father came to visit him on Monday. Mr. Robert Mesmith Caton, assistant surgeon at the gaol, said he was present. at eight o'clock this morning, when the sentence of death was duly carried out in the case of Jackson. rip, examined the body an hour after the execution, and found that the man was dead. Death was caused, in his opinion, ny fracture of the neck. It was practically instantaneous. A Juror asked whether it had not been arranged that the executioner should be retained until the inquest was over. He was informed, in reply, that that course was only adopted in cases of mishap. In answer to another question, the Governor said a dark on the nose and forehead and the bleeding was caused by the rebound of the drop. Jackson reeled forward very_ much at the time when the bolt was drawn, thus getting out of the upright position. The jury returned a verdict that the indolent ot death had been duly executed according to law.

A lithographic printer, named George Henry Dyson. aged 24, of Leeds, employed 1-iv Messrs. Goodall and Saddick, of that town, lies in LT; ham Cottage Hospital In a critic,al condition. On Monday he was travelling by an excursion from Leeds to Blackpool. At Lytham the train stopped a short time, and Dyson got out. Before he could regain the train, his legs were caught by the wheels, and so fearfully mutilated that amputation of both limbs below the knee was necessary. He was to have been married -next week, and the young lady to whom he is engaged was travelling with him. The un- fortunate man is improving as rapidly as can be ex- pected, and hopes are entertained of his recovery.

to inkusA, next year, they would be alike Olarried and renovated by the change. It would the railway companies a better chance, too, if there was less of a rush to favourite places of r'?6c)rt ; and it is a matter of course to say that it /vcnild lessen the risk of railway accidents. Al- though it is true that, in proportion to the number uf People conveyed from place to place, the per- c)e. ntage of accidents is remarkably small, it is linPossible not to observe that railway accidents 410 st frequently occur during the congested traffic of holiday time. The greater the congestion, it Ikta37 With truth be said, and the greater the risk. tis saddening to reflect that Monday last was liot free from catastrophe. The collision at Hamp- tsl Wick Station has resulted in the loss of six'" l'es, and a number of people have been seriously 44lured. The official report states tit a the signal who sent the train of ompties on the wrong neis "an experienced man, and was perfectly taBnber ;" but the probability is that he was over- zect with extra duties consequent upon the extra ; and what may have been a momentary .;ht has been fraught with the most terrible ent4squences. It may be said that railway corn- shouldn't give their servants so much to do; the strain is inevitable when the traffic is con- 452„tsd. Men who know the work are necessarily in to the fullest extent; it is obvious that it °WU be unsafe at such a time to employ inex- telienced servants. The suggestion we make t'h to trying resorts somewhat out of tce ordinary run would, if adopted, cer- InlY have a tendency to relieve certain eetttres of traffic, and in this way there can be no that it would be the means of reducing risks .of holiday travelling. But the main con- Alen is that it would ensure greater enjoy- tt by offering greater variety. Man is a crea- hof habit even in the matter of holidays. There thousands upon thousands who from sheer of habit confine themselves to two or three These people, if they once broke through tt they doubtless look upon as a charmed circle, be surprised to find that there are circles as o which have hitherto been outside their Bank Holiday has become an institution, It should be made the most of The busy in particular, requires at such a time and complete change of scene. There is no Where there is a crowd; it must be sought in sleepy hollows, or by the lone mountains and waters of our beautiful land.

"TOUCH AND GU:. The, Conservatives of Newton paid a visit to Hale, on Saturday. Wonder if there .are any hale Conservatives at Newton?

--- It will be seen that we have received another interestin letter from Mr. Whithatn. He men- tions that Mrs. Hope and her family, who left War- rington a few weeks ago, have reached San Fran- cisco, all well.

Wales is not to have it all to heriielf ; it is said that gold has been discovered in Ireland. This is good news fnr Paddy ; it was thought that all the gold had been taken out of the country to line the pockets of absentee landlords.

Who cares for the rain? It poured at Hnyton, on Saturday, but sports were announced and sports were held. The sports included dancing. Fancy, dancing in the rain ? But they were equal to the occasion; each couple carried an umbrella. They understand sport at Huyton, and know the bliss of umbrella courtship.

Great is Steam, and the locomotive is his prophet! Now that steamers can get to America in six days, and a train is being run from London to Edinburgh within eight hours, may we not ex- pect, as Byron has it, that— soon . Steam engines will conduct us to the moon ?

Temperance men have \been demonstrating strongly both at Runcorn and at Widnes during the past week. At Widnes, on Saturday,' the tee- totallers were in for a good deal of "heavy wet" • but it didn't cause them, when they got home, to smash pots, thrash wives, and finish the night in a police call, after the manner of some when they are in a " moist " condition.

• Instead of what Tennyson calls "a cycle of Oathay,r we have had manceuvring cyclists in this part of the country. The project has not been carried out on so large a scale as was expected; but the raanceuvres have been successful. The cyclists have shown that in time of war, or rumours of war, they will be the right men to " turn about, wheel about, and jump Jim Crow.'

--- The large attendance at the funeral of Mr. Noah Legge, on Saturday, was a striking testimony to tht affectionate regard of those who knew him best .—the men who in various relations had worked with him and under him. Character is everything; but sometbnos it is not till death that its worth is fully realised. Only the adieus rd the just Smell sweet and blossom in the dust..

It was fitting that M. Carnet, the President of the French Republic; should imveil the statue to Mirabeau' the genius of the Revolution which made the Itlpublic possible. It is stated that there were as many as thirty thousand persons present at the Coremlny, which took place at Mont- arges on Sunday. The French are proud of Mira- beau: he was a hero; he covered himself with glory in defying the King, and what could be more heroic than that?

Carlyle liked Slirabeau as he liked all strong men. After describing his appearance, he says— That is the type-Frenchman of this eooch; as Voltaire was Of the last. He is French in his as- pirations; acquisitions in his virtues, in his vices ; perhaps more French than any other 'nail ;—and intrinsically such a maas of manhood too. Mark him well. The National Assembly were all differ- ent without that one; nay, he might say with the despot—' The National Assembly ? lam that.'"

Alderman WiCechnie has proved such an ex- cellent Mayor of St. Helm* that the regret .will be general that pressure of business prevents his accepting the offi !‘a for a second year. The question now is as to a tuccessor, and it is rumoured that ail .clioico is likely to fall,. on Alderman J. C. Gamble, J.P. As his father, Colonel Gamble, has been Mayor of St. Helens no less than five times, he is bound to accept; it runs in the blood. •

The magistrates, of Widnes set an admirable ex- ample by inflicting heavy fines for milk adultera- tion. On Thursday a penalty of 2,5 and costs was imposed on a farmer residing at Halebank. The Bench went the length of intimating that if the milkdealer vim brought up again for a similar offence, ho would be fined in the full surn—C2o apd costs. This is going the right way to work; lot fraudulent milkmen be made to roalisc that honesty is the best policy.

The "Morning Advertiser," the organ of the. license,d victuallers, is delighted to find from the Encyclical Letter of the English Bishops who were recently in conference at Lambeth, that they do- not insist on total abstinence as a Christian duty; and that they do not approve of the practice •of substituting unfermented wine in the celebration of the communion. But what of that Study the record of the votes of the Bishops in the House of Lords, and it will be seen that the way to arrive at a right judgment is to say yes when tha bishops say no.

Councillor W..Pierpoint raised a nice point at the Warrington Town Council meeting, on Tues- day, when he put a question as to something which appeared in the annual statement of accounts just issued. The Mayor said it was "riot quite in order;" hut the contention as to the annual statornont with reformco to the Gas Com- mittee has been that it was presented to the Council by means of the • Annual Statement of Accounts. The issue is still loft, open; but it was sUfficient for'Councillor W. Pierpoint that he had his way in calling attontion to what is undoubtedly. a matter of importance.

The Rev. F. W. Willis, Vicar of Warrington, preached his first sermon,in Warrington,to a large congregation on Sunday evening. He took his text from the lessons, and in the course of his ex- cellent sermon he showed how Rehoboam "lost his kingdom, an earthly one, by trying to rule simply by force." • Amplifying the point, he said—" It is by love, and riot by force or tyranny that we wii. the moral kingdom in the hearts of men." The Vicar meant nothing of course political, and, just. because nothing was meant, it might be all the more serviceable if someone were to send a copy of the sermon to the Prime Minister, and the Chief Secretary for Imiland.

The. expected has happened, with regard to the Gas Committee of tho Warrington Corporation; the majority of the members of the committee re- signed, but their resignations were not accepted at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday. Their keenest critics were emphatic in stating that it was not a question of losing confidence in the committee. • But if the members of the committee had a doubt•on the subject they were of course within their right in having that doubt resolved. The Committee and the Council have "kissed again and made friends."

• Alderman Davies spoke like an Alderman in re- ferring to the ratepayers; he knows he does not depend for his seat upon their suffrages. There is no doubt a great deal of ignorance—even amongst editors. For mstance,we have repeatedly confessed that we cannot understand how it is that a leak- age reported to be 71 millions (or 4 per cent.) in 1886, should have risen to 28 millions (or 14 per cent.). in 1887. Seeing that Alderman Davies turned on the leakage tap,would not it have been as well if he had let out an explanation of the phe- nomenon? How are ordinary mortals to get rid of their ignorance unless Councillors Aldermen, and other superior persons condescend to enlighten them?

The sum of 010 1'44; Cr a penny in the pound in the rates, and, het er than incur such an expense for such an ob- tltki *e do not doubt the inhabitants will con- that the Town Council has taken the right " in again shelving the proposal to deal with •lat , _

not within the borough of Warrington be amalga- mated with the parish of Grappenhall. (2.) That the parish of Grappenhall (so extended) and the parish of Thelwall, in the county of Chester, and now in the Union of Warrington, be transferred to the Union of ;:tuncorn, in the cOunty of Chester. (3.) That the parish of Latchford (altered as hereinbef ore provided), in the Union of Warrifigton, and in the borough of Warrington, and now in the county of Chester, be transferred to the county of Lancaster. This •means that, for the future, if tho Com- missioners are to have their way, the boun- dary line- (in ,Latchford), of the borough of Warrington; will also be the boundary line be- tween the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire. But this leaves no room for the extension of the borough, in this direction, without raising the difficulty of going out Of one county into another. And what of the Ship Canal? Has it to be utterly ignored, although so likely to be a striking feature as a dividing line? It is not, perhaps, of Much: moment that the parish of Grappenhall is to be extended by taking a slice of the parish of Latchford ; but it is of moment —of great moment—that it is proposed to take the parish of Grappenhall (so extended) and the parish of Thelwall out of the Warrington Union and transfer them to the Chester Union.- It will be a monstrous injustice to the poor of both these parishes. At present they can get to Warrington Workhouse to make application for relief by making a short journey; but if the applicants are required to go to Dutton Work- house they will have to walk seven or eight miles Let any person who is interested in the matter look at a map, and he will see how absurd it is to propose such a change. The fact is, the poor arenot being taken into account at all. The proposed altera- tion is in the interest of the Cheshire Squires, who do not desire•to be associated With Warrington— except as a place where they make a pile of money. But the poor have voices, and they have votes ; and if they will use the powers they possess, and use them speedily, .they will make short work of these ridiculous recommendations of the Boundary Commissioners.
