UNITED TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES.

The annual demonstration of the temperance so- cieties of Widnes. took place on Saturday. Unfor- tunately the weather was eery unfavourable, rain descending during the w'mle of the afternoh, but nevertheless about a t houstind teetotallers assembled on the 'promenade. We. t Bank, at half-past two. The procession was healed by . Rey. It. Burdoh (Wes- leyan), R. Yeatman (Baptist). E. Hall (Free Church), and a number of old temperance workers. Next came the Jubilee Brass Band in their new uniform, and then followed representatives of the organisations named in this order :—Blve Ribbon Mission, Lacey-st. Band of Hope, Zion Band of Elope, Parnworth Wesltlan Band of Hope, Baptist Band of Hope, Albert-road Band of Hope, Bitten Wesleyan Band of Hope. Oakland-st. Brass Bawl. Loyal Juvenile Temple ()award Juvenile ! Temple 1.0.G.T., Star of Widnes Lodge Semis- titan Lodge Hope of Appleton Lodge 1.0.G.T., and the Recbabites. The temperance 'organisatioas iii connection with the Church of England did not take ' part, as they held a demonstration on their own account later. Numerous banners and bannerettes graced the procession, but -umbrellas were a very conspicu- ous feature of the display. Thte proeession marched through the main - thoroughfares to Appleton, where Mr. H. Wade Deacon had kindly lent a field for the re- ception and use of the Large party. An open air meeting was held tinder the chairmanshin of Mr. J. It. Lich, president of the. St. Helens Band of Hope Union. Amongst those on the temporary platform wore the rev. • gentlemen previously, mentioned, Messrs. J. Brock, J.P., T. S. Smiles, S. Owens, John Shaw, The Chair- man bristly introduced Mr. BroA, who said they had had as inueli water as any ordinary teetotaller mild de- sire. (Laughter.). He thought the people were very courageous to come reit on a day like that, but there were many reasons willY they should coulee:at and show. 'the publiethestrength of theireonvictions. (Hear, hear.) In • little time to come they would be cailed upon to elect under a new Government Bill certain enunty c ma- eillors. The temperance me t aad men:fore, ought to be very careful vraorn they sent to represent them, as the liCensing clauses, which had been elimina- ted from that Bill, Arould he certain to come up again , before long. In that, he felt sure they would have the ! support of the better class of publicans. and some of the publicans would be only too thankful if thy were allowed to close their homess SundaY. (1/ear. ear.) He considehel also that in face of recent legal decisions' that there was no legal right t,-) e:imeensation. There , may be a certain equitable right under, certaia circum- stances, and then comeemsatioa. if it b given. Must be restricted in time. Ten years had been mentiened dor- • in.; which time this restriction was to work, and at the end of that time they must :ease altoeether, and if they ! took care to send suitable man to these comity emaeils,

he had i o doubt there would be a wonderful improve- ment with regard to the drink traffic. He could not say that he was a staunch teetotaller, but he was a temper- ance man, and that was applicable to many other things besides simply to the drink traffic of the country. They all had in their sphere a certain amount of influence, and if they would only bring their induence to bear on this matter, they would make a decided improvement. There was a grand opportunity coming if they only totk care to seize it, and if they would be reasonable About it, they would have the matter in their own hands. It would all turn upon the kind of representatives they sent.' He warned them to take care in that neighbour- hood, and, therefore, to send proper representatives. (Applause.) Mr. Bu don, said he was very glad to Mr. Brock as a strong teetotaler, to move a vote of thanks. The princi- pals he had kept up had injured no one, but they could not say that about the publicans. He wanted them to think about the widows and orphans whose ten thous- ands of hopes had been blighted; and if they compen- sated the publicans they must compensate all rotind. Look at each individual case, And have a proper repre- hentat i ye board.

- Mr. Swales seeonded the vote, and said 'he would give , them one year's compensation and no more, and that evtrything onght to be tried on its own merits. • The Chairman, in putting the vote to the company, said he wasglad to think that one of the leading magic- ates the county was showing them sqch a good example. The von was carried with three loud cheers. Mr. Brock, in resporoing, thanked them for the hearty way in VZ-hicli they had received him, and for the vote Of thanks. He saw a great number of cases from time to time in the courts, and that was quite sufficient to make any man into a teetotaler at once. . There could be no legal right to compensation what ever. (Applause). The Chairman said before they went he wished to con- gratulate them on their appearance that day. The pro- cession did credit to the society who formed it. There wereh great numlior of young people growing up" to be temperance workers, and that would tell a tale upon Widnes in a future time. Many of the widows and orphans and others they observed about them were the result of the drink trade.

A vote of thanks to Mr. Leach for presiding, and to Mr. Dea”a'for the loan of the ficla, concluded the pro- ceMingi. • The childkn were narched to their respective 'school- rooms, vehere, bun., and coffee were supplied to them, and they wee afterwards allowed to amuse themselves in a ntunb.!r of gams dear to the juvenile mind.
RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. ANNUAL DEMONSTRATION.

T'ee members of this temperance organisation held their annealdemonstration last week end. On Sunday afternoon about 200 members assembled in Devntishire-sqeare, where short addresses were delivered by Messrs. S. Ashton, T. Cooke, D. Bis- brown, W. Hetherington, and S. W. Timperley. The singing was conducted by Mr. James Stubbs. After- wards the members walked in procession to the Parish Cherce, where a special service was con- ducted, and the Vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, preached an appropriate sermon. On Monday the bretheren met at Regentest. School-room, and formed into nroceseional order. In front were two mounted marshalte, Messrs. T. Heason, and J. Lea, ; then came the Weston Wesleyan Sunday School Brass Band, and the beautiful bannerol the division. The silken rib- bons oF the banner were held by four children :—Annie and Aliee Cenke, Mageie Hetherington, and Lizzie Bisbrown, who were attired in white dresses. The cords were carried by Misses Randles, Guy, Hulse, and Hind. Following were the Daughters of Temperance, the charter being earried bY Mr. Jabez Stubbs ; then the Life Boat Crewe Division, the charter being carried by Mr. S. Ashley aild Mr. Jams Bisbrown. In the rear werewthe members of the Cadet Section "Guide to Youth." It was estimated that therewere nearly 400 per- Sens in the proceseion, and it was marshalled throtighthe principal streets by Messrs. T. J. Holt, James Johnson, J. Crank, T. White, S. M. Timperley, D. Bisbrown and T. Coolte.-secretary. EAreete, stoppages were made at the residences of Mr. Thomas Kirkham, Leinster Gar- dens; Dr. Melanmane, Lord-st. ; Dr. Robinson, Belve- dere; Lee's Temperance Hotel, and Dr. McDougall's, High- , se After sivindine a short time in a field kindly lent by Mr. T. Kirkham, the precessionists returned to Bethesda schoolroom, where tea was provided. The tablas were presided over by Mesdames Gibson, Pendlebury, D. Bis- brown. Royle, Watson, and Bandies; and Misses Stubs, Bandies., Ellis, Guy. Price, and Either Millington. Sub- sequently a public meeling was held in the same build- ing, and there was a crowded audience. Mr. F. J. Nor- man, presided, and there were on the platform the Rev. E. Hall, Messrs. T. Reason. S. M. Timperley, E. Key, S. Ashley, J. Crank, T. White, D. Bisbrown, J. Bis- brown, R. Thomas, J.. Boyle. T. J. Holt, W. J. Hethering- ton, and T. Cooke, secretary. The Secretary presented the annual report, which stated that order was making progress all along the lin . Durine the year 20 new divisions had beeninsti- tuted, and 22 cadet sections, a net increase of nearly 1,000 in their memhership, and an increase of £6,477 ss' 9d in the funds of the society. (Applause). The roll of membership was now 22.931, and the amount of funds £79,231 6s LI. (Applause). They had in connection with the juvenile branch 4,680 members, with funds to the ameunt of £2.231 HA. Durine tha year the order had paid away sickness £16,762"13s sd; and in death claims £2.755 10s, awl had. given away to deserving members in distress, £317 7e 7d. (Applause). In their own local division at Runcorn, whose anniversary they were tedebratine that day, they numbered 240 members in good standing and about 120 cadets, or juvenile mem- bers. (Applause). During the year they had received from the members in eintributiorte £297 7s 70, and had paid away in sick claims .£1513 19s, in death claims, £56; had given away to deserving members in distress, £1 5s 70, and had sent £2; to the central fund, leaving a , balance in the treasurer's hands of £62. The sickness throughout the year had averaged a little over seven days per member, and their death rate 7.19 per thousand whilst the death rate of the juvenile sections had only !averaeed a little over 2 per 1,000. They must each of them feel somewhat enconrage'l by this year's success of the order, and he trusted that they might be stimulated to still greater efforts difring the coining year. (Ap- plause.) Let each of them work to gather in new mem- bers, not forgetting that it was part of their labour as the direct means of extending it benefits and blessings. -(Lond applause)._ The Chairman then delivered an. address, in which he said he woet I deal with two particular points—the ad- vantages of time-Sons of Temperance Society and the pre- -sent Parliamentary view of the temperance question. With regard to the advantages of the society, the princi- cipal on which it was based was the joining together of teetotalism and thrift, and two happier companions never yet merit together. (Applause.) Those particular tiocieties had been carefully weighed up by scientific men. for it was obvious that the leading doc- tors, amongst them being Dr. Richardson, had arrived at the conclusion that teetotalism. from the standpoint of health, was the right and proper thing. (Hear, hear.) Teetotalism was conducive to health, and he felt that if the society noidd get more people to • become teetotallers the figures would prove conclusively that the advantages were very apparent indeed. With regard to the Parlia- mentary aspect; the Chairman said they would remem- ber that two years ago he expressed the greatest dissatis- faction at there not being :any organisation amongst temperance people to obtain 'legislation in their behalf. He could not help thinking that if they had temperance leaders to pitch the question forward they would be suffi- ciently strong to get what was wanted in the shape of legislation'. A short time ago the present Government brought forward a measure which proposed a system of compensatioa to the publicans in this country. Those present knew what the temperance party did in the mat- ter. (Hear. hear.) They were sufficiently strong to prevent the linveinment from giving that compensation, and it only required the same unanimity on the part of the temperance party to bring about what they now de- sired. They did not get temperance legislation, because their leader e did not stand together sufficiently. If they went to Mr. Gladstone and toll him to put the theory he had advanced some years ago in practice, and they would stand by him, and he declined, let them go to the Tory party to ask for legislation. Mt did riot grudge Mr. Parnell his snecess in mead to his fight for the question nearest hie heart, but he certainly said they as teetotaler; should take a leaf out of his beek, and if they had done so twelve months ago they would have found that tem- perance legislation would have been brought un to the standpoint they desired. (Hear, hear.) If they only worked they Meet sueceel. for Gai was on their side, therefore their triumph must be speedy and very corn- plate • (Applause.) The Rev. E. Hall, in the course of his address, stated that it was 21 el 22 years since he became a member of the Sons of Temperance, and he was still one, although for certain reasons, which he evplained, he was not a 'member of the local lodge. When they spoke' on the temperance queetion, they certainly spoke of a most im- portant social question of the day. They knew that so- ciety was so bound together that the innocent sitffere.d with the guilty. How merle mothers a.nd fathers were there who had abandoned themSel yes to habits of intern- penance ateLzice; and who were starving their children in mind arm Leidy ? How many houses were there that , were made homeless, and the workhouses, asylums, arid , gaols filled in consequenc'e of the evil of intemperance? 'George Cruikshank. the ereat temperance painter, had attempted to paint the misery' and others had tried to describe it ; but it beffl the' genius of artists, the literary powers of writers and others to do it anything like justice. (Hear,' hear.) Thee must catch the spirit which hed been -previously meetioned, and Tierce the Governinent to do sem for the mitigation and suppreseien of that wee. (Applause.) The House of Legislature was a servant of the nation, and must sooner or later do' the bidding of the people. (Hear, hear.) They hal only to'spAlr an I show their determination by raising their voice,. and they would get what was re- quire 1. Tileir•quairo. wai not with the men a9d women who -were (melee] in the trade, bet with the tradie. It was unworthy of them, it war and it was cowardly and uueiea to stand by all not put out a help- ing hend to th iso mom were perishing, and it made them participators in their ruin. (Hear, hear.), • It was

inot sufficient to sign the pledge ; let them go forth and rescue those who had fallen into the evil. There were two things for them to do—wipe their hands of all complicity with that traffic, and use politi- cal, social. and moral nalluence in order that they might bring others to their way of thinking and living. (Hear, hear.) They must remind the Government of its duty as defined by one of the most enlightened statesmen this country has ever produced. He wished that statesman hid shown his enlightenment on the temperance ques- tion; but that was his weakest point, and the blot on his escutcheon. (Applause.) He had told them that tho first duty of a Govrnment was to make it easy to de right, and hard to do wrong; but it had not been so in the past. He (the rev, gentleman) did not think the . temperance question was a Utopian movement; they be- lieved that it had succeeded, and had God's blessing upon it. (Hear, hear.) They were making progress all along the line. When they found that a Government had the temerity and the audacity to talk about com- pensating publicans, it seemed to him that there was urgent necessity for being up and doing. It was not for them to pay compensation to publicans when they closed their houses; it was for the publicans to compensate the poor orphans and others who had been dragging on a miserable existence, and for them n to repair the wrong they had done—(hear, hear,)—and then talk about com- pensation Compensation was due rather from the pub- licans than from the people. In concluding, the rev: gentleman invited those present to push forward the noble work, and he was loudly applauded on resuming his seat.

Mr. Temperley spoke in behalf of the cadet section, and said if they kept the yoUth from the accursed drink the publicans would shut up of their own accord, and there would be no 300 millions required to compensate them. (Hear. hear.) That would come about in a very few years, and if they could only keep the children from the drink, public-houses would become empty. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Boyle made a speech in advocacy of the Daugh- ters of Temperance, and the meeting concluded with the usual votes of thanks. The proceedings were enlivened with a number of songs and recitations given by the youhg members of the society.

WOMAN'S KID FRACTURED WITH k STOOL —At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Killalea, of 2, Sankey-st., was brought up under a warrant charged with having, on the 28th July, unlawfully and maliciously wounded Bridget Glynn, with intent to do her grevious bodily harm.—Mary Ann Glynn said she was the daughter of the prosecutrix, and lived at 23, Sankcy-st. Her mother was very ill in bed suffering from a brokerurib, and she had also a rib "staved in." The prisoner caused the in- juiles by striking her with a stool, which was broken by the force he used.—Dr. Hutchinson certified that the woman was in a very weak state, and would not be able to attend court for at least a fortniglit.—The prisoner was remanded for a week. _

The Committee rooorted that the total sales for the half year entied'itme 30,h amounted to £33,529 16s 3d, being an increase of £773 on the corresponding halfsyear. The net profit amounted to £l,Bll 3s 111, and . they recommended a dividend of 2s 61 in the £ on £38.392 of check account books brought in. which would amount to £42,739 2s 61. The balance of £l2 OA na was added to the reserve fund. The report was adopted, and no comment was made with regard to the dividend.—A proposal to erect a cen- tral stores at Widnesat acOst of about £3,500 waslost by a large majority. The retiring members of the committee were Messrs: W Cropper, S Stubb.4, W Whitehead, and T Watson, and the following were elected in their ,places :—Messrs. R [byte, Thomas Riley; W Dwm and W. During the meeting the Widnes members left the room in a body because Mr Fitzpatrick, who was making a. proposition that the tialf-vearly meeting should be held alternately at Widnes, could not obtain a fair hearing. WEszoN CHURCH ScHoors.—The riria fete and sale of' work realised the highest anticipations of the promoters, and the proceeds will more than clear off the debt of 020 existing on the schools. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—Mrs. Taylor, wife of John Taylor. confectioner, Widnes-road, fell down in a fit near the Post Office on Tuesday. She died whilst being conveyed home on a stretcher. LIVER ALKALI COMPANY. WIDNES.—ThiS company pro- pose to shortly extend their works in Ditton-road by the erection of plant for extracting sulphur gas from waste. It Is estimated that .£lO,OOO will be spent. ALLEGED ROBBERIES AT lILINCORN.—On Thursday, at I Runcorn Police Court, Edward CoMtn was charged with having stolen 21bs of beef, worth Is Eld, the property of Henry Greenwood, a clogger. He was remanded,for a week..—Jelin Knight, a labourer, was also remanded for a week on a charge of having stolen a • vest and a silk handkerchief, the property of John Hornsby. ' • CARRYING LOADED ARMS AT SuTToN.—Albany Potts, a young man who was respectably dressed, was brought np at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, charged with having on that morning been found at Siam( with a re- volver In his possession, with intent to'commit an un- lawful act. Prisoner was remanded for a day to allow inquiries to be made, and yesterday Superintendent Hollingworth informed the Emelt that the inquiries were satisfactory and he was discharged. - -

• . THE POLISIT EI:WEST:TNT I%T Wipeze.—At Wienes ! Police Court, on Wednesday, Maggie Liz hie, 45, Crum- 'well-st. Frank Ifeas. 11, Bare-st., and William Danvi- latis, of seine address, wore charged with stealing a large quantity of article, the property of Alexander Lizdas, husband of the female prisoner, and of William , Vaenites, .a lodger. Tint particulars of the case were given last ir:•A, and a: the Beath committed the prisme-e; t e'te. their trial at the'. Quarter Sessions. RTINCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.—Mr.j:•E. lemeshaW, the secretary, has just issued ' a list or the fixtures of the Runcorn Club for the coming season. ' It. is got up in good style, and takes the form of a book. Art important feature is the addition of the laws of the Rugby game and the rules of the Rugby Union, while the space pro- vided to properly record the result of, each game will be very useful. The fixtures are a capital lot, and include matches with four Cheshire clubs; eight Lancashire clubs, and clubs, in Yorkshire, Westmoreland, and the Midlands. A match has also been arranged with the Maori team, which is expected to visit \ Eagland in the winter.. JUBILEE OF TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN, —This year will have completed the fiftieth anniversary of the eree- fion of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn; and ee was deter- mined to c•lebrate the jubilee by removing the organ from the gallery, and be having the instrument tho- roughly repaired, aryl new steps added. Comfortable chancel stalls ' have ' bem provided for the choir, and the general interior of the church has 'been renovated. During the ..past fifty years there have been seven vicars of the church. In commemoration of the jubilee a special service was held on Thursday night,- and was conducted by the Rev. W. Preston. The choir was augmented for the occasion, and Mr. E. G. Smith, of Manchester, 7presided at the organ. The Rev. Canon Burbridgepreaehed a sermon. After the service Mr. E. U. Smith gave a recital on the organ. - • ' DROWNED IN A RUNCORN D3ClA.—'gr. J. E. Worsley,, coroner, on Saturday held an. inquest at the New Inn, Runcorn, on the body of Thomas Goode, aged 11 years. —Thomas Goode saia he was the grandfather of the de- ceased, and lived in Back High-street. The father of the deceased was a boatmen and had no residence. On the previous day the deceased and his brother, aged seven years, were playing on board a narrow boat belonging to the Marston Hall Salt Company, which was lying in the Old Dock. Witness cautioned the boys to be careful, as .the plank they were running upon .was only eleven inches wide. Shortly afterwards the boys 'caught hold of each other, and fell over the side of the boat into the water. James Wardle, E boatman, inimediately -grasped the younger brother and saved him, but the deceased sank underneath the boat, and did not rise to the sur- face.—The Coroner observed that it, appeared to be a dangerous way of plavine, and asked whether it was customary.—iVilliam Bebbington said it was very com- mon. Little children about three years of age might frequently be seen toddling about the bont4. DROWNING MYSTERY AT WIDNES.-,-:DG ThUrday Mr. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Widnes Police Court, on the body of James Richard Bond, aged 28, a waterman of no settled abode.—Martha Ann Bond, widow of the deceased, stated that on Tues- day afternoon, at three o'clock,- she saw the deceased in , Waterloo-road. He was then in drink, and went across the fields towards the canal where the boat he usually worked on was.—Samuel Holden, of John-st.. West Bank, said he was master of the flat Diana. The deceased had Made one trip with him and that was On Monday the 6th inst. The flat returned on the. Tuesday. He saw the . body of the deceased in the canal on' morn- ing. He had no right to sleep on the fiat.—George Web- ster, of Rigby-st., St. Helens, said he slept in the flat Diana from 10 o'clock on Tuesday night. He heard no disturbance and saw nothing of the deceased. On Wed- nesday morning he saw a doe., a hat, and a belt in the small boat of the flat, and the body of the deceased was found in the canal.—P.C. Davy deposed that he saw the deceased at half-past eleven o'clock on Tuesday night. , He was slightly in drink, and he said he was going to sleep OD the flat Diana.—A verdict of found drowned was , returned. ITCSPECTION OF .CHESHIRE VOLUNTEERS.—Tbe Earl of Chester's Rifle Volunteers, composed of com- panies from Chester, Frodsam. .Weaverham: anti Runcorn, who went. inte camp at Rhyl on Sattirday, were inspected on Friday morning by, Colonel Pat- ton. The weather was magnifieent, and there was a large et tendance of spectators. There were over 600 men on parade, untie- the conruand of Calorie' Ashton and Major Hazlehurst, At the conclusion of the manmavres .Colonel Ashton expressed his high approval of the bearing and conduct of the men. • I STUBBS' FURNITURE CRRAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with hilt the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. sold hi bottles, and 31.—Isaac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Run corn .—Adet. THEFT FROSE A " PApDY-Rousic."—At. an Occa- sional Court. held at Warrington, .on Thursday. be- fore Mr. Z. Armitage, amyl named Michael Feeney, described as a farm labourer. from Widnes, was brought up in custody charged with having stolen from a " Paddy-house," on Cuerdley, Earn), a pair of beots, a shirt, and a coat, value in all ss, the property of Walter Foy and Patrick McHugh, labourers on the farm. It appeared from the evi- dence that the prisoner, who has been previously convicted, went into the "Paddy-house" while the men were absent, and helped himself to the articles in question. He was committed to take his trial at the Quarter Sessions. MARRIAGE OF M. YERBITHCIIT,' M.P.—The mar- riage between Mr. Robert Yerburgh;.M.,P. for Ches- ter, and Miss Elms. Thwaites, only 'daughter of Mr. Daniel Thwaites, of Addison Lodge, Lon- don, and Woodfold Park, Lancashire, late M.P. for Blackburn, was solemnised at. St. Barnabas's, Kensington, on Wednesday. .The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Oswald Yerburgh, curate of St. Peter's, Raton-square, brother of the bride- groom. The Rev. RochfOrt Yerburgh, rector of ' High Bickington, North Devon, accompanied thel bridegroom as best man. The .wedding was very quiet owing to the serious Binges of the bride's father., Mr. Thwaites is a million:hire brewer, and ' Mrs. nirburgli is his only child. • A CYCLIST'S ADVENTURIC—Mr. J. B. Warren, the long distance cyclist, of Sr. Helens. had a curious Bank Holiday edventure. 'Precisely at midnighron Sunday, he set the wheels of his little Rudge tri- cycle in motion. Warrington 'MTN passed safely, and all went well until Hoo Green was reached (1-25 a.m.. 18 miles), when Mr. Warren's passage was completely blocked by the abrupt appearance of several pointed bayonets. Not 'relishing the idea of running into cold steel at the rate of 14 miles' an hour (this being the rate at which thescyclist was then travelling) he eased of?, hut before he hal time to recover his senses, he was dismounted and made a prisoner. Fortunately, his aggressors turned out to be Volunteer Cyclist sentries, who, after examin- ing his person, and closely inspecting his machine. satisfied themselves that he was not the " hearer of despatches to- the front," and with the welcome words, " Pass on, friend ; all's well," the cyclist was allowed to resume his peregrinations. Mr. Warren then proceeded through . Kentsford and Holmes Chapel to Church Lawton, where he took a wrong turn, and ultimately found hi to sel tin Talke- on-the-hill, Staffordshire. He made this the tern- jog point, and started back for Wiirrington, which was reached again at 6-5 a.m.—a good performance, a distance of 75 miles having been covered in airs. smine during the greater portion of which rain fell heavily. A stoppage was made at the Norton Arms Hotel for breakfast, after which another start was made, Mr. Aarren being joined' by 2ileesrs. F. W. Wilson and A. Makin. Proishara, was passed through, but on arriving at Chester. Mr. Warren, who was now scarcely eecognizable from the quan- tity of mud and water with which'he was covered, was strongly advised to abanden his ride. and, as the rain was then descending in , torrents. he re- solved to return home. via Frodsbam awl Warring- ' ton —total distance, 127 miles. It is to he regretted that " the pelting of the pitiless storm " rtiviered Mr. Warren hors de ront!mt, a.,A his achievement for the first 75 miles presaged tie ammulkliment of 1 the task which he had eet himself, viz:, .240 miles in 24 hours. All being well, Mr. Warren .expects to start from Land's End on his tricycle on 'Sunday (midnight), 12th instant, fx: John-e'-Groats. and will probably pass through Warrington late on Tuesday night or during the early hours of Wednes- day morning.

Mr. A. JORDAN, headmaster of ;St. Mary's Roman Catholic School, Warrington, has passed successfully the recent examinations for the -first B.A. degree in the University of London. He is, we understand, the only Catholic elementary schoolmaster ;who has obtained this distinction. SERVICE OF SONG AT HAVDOCK. On Sunday afternoon the choir of the Ettrlestown Primitive Methodist. Chapel paid a visit to the Primitive Methodist Caapel-at liairdock, for the purpose of giving the service of sacred song entitled "Rare , Metal." The chapel was 'crowded, and the manner in which the solos and choruses were rendered gave evident satisfaction. The choir was under the ' ;leadership of Mr. W. Banton, and Sir. T. Ormand officiated as reader. The service Was in aid of the trust funds. ANGLO-DANISII EXHIBITION AND FETE. The ; improvement in the weather has taken many thousands of visitors to London, a large proportion of whom have availed themselves of the opportu- nity of once more visiting the beautiful grounds at South Kensington attached to the; Anglo-Danish Ex- hibition. At dusk the grounds are converted into a veritable "fairy land!' The myriads. of prismatic gem lights, arranged in georgeous designs by Messrs. Pain awl Sms, the magnificent military I bands, the beauty. of the gardens' and lakes, the tasteful arrangement of the flowers, the oat-door amusements, provided With a lavish hand, the tab- bleaux vivants illustrating the fairy lore of Den- mark, form a combination not easy to excel. Ex- carsions to London are now frequent., and through tickets, including admission to the Exhibition, may bc Obtained. THE VACANCY AT LIVERPOOL.—Lord Claud John Hamilton. who has hithetto represented the West Derby division of Liverpool, has placed his resigna- tion of the seat in the hands of local Conservatives. The lion. W. U. Cross, eldest son of Viscount Cross has been chosen as the Conservative candidate for the West Derby Parliamentary Division of Liver- pool. On Tuesday evening Lord Claud Hamilton took leave of the constituency at a crowded meet- ing held in Beacon hall, Wavertree-road. Hon. ,W. H. Cross, in an election address issued on Wednesday, claims that, as the son of Lord Cross, who represen- ted• South-west Lancas:iire, he is no stranger 0 the constituency. Ile is an earnest supporter of the Church of England. He considers the maintenance of the union of England and Ireland under one Par- liament the question overshadowing all others, and acknowledges the loyal co-operation of Lord liar- lingtnn and the Liberal Unionists in support, of this policy. AZ, Liverpool, yesterday, the lion. William Henry Cross was nnminated, and was elected un- opposed for the West Derby Division.

Write for price list to the Sole Mannfaeturers, Coleman and Co., Norwich, who pay car- riage on any quantity to any part of the United Kingdom.- 4455. INQUICST ON Da. RIDLEY. Extraordinary evidence was given on Wednesday at the inquest on Dr. Ridley- Mr. William O'Brien, who was under examination the whole of the day, said Dr. Ridley was pale, frightened, and thoroughly wretched all the time he was in Tulla- more gaol. In fact the doctor told him that he had an uneasy, haunting feeling that it would end badly, and. that the govenor and every official in the gaol shared his wretchedness. It was monstrous and unnatural, Dr. Ridley said, to treat men in that manner ; but what could he do ? Every official, indeed, seemed to have a superstitious terror of the Prisons Board, and showed suspicion and distrust of each other. Palpably, Dr, Rid- ley thought of resigning,. When examining him in bed, and finding the suit of clothes, Dr. Ridley said : My God! wa are all ruined." Mr. O'Brien then described his treatment in prison, and the torture he suffered for weeks in suspense lest be should be attacked. Mr. Lane, M.P., deposed that when in Tullamore Gaol he was visited by Dr. Ridley, who told him that he was closely watched from Dublin, and asked him to 'give him per- mission to certify that he was fit for punishment. Wit- ness gave him that permission. Dr. Ridley brought to him roast fowl and sandwiches tied up in a hand- kerchief, and told hum that he had got into trouble and reprimanded for giving him exercise. Not only Mr. Lane, M.P., but Mr. Hooper, M.P., made sonic singular disclosures as to their harsh treatment in prison, andthe kindness they received from Dr. Ridley-, though every- thing he did to lessen their hardships seemed to 133 over- shadowed by fear of the authorities. It was Mr. Hooper's Opinion that Dr. Ridley had over-estimated Mr. Mande- ville's capacity to bear punisluneut, and that he dreaded investigation, and felt something akin to remorse. •

div.p: :BIOK FROM DRINKING PARIS WATER.

Mn. R. W. WOODRUFF, of 33, Glatney Esplanade, St. Petersport, Guernsey, writes :—" In 1879, by drinking the water in Paris, my blood was poisoned. I was taken sick there and had very hard work to reach Guernsey; when I did, I went right to bed and sent for a doctor, who, on seeing me, said I had rheumatic gout and that it was caused by my drinking the Paris water. After I got to bed it was three weeks • before I could raise my head from the pillow. In 1880 I was blind and helpless. In 1882 I' was helpless for six weeks; I had it every year from 1879 to 1836, and was a great sufferer. Nearly all this time I was under doctors. The latter ,lart of 1885 I be- gan to take "Warner's SAVE Cure" and am still taking it. since which I have had no rheumatic gout and have not had to call in the doctor. lam enjoying better health than I have done for years, and am sixty-nine years of age." The remedy which cured Mr. Woodruff can be pro- cured of all chemists, at 4s 6d per bottle, or of 11. If. Warner and Co., 86, Clerkenwell Road, London, EC.
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Holmes and Burgess. DRUNKXNNLSS.—James Kelly was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Irlam-st. on the previous evening; Mary Kelly, tramp, charged with a similar offence in Scotland-road, was dismissed on pro-

seising to leave the town. CHALLENGING THE WORKHOUSE Porerra.—Win. Parker, a rough-looking tramp, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at the Workhouse on the previous evening. It appeared that defendant applied for admit- bance, and as he was drunk the porter, Currie, refused to admit him. Prisoner attempted to fight him and a policeman was sent for, and the man was taken to the police station.—The Bench sent him to gaol for 14 days, with hard labour. Scnoot ArrEvnaxer Casxs.—The following cases were brought forward, Mr. Geo. Riley prosecuting on behalf of the School Attendance Committee :—The son of Thos. Harrison, coal-heaver, Winwick-road, was sent to the training ship •' Clio." Joseph Ellis. wiredrawer, Guar- dian-st., fined ss; Thomas (Heave, brewer, Erveiod-st., lined 5s for the third time; Edward Murray, forgeman, Winwick-road, fined 5s • P. Downey, forgeman. Pinners- brow, fined ss; Michael Flynn, forgeman, Bewsey-road, fined se; Joseph Knott, forgeman, Winwick-road, fined ss; William Jones, wiredrawer, Tanners-lane, fined ss; John Harrop, glass engraver, Battersbv-lane, fined ss. A warrant was issued for the apprehension of Wm. Higham, forgeman, Winwick-road. who failed to appear. MONDAT.—Before Aldermen Harrison and Holmes and Councillor Greening. DRUNKENNESS.—The following people were dealt with for this offence :—Sarah Wilkinson, near Sixpenny fields, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs; James Sullivan, in Scotland-road, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs; Eizabmil Brown, in Horsemarket-st, on Saturday even- ing, fined 5s including costs; James Barrow, in Butter- market-st. on Saturday night, fined Sc including costs; John Donlan, in Buttermarket-st. on Saturday night, anti for assaulting William Burrows whilst assisting the police, fined 40s and costs or one month with hard labour; Joseph Warburton, in Winwicn-st, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs; Ann Whatley, in Winwick-St, on Saturday night, fined Sc and costs; Patrick Egan, in Irlam-st, on Sunday morning, fined 5s and costs; Mau- rice Lynch, on Friars' Green, on Sunday morning, fined 5s including costs. BRUTAL TURATMENT OF A MOTHER.—JOIIII Conway was charged on warrant with having used threats to Nomh Conway, his mother. Prisoner said he did not remem- ber whether he did or not; he was drunk. Complainant stated that the prisoner broke two chairs and a table over her. The magistrates ordered him to find two sure- ties of £lO each for his good behaviour, or to go to pri- son for a month. EDUCATION PHOSECUTION.—John Hiram was brought up on warrant, charged with having neglected to send his child, James, to school. The boy, with the consent of the father, was ordered to be sent to the ship " Clio." SUSPECTED THEFTS FROM FARMERS.—WiIIiam Yates was brought up charged with having been drunk in Lyme-st, on Saturday night. Prisoner, pleaded guilty. Tile Chief-constable stated that the prisoner might have been brought up on two other charges, but he was not held responsible for his actions, as he was subject to ser- iolsl fits. On Saturday afternoon, the prisoner, who was a carrier and errand-man for the Market people, was in- structed byjames Woodward, farmer and cheese-factor, Weaverham, with a basket containing 14ilbs of cheese, of the value of 10s. This the prisoner was ordered to take to a man named Aaron Jones, in Stamford-st. The prisoner returned to Mr. Woodward, drunk, and said that he had taken the parcel, but it was discovered that he had not done so. The matter was reported to the police and the prisoner was arrested in Lyme-st. The basket containing the cheese was found late that night, after Yates had been taken into custody, on the Market Hall steps. The prisoner had also been entrusted by James Heyes, a Penketh farmer, with a parcel of grocer- ies, to be Laken to the 'bus near the Blackburn Arms. This parcel also had not reached its destination. There was, however, no evidence to show that the prisoner had deliberately stolen the parcels, and so he was only brought up on the charge of drunkenness. He (Mr. Hunt) thought that people should not trust Yates, as he was not deserving of any sympathy. The Bench ordered prisoner to go to gaol for a month, with hard labour. WEDNE3DAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough and 'Alderman
Burg.

ASSAULT BY A SHIP CANAL 7 NAVVY.—John Stringer, a labourer on the Ship Canal, was charged with having I been drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road on the previous night, and also with assaulting P.C. Evans at the same time and place. It appeared that the constable found the prisoner drunk in a tripe shop in Wilderspool- road, where he was creating a disturbance "about some change, and frightening a little girl who was left in charge of the shop. On the officer putting him out, prisoner became very disorderly and struck him several times, tearing off three buttons from his coat, and snatching his policeman's whistle away. Prisoner said that he did not remember the assault at all, as he had been very drunk. He was fined 5s and costs for the drunkenness, and 103 and costs for the assault. BEGGING EXPOSED.—JamPs Casey was charged with begging in Rylands-at. on the previous evening. P.C. Monaghan stated that the prisoner had with him two ,children, whe were singing whilst prisoner was begging for coppers. He spoke to the children, and found that Casey had brought them from Manchester to sing for him. He allowed them to go on promising to return there. The prisoner made a living in that way. The Bench ordered him to prison for one month. with hard

labour. CHEAP RAILWAY TRAVELLING.—John Crompton, an old man, was charged with having traVelled in a third class 'carriage from Widnes to Warrington without paying his /are, thus defrauding the London and North-Western Railway Company to the amount of ed. The Chief Constable said he did not believe prisoner was respon- sible for his actions. Several questions were put to the prisoner by the Bench, which he answered in a rambling manner. Ile was ordered to be taken to the Work- houSe. THREATS.—Thomas Hennessy was brought up on war- rant charged with having used threats to Jane Riley on the 29th July. Complainant said that she and defend- ant had been neighbours, but she had" flitted "for fear Of him. The magistrates ordered defendant to find a surety of £5 for his good behaviour during the ensuing six months. TIMSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Councillor Greening. THErr BY A CARTER.--James Ward, a carter, was sent to prison for a month for having stolen a cardigan jac- ket belonging to another carter named Reuben Wilson, whilst in St. James-st., Latchford. She said that.because his dinner was not just ready her husband struck her and threatened to kill her. She denied having said to him when he came home "no work, no grub." div.head: NOTES BY ME WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY ME WAY.

On Wednesday the third days' play in the contest be- tween Yorkshire and Middlesex was commenced at Bramall-lane. Overnight Middlesex had lost three wickets for 84 runs, having seven wickets to fall and 54 runs to obtain to win. Forty minutes' play was sufficient to settle the encounter, Middlesex gaining a well-deserved victory by six wickets. On the same day a highly creditable victory went to the account of Gloucester at Clifton, Sussex losing ths return match by seven wickets. In direct contrast to the matches decided re- cently, the one under notice has produced some heavy scoring, and in all the 33 wickets that have fallen have produced as many as 951 runs or an average of nearly 30 The Kentish eleven suffered defeat at the hands of the Australians. Only twenty minutes' play was neces- sary to finish the game, the last three wickets of the home team only adding 15 runs, and the innings closed for 80, Australians thus winning by 81 runs. The match Notts v. Surrey was soon over, and Surrey gained a de- cisive victory by 78 runs. Notts, who had four Iwickets to fall, lost them in less than half an hour for 14

The Warrington Cycling Club have their fifty miles road race to-day (Saturday). About a dozen entries have been received, and, as the prizes are valuable, a god contest is expected. Considering the state of the weather on Monday, the Warrington Football Club scored a success in their annual athletic festival, which was attended by a large number of spectators. The events were well conteNted, and were watched with interest, but the weather was sufficiently- wet and dull as to damp the spirits of most people. Details of the sports will be found in another column. .

It seems to be generally admitted that the cyclist vol- unteer manceuvras have gone far to demonstrate that cyclists may be useful from a military point of view even in face of adverse conditions. They show, at all events that the wheelmen can keep the road and do a very creditable forced march even in spite of wind and rain and mud and darkness. It is true that twenty- eight or thirty miles—the distance from Crewe to War- rington—in five and a half hours is far from record time, yet it is doubtful if any other branch of military ser- vice could have accomplished thy feat under similar cir- cumstances. .

Most of the amateur warriors when they reached War- rington on Sunday morning were in a sorry plight, and in turning out a few hours later to clean the mud-bespat- tered machines and accoutrements they had a rather un pleasant foretaste of the exigencies of military life. In most cases, however, the inconveniences were cheerfully put up with though it is said that in one in- stance at least one of ;he contingent "cleared out" al- together on Sunday mornin., disgusted, as he expressed it, at "the whole blooming business." This young man had evidently mistaken his vocation, which was not to be one of the defenders of her Majesty's realm, but one of the defended.

Har- rison; Councillors Dakin. Greening. Jolley, Dixon, Blackburst, J. V. Taylor, Barker, HutchinEon, W. Pierpoint, Monks, J. Pierpoint, J. Slmw Green, Wright, Ashton, Bolton, Heaton. J. Taylor,. STREET INPROtEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE.

This committed recommended that the following plans be approved —Shop in Sankey-at., for Mr. Hutton Wright; iron shed in W-st. for Mr. Thomas Williams; workmen's home in St. gary's-road, Latch- ford, for Mr. A. Bruchemite ; alterations to building in Rose and Crown-st., for Mr. Joseph Dobson ; stables (amended plan) in White-st., for Mr. Henry offices, and addition to works, for the Castle Rubber Company, Limited. The following report of the Ligh- ting Sub-committee, which was approved and adopted: —The Lighting Sub-committee recommend—that two lamps be erected in Lincoln-st. ; that two new lamps in Leonard-st. ; that one new lamp at borough boundary, Manchester-road. Resolution "that, in the opinion of this committee it is desirable that so ninch of the surph.n land in Bridge-4, south of the Roe Buck Hotel, as will enable the Corporation to construct a street through that land to Wilson Patten-st., be not sold at present.' Also, "that the offer of Mr. J. B. Isaac, for the purchase of a plot of surplus land in .Bridge-st., at £1,?06' 13s 4d, be accepted. Councillor PLArr moved the confirmation of the minutes. Ile said the Council would be glad to-see that at last the Corporation had been able to sell a portion of the surplus land in Bridge-st. The price- was not quite so much as the committee would have liked, but it was the best offer they had got, and probably the first pur- chaser had got anadvantage. Taking into account the whole amount of land, back and front, the price amounted to £2 lOs per yard, but if they considered the front land to consist of about 70 feet, it amounted to about £3 per yard for that portion. The plot sold im- mediately joined the site of the Roebuck Inn on the Market Gate side. Referring to the recommendation of the committee with regard to the proposed street from Bridge-st. to Wilson Patten-et., he said it must not be lost sight of that they had no right of way for carriages or vehicles around by Arpley Station, and on certain days in the year the London and North-Western Railway Co., to preserve their rights, stopped up the road and made people ask permission for using it. Some years ago there was a great outcry against the dangers of the shunting operations which took place at the bottom of Bold-st., and that might be revived at any time, for the railway company had the right of shunting, and they would be within their right if they blocked up the road- way entirely with their wagons with the exception of the footpath. Mr. Platt also referred to the advantages of the proposed new street in case tramways were to be introduced into the borough, as it would enable :the trams to go right along, to Penketh without coming into the narrow streets at Market Gate. The committee had already offers oh hand from all the parties interested in the land over which the new street would go, but these were not yet accepted, and having entered into details as to, the various items, he said the total cost, including paving, &c., would be about £4,606 ss. All the Council was asked to do that night, how„ger, was to sanction the proposal of the committee that so much of the land in Bridge-st. as would enable the Corporation to con- struct the street should not be sold at present. Referring to the plan of Mr. Hutton Wright of a shop in Sankey- st., Mr. Platt added that Mr. Wright was not willing to set the shop back 4ft. 6in., as it would place the shop in a recess, but he thought the committee would get two feet or three feet at a reasonable price—£.20 or £3o— they were prepared to take that rather than nothing at all. Councillor GREENING seconded the adoption of the 1 minutes. Councillor JORN PIERPOINT thought they ought to have property set back to lines that would be convenient to the public., He thought that and other matters that had happened within the past few years showed the desira- bility ,of the committee being alive to the propriety of making provision for the widening of the streets of the borough.
Councillor WRIGHT quite agreed with the remarks of Councillor J. Pierpoint, but said that to set the shop re- ferred to so very far back would very much reduce its value. •

Councillor MONIS hoped the conunittee would have the shop set hack to the line ultimately intended. In a case not long ago the committee insisieci on property being set back to a line to suit the requirements of the town, and he did not see why Mr. Hutton Wright should not be compelled to do the same thing. Councillor PLATT, in replying, said he thought the im- provement in the width of Sankey-st. would have to be made on the other side. At the same time they would like to get the shop in question in a line with the corner of Legh-st. which would take about 4ft. 6in., but any one could see this would be a very great injury to Mr. Hutton Wright's property. . The MAYOR thought it would be advisable to take 21 t. or 3ft. if they could get it. The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

This committee's minutes contained following items : —That at the request of Mr. William Pierpoint, the brook running in front of his house in Wash-lane be covered in; that the tender of Messrs. John Collin and ' Son, for the erection of house, office, storeroom, and boundary wall at the.rard in Wharf Meadow, at £520. be accepted; that the Borough Surveyor prepare plans, specifications, and estimates for the forming and paving of the following streets t.—Gerteral-st., Eldon-st., Wil- liam-st., Back William-st., Back Crosley-et. ; that the Town Clerk serve the necessary noticiN, and take all proceedings under the Public health Act, for the form- ing and paving of Selby-st. and for the recovery of the , expenses incurred by the Corporation in the event of the owners being in default. Alderman DAVIES moved, and Councillor Asirros seconded the confirmation orthe minutes. Councillor F. A. Ile be- lieved that this ejector had only' been worked intermit- tently during the past three years, and. he. failed to see why the Paving and Sewerage Cbmmittee. should allow such charges to be made on its funds wheulthey got no- thing in return. The MAYOR pointed out that these charges:had nothin to do with the minutes of the committee. Councillor W. PlaripoiNT said he.had been' assured in that chamber and out of it that those' annual accounts were presented to the Council; and in. that case he claimed his right to call attention to any single.particu- lar in them. The MAYOR said the charge,: had'been brought before the Council in the committee's minutes, Councillor W. PIERPOINT had no doubt they had, but that was the first occasion he had' had the opportunity of calling attention to them. • The MAYOR: Ido not think you are. quite' in order; these have nothing to do with the present minutes, Councillor W. PIERPOINX said he had said nearly ail he wanted to say. The MAYOR said he wanted VS call attention tothe-fact that there was nothing on the minutes bearing regrence to those charges. Councillor W. PIERPOINT : You rule then thatthese•ac- counts are not presented to the Council. ' The MAYOR: Not now. Councillor Bovroit : They are ,only. waste paper. (Laughter). Councillor BARKER: IS it true Aar thi:s ejector. has only worked intermittently during the last three years.? The MAYOR: That is a question that may be asked the Chairman. Councillor Mcevits: But it is not on the minutes. (Laughter). Alderman DAVIES : Never mind, the technicalities: of

• debate; I will give the best reply I can. In the first place with regard to the cellar mentioned by 'Mr. W. Pierpoint, they were now advised by the Town Clerk that it was within the responsibility of the, committee to deal with the cellar, and they would therefore, act upon that advice. (Hear, hear)... With regard to the top ejec.- tor—that beyond Black Bear bridge—it had only worked intermittently, and he thought that' had: been brought about by the extraordinary demands uponthe powers of' the engine at the gas works to eject the excreta from 'the intercepting depots. (Hear, - hear, and a. voice: It should have been charged to the Sanitary Committee). They would make some further inquiries as to whether. they were being " done " by the, Gas Committee: (Laughter). With regard to Councillor F: %A. Roberts" reference to Knutsford-road, the macadb.rn for the necessary repairs had been bought and was on its was,. and in fact the work was in hand. The minutes were then confirmed. At a meeting of the To;;;;; 11111111 l Park, and ' Baths Com- mittee, the BATHICREITIL reported that the income ffom. the Baths during the past six weeks was £313.4 VP: and for the corresponding period last year £836 lid. The committee resolved " that the wall in front of the :Town Hall be removed, and a suitable palisade substituted in Lieu thereof, in accordance with the plan NO. .1; at an estimated cost of £470." Or, as an alternative : "That the wall in front of the Town Hall be removed': and'a. suitable palisade substituted in lieu thereof, in fieeor, dance with the plan No. 2, at an estimated 'cost of £250." _ .

The MAYOR proposed the c.onfirmation of the minutes. Plan No. 1, referred to in the minutes, he said, provided for taking down the wall from gate to gate: andthe. setting back of the palisading 20 feet: The alternative. plan provided for the taking down of the wall between the shrubs, and the making of the proposed paiSades on the same level as the present wall. The public seemed to be in favour of the wall being pulled &into Aid he thought that it would prove to be a great benefit. Alderman 114RMION seconded the proposition: Councillor J. Fle did not think that the expenditure of £470 in this way would be of any• benefit to %the street. lie did not thiiik it right to the ratepayers that they should spend £470 in that manner on a thing that was not absolutely necessary. They could not affprd to. pay for a fad of that kind. Let.those who wished tepult down the walTpay for it. The Towx: Creaa, in answer to Counieittor Grrenitig, said that they could not take any part of • the recreation ground without the consent of the Treasury; and possibly - the Charity-Commissioners also. Councillor.PLATT thought that there were plenty better ways of spending the money than by pulling dbwn the wall. rte-dld not think that either of the proposed pilule, was the right one to adopt. Councillor Jor.LEy said he thought it was thepopular, wish that the wall shan't /come down.

Councillor F. A. ROBERTS pointed out that when the jubilee•subscriptions came in the committeefbund that the wall scheme had not opened thepurse• strings of the public, so widely, and the sum contributed was only suf- ficient to defray the cost of the demonstration. Councillor BARBER. said that he should support the pulling down of tho•wall if the committee hada definite plan in view. Alderman Hotxr,s' thought it would be an unnecessary k expenditure. He added that the cost of paving the street ' after the wall was• milled dawn would be about £230, in addition to the £1170.• Councillor Heaton, Councillor Pereira, and Councillor Francomb having spoken on the minutes, The MAYOR said that the £47o* did not include the making of the street, which corould cost about £l4O. Alderman ffautusoN said that not to remove the wall

was a reproach to Warrington and a slur upon its good taste, public spirit, and enterprise. He hoped that the commonsense of the Council would vote in favour of its adoption. Couneiflor MoN-Es suggested that the committee should withdraw the resolution, and bring forward a well matured scheme for opening up the front of the Town Hall in such 4 manner that it could be utilised either in wet or damp weather for musical performances. Alderman DAVIES thought that about one in a thousand desired the taking down of the wall, and that about 99 per cent, of that one in the thousand were writers to the newspapers. If it was decided to pull down the wall it would be a success of agitators, and not the voice of Warrington. The amendment was then put. div.p: MARKETS COMMVTEE..

At a meeting of this committee it was reported that the total income from all sources daring- the four weeks ending 23rd July was £289 1.7 s 11d. The report was adop- ted on the motionof Councillor Daatti;.second'edby Coun- cillor BLACKIIIIR:ST. GAS COMMITTEE: RESIGNATION, OF /MISERS. The minutes of the' Gas Committee comprised the fol- lowing letter from Mr. Paterson :—t' Warrington, 6th July. 1838. The members of the Gas Conurittee. Gentlemen,—l feel that I cannot leave•without con- veying to you my very cordial thanks for many past favours, and my best wishes for year future pros- perity. I regret T cannot accede to the • conditions im- posed by the Town Council, and venture to' hopenay re- fusal will not inconvenience you.—Faithfully yours, James Parnasof.',' [On this date Mr. Paterson,retired from the management of the works, and Me: laddock commenced his duties as gas engineer.] At' 3 meeting held on the 10th July, minute: The Gas Committeehav- ing received the amendment passed iv; the Town Council relative to the report presented by them, and consider- ing that it is a direct vote of want of confidenceriwthem,i the following members of the committee hereby'tender their resignations : Aldermen Holmes, Webster, Pick- mere, and Chandler; Councillors Barker; . Greening, F. A. Roberts, and Wright. ' Alderman Flozat' as in proposing the confirmation of the minutes of the Gas Committee, said it would tern- membered that a very strong discussion took place in-the Council over certain proposals which the Gas Conireittee made as to the future management Of the as works,but finally the committee carried their resolution. Unfortu- nately, immediately after that an amendment was pro- posed to their. minutes asking them to withdraw the re- solution which they had proposed before, and bring, in another recommending that the allowance to Mi. Pater- son should be continued for only twelve months. It was. utterly impossible for the committee, having considered the question so closely, to bring forward a fresh scheme for they had told the Council very emphatically that the scheme which they had erg carried was what they con- sidered to be the best under the circumstances; niAhe interests of the Gas Committee, and, through theing.of the ratepayers at large. They, therefore, considered that there was no other course open to them than to plate. themselves before the Council, to give them a chance,, if they saw cause, to accept their resignations. If;the Council chose to accept the resignations well and good;. but if, on the other hand, they chose to retain their con- fidence in the committee, the latter would continue -to work for the interests of the welfare of the town, an they had worked in the past. Councillor Winarr seconded the adoption of " the. minutes.

Alderman DAVIES, prior to moving a resolutionil.saidi that at the time the Corporation bought the works he total quantity of gas made was 119,008,500 cubic feet, of which there was sold 102,005.208 cubic feet, showing a leakage of 17,003,294 cubic feet, •or 148 per cont. ; -so that the management of the works whilst under.theo control of the Gas Committee had shown no depreciatibn ' whatever. The•leakage he had mentioned included loss- I, on publiclamps—that was, the difference between.the quantity charged for and that actually consumed. That .had remained to this day, and it was a fact that there had absolutely been a loss to the Gas Committee on.o.the :charge for the lighting of lamps in the borough. In are- port published at the time the works were purchasedi.he read, "We may here observe that the company's pro- perties and effects are in first-class order and condition;: indeed, we have learnt that the plant has been airiest entirely renewed during the last twelve years." That 'statement upset the theory that they were buying old , land rotten works. The next thing was that they-not , only-bought a company which was, or its effects were; :producing £6,661 a year. but they bought a concern ,which had a balance of £lO,BOO to its credit. He admit- tad that it was affected by a loan of £5,000 and likewise by a sum Of £2,700 which they paid in cash, but'the fact remained that there was an income of £8,6611. for. which they gave £0,120, leaving a margin of abont•£s4o" per annxtur in the interests of the borough. (Hear,, hear.) The Committee which drew up the report from which he quoted estimated that in ..eight. ,years it would end in a profit of £7,'128 to the-Corporation. At the end of last year. after the, 'annuities and sinking bind, which amounted to £.111:008',. had been paid, the surplus was not £7,128, but £113;3191 ft addition to that they had reduced the price of gas-no .less than 3d per 1,000 twice over—that was, -fiel-per 1,000 less than perhaps it would have been had the company still owned the workii. could well understand that the feelings of the Corn- mittee had been very much annoyed and grieved ba the action of the °outside public who had contributed letters to nevrspapers. He WAS pleased to think that the. Conned was independent of any adverse influences from such people. The letters and the action of the people he- referred to had done a great amount of injary;.for. 'they appealed to the unthinking portion of the public:. and' put then] against those who were trying to de good' to-the-town. There was a great amount of mischief' done-by ignorant people to a class even more ignorant tharutheinsetves. He had seen a placard on the walla of the- town 'fivgrgich the names of the best men in that Council' were set forth to be kicked out on the first op- portunity. Did-they moan -to tell him that was, a4proper thing forth* outside public to do in regard toa,•.commit- tee which had done all he had mentioned for the town?' Proconsiclered that it was most offensive, annoying;,and, very-wrong indeed. Taking all those facts into conside- ration, he nonsidered the Council would be perfectly. justified in passing the followinc, amendment•-i--"-That the minutes of the Gas Committee be confirmed; withit the exception of the minute of the 10th July; which reads as' follows :—"The Gas Committee having-received the amendment passed by the Town Council' relative to. the-report presented' by them, and considering that- it. Is• a direct vote of want of confidence in them,‘ the-follovx- ing•members of the-committee hereby tender their-resig- nations :—Aldermen Holmes, Webster_ Pink-mere,. and , Chandley ; Councillors Barker, Greening, Roberts: and Wright ;' and that the Council now expresses unabated and unreserved confidence in the committee, with the earnest request that all the members of. the-committee wilt continue to Mit* their valuable services as hereto- fore-for the benefit of the Corporation, town, and neigh- bor:l.llo°d." Councillor Ptsvor seconded the amendrnent,, and said he had the fullestconfidence in the ceirunitteftailialloPed tlika• would continue the work In which they had been of the. very greatest use to the town. In moving hisansend- ment on the previous occasion heohad- noiniteation of expressing anyvote of want of confidence ia the com- mittee. (Hear,.hear.) Alderman CIEDISFIELD said he should be grieved beyond everything if Alderman Holmes thought the. Coutteil had in any- way lost confidence in him, Alderman Holmes had been one the most valuable servants of the Cor- poration he had known for tee, last 3Ct years, and it would be base ingratitude on the • part of the Council if they did not respect him. He supported Alderman Davies's amendment, and trusted the Chairman of the ' committee. would be satisfied that the Council had just as much confidence in him as-they had ever had. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON was sorry to think the members of the Gas Committee were sovery thin-skinned as to want a vote of confidence passed in them. If that was the kind of feeling which existed,, the members of the Council ought to accept their resignation. At the same time he should be sorry to) see them retire•in such a spirit. Councillor F. A. ROPRIITS said he- admitted the right of the Council to criticize. the action of the Gas Or any other Committee. He was glad the Council took such AA in- terest in the committee of which he was a member,, and made them give a good reason for everything they did ; but he said deliberately, as a junior spember, and with- out having had the same experience others had hack that the Council had made a mistake they could not rectify with regard to the expenditure. A letter appeared On the minutes from -Mr. Paterson declining to accept the resolution paiied at' the last meeting of the Counpil, and refusing to remain under any terms practically as con- sulting engineer. He said deliberately that in his opinion Warrington had lost £4OO or £5OO a year by the with- drawal of Mr. Paterson's,. services. ("Oh,. oh.") Other gas works would only,have been too glad to engage Mr. Paterson as consulting engineer at a sum considerably higher than £lOO a year. Alderman HARRISON said he thought Councillor Roberts had taken an extreme view of the question. For him to say they had lost £4OO or .1:500 a year because Mr. Paterson was leaving them, absolutely gave the lie to what Mr. Paterson himself had Said% for when he rer

commended the Council t take Mr. Haddock he charac- terized hilin as a person fully competent Lu every respect to discharge the duties of the office. He (Mr. Harrison) did not believe there was a committee of the Council which took a more earnest or a more conscientious in- tere:it in the welfare of the town and in the duties en- trusted to them than the members of Hi., Gas Com- mittee.

Councillor F. A. ROBERTS : I did not reflect upon Mr. Haddock. or his management. I believe he will be a good Manager. The proposition of Alderman DAVIES was then carried 11/13/IiIDOLISIy. THE CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The minutes of the ilivers Committee contained the following report of the borough surveyor, prepared at the request of the committee :—" I have carefully con- sidered the Ship Canal Mans and Act as far as it affects Warrington, and beg to report that matters appertaining to the borough are well protected by section 88, pages 126 to 133, in the Ship Camel Act. As far as your com- mittee are concerned, the company are bound by sub- sectimt 14, sec. 88, to dredge the bed and banks of the river between the eastern and western boundaries of the borough to give a depth of eight feet of water at low water of spring, tides, and to ever after maintain the same. This will enable vessels cf, say 150 tons, to lock in and out of the proposed canal at any period of the tides. , The distance between the principal outlet SCVPIT of the borough arta the deepening at the western boundary is 880 yards. How far this will perneit the deposit of sew- age matter le what may be termed a pond experience will have to prove, but seeing that the Corporation have the jornt control over the sluices which have to he constructed in the locks at ITalton and Latchford (see sub-sections 15; 18, 17, 18) for the purpose of maintaining the water at a depth of 0 feet, and also to ensure the flow of water mentioned itr sub- section 12, I do not consider there is ant" cause for alarm in connection witlethe impounding of the sewage. The principal sub-sectictr which affects your 30mmittee is No. 12, referring to the abstraction and diversion of the water flowing down the river. The minimum quantity stated, viz., 100,000,000 cuble feet in 24 hours,ds abave what may be termed the dy weather flow. I consider it would be advisable todake observations, and obtain the flow of water before any diversion of theriver waters takes place, and that the mode of guaging should be de- cided upon, and overtures then made to the Ship Canal Company to carry out sub-section 13 of sec. 18." Having, regard to the contemplated immediate disuse, of the Old' Quay Canal by the Manchester Ship Canal Co.:, the com— mittee resolved "That th'etown clerk and borough sur— veyor be instructed to correult Mr. J. Wolfe Barry upon the Warrington Clauses or the Manchester Snip Canal Act, particularly with respect to the sections as to the abstracting of water from the river, and the fixing of proper guages for testing the flow of water past Howley ' Quay."

div.head: LATH MR. WARRINGTON WOOD.
div.p: THE LATH MR. WARRINGTON WOOD.

With reference to the Offer of Mrs Warrington,wood , of original plaster casts from,the works of her late hus- band, the MAYOR reported that Mr. Chorley had ar:Anged to have one cast brought from, Rome to Warrington in order to ascertain the cost of trtusit. The Council then rose.
WARRINGTON AND TifF. SHIP CANAL.

It is generally admitted that the future of War- rington, with Ls various trades and interests, will be "for weal or woe very deeply affected by the construction of the Ship Canal. The Corporation, or at all events the River Committee of the (~orp- oration have, it will be seen from Sour report of the meeting of the Town Council held this week, had under consideration some of the possible conse- • quences to the town of the making of the canal. , The Borough Surveyor report& to them that " mat- 1 ters appertaining to the borough are well protec- ted" in the Ship Canal Act. ia independent peru- sal of those portions of the Act having reference to Warrington will, we should thiak, amply confirm the opinion of the Borough Surveyor. Apparently those who had the framing of the clauses of the Act for the "protection of the Corporation, traders,&c.," of Warrington, have, as far as human prevision can go, very effectively safeguarded the interests of the borough. In the present article we will briefly glance at tone of the provisions•ia the Canal Act for the protection of Warrington. RIGHT TO 1.1,5 E THE:-CANAL.

"The traders, manufacturers, and all other per- sons now or hereafter carrying on business at or near Warrington" will, in the future, or at all events as long as the proseot Act ,holds ,good, have the right to use the portion of the ,Ship Canal between the entraree to Warrington docks and Eastham, and also the entrance locks to •the canal at Eastham when available, and when these locks- are not available they.tizill have a right to enter the canal from the Meney estuary at any of the locks between the Old Qesy docks, at Run- 'corn and Eastham. After the Mersey has been 'deviated from its present course into a new channel which is. to be cut across Arpley Meadows, part of the-old channel towards Wilderspool will be utilised in the making of the Warrington docks. At the , south eastern end of the docks,..not far from the village of Lower Walton, there will be a communi- cation by means of locks between the docks and the Mersey at. the point where it will again run into its old course neat Walton Arches. The right to use this means of communication between the docks, and the. river is secured!.to the "traders, manufacturers, &c.," of Warrington for any vessels which are of not more than one hundred and fifty tons burthen upon payment of atoll for each jour- ney up and down the canal (inclu4ing the use of ,the locks) of not exceeding fourpence per ton of cargo. In, case the vessel carries no cargo, or less than twenty tons of cargo, the toil-it shall be liable topay will not exceed rive shillings for each jour- ney. And, farther, in case toll to the-amount of not lessthan one pound has been paid in respect of a cargo carried: up or down the canal the vessel will be-entitled to-return without any. cargo free of 'toll. These conditions and tariff are, however, only ap- plicable to vessels solely employl.,•d in navigating or trading between the eastern boundary of the borough of Warrington and any dock or place situate on the Mersey. below Warrington.. The traders and manufacturers of Warrington will have the same rights to the. use of the canal and locks with regard to, vessels that may be engaged in conveying their :commodities, to, any port outside the-Mersey, or from any port outside the Mersey to Warrington, but the toll they may be liable to pay in this case will be . dloubled—that is to say, eightpcnce per ton of cargo. I It is laid down that the tonnage butrthen of a vessel ,isto be ascertained in the follcwing manner. The. I master of the vessel will have to-deliver to the per- son appointed by the Ship Can.alCompany to receive .tolls, a declaration in writing stating the greatest weight of cargo which such .vessel is capable of !carrying, and the weight of sv.k.li cargo will be taken :as the tonnage burthen of the ~vessel. Any master. who shall fail, to deliver these-declarations or certil6l cates will, be liable to a penallyaust exceeding forty shillings,, and for delivering al• false certificate he• will be liable to a penalty not exceeding twer' pounds. BIGHT TO PRIVAIR WHARVES.

The Can-al Company will not be entitled to charge wharfage rates upon any gocds or animals land at or shipped at any private quays, wharves, or Ica, ding places now existing won the banks of the Mersey,at Warrington, between Bank Quay and the. eastern.boundary of the borough above Rowley Weir, cr at or from any pritcate quays, &c., which .may hereafter be constructed upon the banks. of the Mersey at Warrington, including the diverted: courso of the river across Arpley Meadows. ITzcept by the consent of the owners or other persons using thesoprivate quays, the tAnal Company will, "not be entitled to.any exclusive or other right obload- lug disbharging vessels., thereat, or of performing any services whatever in aonnection with the-same.' It la farther provided, however, that any oh these private quays, &c., which may be hereaften• con- structed must be constructed in accordarce, with tkoprovisions of the Canal Act with respect to. the construction of wharves by owners. USE OF BRIVATE TUGS.

Subject to the grant of licenses by the Canel Com- loony, and to their bye-laws, the "traders and. manu- facturers, or other persons now carrying on business at or near Warrington" will be at liberty to use within the canal or the Warrington dock, the steam barges, tugs, or other power belonging to, them and employed for towing barges, lighters, or flats with- in the same. In the event of Iliffmeaces arising with respect to the graWing of these- licenses, the differences are to be referred to some, person nomi- nated by the chairman for the time being of the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners, whose I decision shall be binding on the parties. NO HOSTILE TARIFFS.

Experience has shown that great carrying corn- panies—sueh as the Ship Canal o:ow:Reny will be in time to come—have often the power, if they are so minded, of doing very material injury to a town or district, or to particular classes of traders, by setting up hostile or differential tariffs. Warrington is. however, proter;ted from contingencies of this de- scription by the terms ot the Canal Company's Act. It is there enacted that "it any reduction be made by the company in the maximum canal tolls, autho- rised in the fourth schedule to this Act, upon cargo conveyed on the canal to or from Manchester, or if any reduction be made in the tolls which may from tithe to time be actually so levied, the com- pany shall, at the same time, make a proportionate tt.a.telnent in the tolls to cargo conver4 ia tike

manner to or from Warrington ; so that, in all eases of reduction in the company's saidltariff, there shall be charged in respect of Warrington traffic no more than the proportion of the "ales fixed in such schedule as between Warrington and Manchester traffic."

div.head: ARE DOCTORS INCREDULOUS?
div.p: ARE DOCTORS INCREDULOUS?

'Mrs. E. A. lligham, 58, Brougham-st., West Gcr- ton, near Manchester, relates a most remarkalAe coincidence respecting her daughter, aged twelve years, who fell and injured her knee so badly, that her medical attendants, in consultation, decided that it would be necessary to perform an operation on the knee, to replace certain ligaments which had been severely in- jured and distended. To this the family strongly objected.. She was taken to the Southern Hospital, Clif- ford-st., Otford-road, where the combined medical faculty dixided it was a case of paralysis of the knee, and that she would doubtless never walk again. She was accordingly discharged as incurable', a confirmed cripple. Some time after this her parents. were induced to try St. SactAls Oil, which greatly benefited her. In a month she began to walk with the aid of a stick, and three weeks kter she was able to walk as well as ever, being perfectly cured. This was in June, 1888, but the mother did not make the fact known to the proprietors of St. Jacobs Oft until December 10th, 1887, as the doc- tors told her at the hospital that it would not be a per- manent cure, but as the child has continued strong and well for over a year and a half, she feels perfectly strfe in stating that a compete cure has been effected mlely And wholly by the use.of St. Jacobs Oil. The motherstates that tho doctors and others who did not think she-would ever walk agaia have called to see her, for they- could hardly believe that a cure had been effected.
