div.p: CALIFORNIA AS A PLACE FOP); EMIGRANTS. BY M. WHITIIAM.

The importance :at this question demands that it: should receive further' notice. I find from recent issues of the "Examiner,' that Mrs. Parker has been' ' compelled to admit im her lectures, that it was not advisable to direct farther emigration towards San Francisco, and Los Angeles. This, your readers will remember, was the advice-I felt called upon to give . during the time this lady was helping the b.)om that was Started in the interests of land speculators. In your issue a March 'MTh, "One who likes fair- play" thought it right to call in question not only my statements, but those-of a gentleman resident in Los Angelos ; I hope the-report of the Leeds lac- tare, to which I refer, has- helped to satisfy the gentleman as to the truthlof my statements. Booming in California is a peculiar institution. Its, peculiarity arises out of the fact that large sums of money are spent by land speculators, who, in their turn, are helped by the railway authorities. It paysthe two to arrange fore "Free round trips" to certain districts, where "free lunch is provided. liaise. pays to give premiumeto parties having pur- chased "lots," to hicluce others: to do likewise. Hun- dreds of "lots" are bought unseen, and thrown up again by the purchasers rather than pay taxes for land far away from water or irrigation. The rain- faith} certain districts of the- State is limited to about' three months in the year; and with an almost vertical san, your readers mayguess what the re- sult'is.. Fruit growing is the, chief industry fol- lowed, but the labour attenditlg this is not sufficient to-attract emigrants. Fruit is plentiful, we in the . city having apricots and peaches. ad libitum. I am told I can know nothing of LGlii Angelos, it being 500Aralea away. In a sense this may be so, but • wnat can Mrs. Parker know of it? A lady in her position, must of necessity be entirely in the hands ob her acquaintance. and these are itist the people who have to gain by the"booming'frand. When Mrs. . Pdrker first set out on her mission, her statement thet "lady helps" were required.. The phrase was newt°, us in England, and contained a hidden mean- " lonesome wealth" requiring com- pany, and a little drawing-room fussiness. As a r matter of fact, what was wante6 were strong girls, for downright hard work. "Servant girlism " is not known here as it is in England) My own girls have been told that" If they wanted their day oat they had better go back to England for it." High wages are made up by employing fewer-servants, in large houses.. Mare than this, Los Angeles, beautiful as it is as a place for residence, is not devoid of the curse-of large towns, the social evil claiming whole streets for it* own. Thinking men need no infor- mation as- to' where the supply of 17ictims comes from. Mrs. Parker-states in one of her letters, March 28th, " It is very easy- to make an erroneus statement, but it is not so easy to-erase the impression suchla statement makes." ' Msvds giVo an example? A strong...hearty young man, a native-of Whitley, near Warrington7,-.J.. Rovrbotliam by nart.tro-indhcecl through reading the glowing ac- counts-given by Mrs. P. of Los Angelos, to tryhis " hick," sailediforloa Angelos. A carpenterby trade, he seemed just the-man- to succeed. Well, for weeks he walked about seeking a job; not a building going .an in the wle-A- district, but he visited it. On one job, at eleven,olelock in the forenoon, he was toM that no less than 27'carpenters had been that morning- seeking work. These-are-facts ; I have them fromsthe man himself,who receiving the- "' Examiner" from his friends*, noted my address and sought me out. /leis the, right sort of man ; to get on, and will soon find work in this city, I hope. WFenithese booms are started the soon flood a place Los Angelbs,with a population of, I think, MOOG. has 5,000 carpenters in it. The same law which rules in the world' of supply and demand respecting male labour, i,villdeterminethat of female labour. Wages. may keep up, hut in these outlying districts cost of Hying is some- thing wonderful. My own girls have jnst left their first situatien, here,, where they reeL-oiVed each per month 15,dollars or about 15s per week.- Qne Annie, immedi- ately engaged to another lady at aidoll"ars, or £3. 55 per week: Dgivehoth sides of the -question, bat I state-, antl-T wish, to' state it as stronglras possibly—working- men, without capital, should not, come out hero, unless they aro sure as I was, of meeting a real friend, ready to •,.grasp. them by the hand, . and coach them into jeb, The supply of labour; more than equals' the-demand.. Capitalists must- come first and then fahour,.both el which I assure yotearc to be found in the eastern Statzs.

, Migration will not long be tho.parret cry of Exgfish CdUservatives, enabling them ta.stave off the only,legiti- mate remedfes for improving British trade. The land- id' S time, is over for singing— And, the farmer plows, and the farmer sows. And he toils with care and,paia; 'Tls for me he plows, and he •reaps and mows, , And gathers the golden gsaln. ' Thetime‘iisnear when the effects of what is here called "pauper-emigration" will be severely felt in the aates, and thaw ltgistators will, at the people's demand, take hold of it. Ireland, Germany;, Italy, Spain, Norway. and Swetien have for years poured in their millions of poor workers. A strong feeliVis growing up against the•systrem, which depopulate,seue country at the ex- pense of another. Since. writing the above,•,li have received a visit from .T. Rowbaham, and P am pleased to say he has found, a. jbb. Previous to cfoing soy however, he aaswered an aavertisement. and when he reached the sob, soon after nine, twenty men were waiting. It was only a i small' shanty. He s noworaployed on the raihray, and gets, 3 dols. a day, Nrorking seven days a week. Ife will very likely be in Warrington before next Christmas. Letters- addressed as under will reach him. I hope L have, made it clear now that it is simply folly-to eornet out here expecting to jump at once into a gold mine. A short time ago a young man, whose name. I forget, from the neighbour- hood of Warrington, apd related to the Harris's of Pad- gate, called upon met:' He was wanting work, but I couldn't help him to WA. Ile seems to have cleared out, as I have not seen hin, since, and feel rather anxious as to his whereabouts.

A question which sooner or later will seriously disturb the labour market here is the one known as the Chinese question. The" ion-eye" arrives here each week by hundreds in spite of all law to the contrary. It is the speck no larger thstr & man' e hand which may yet cover the whole politicalthorizon. 'Not only here, but in the British colonies popular indignation is _lacing roused at the introduction of a coolie race who areyttle else than slaves. Several vessels have recently arrived in Austra- lian ports laden %ith Chinamen, and resolute opposition was shown to their landing. The New Zealand Govern- ment is deterrainoct to prevent an influx of Chinese, and has passed a bill to that effect. Yet, in spite of this, Salisbury responds with the assurance that" the home Government will not give its support to arly immigration laws passed by the colonies, independently of the Imperial Pairlilament, and will especially oppose any such laws directed particularly against the Chinese Thus it is seen that- not only the States but the whole of the civilized world is likely to be called upon soon to consider seriously- what shall be done with the Chinese, not only a nation but in respect to treaty making. Is a civilized power justified in making a treaty with a nation such as China? Certainly not, when it is known that wherever Chinese settle they isolate themselves, and two races which do not intermix cannot exist side by side. Where the Mongolian fixes himself emigration from Europe will cease. Why. should the European leave his native home to enter into competition with a pagan me, whose chief object is to scrape money enough to- gether to take him back to China. These "things" will k work for fifty cents 4 a day, and will work long hours. ' They will burrow in the earth like rabbits, seldom seeing daylight. At the street corner and on the side walk they will fix their cobblers stall. Good at imitation, they are thrusting themselves into alrnostevery trade. Streets without number resound to the click, click of the sewing machine. Down every alley ancl up every back :street the Chinese laundry man is seen ; clad in a suit of white loose things he is thocheap, and servile tool, or servant. of the olose-fisted. As mar- ket gardener, he will trudge tho city round with his sad- dle and hartipers. There am now in the Statea 9240Q0

Chinese laundrymen, and 12,973 laundresses. earl'' 26,983,840 dollars annually. But for the competo these Chinese the 60,000 women employed in Anierit` laundries might be quadrupled. Men go round country exhuming and gathering the bones of definair celentials for exporting to the flowcry land. A ti consignment has just arrived in this city ready forth, blessed land. Mayor Hewitt, of New York, sa.Ys are persons who are brought under contract to is`"" whG are practically owned and managed by contneo who hire them out in competition with the free 13l)001 the country." The manager of a fruit canning facw_, an Englishman—took me through his place, ann,.. surprised; none but Chinese were employed, sv!l-E them stoning and canning peaches for export ployers and workmen all Chinese, the inanW7l English—all for fifty cents a day. I soo that in 11 o fund of £128,000 was formed for the purpose hi , tprblishing a Christian institution in China, but a n• difficulty prevented it from being used. Thert 1 in attempting such work—better throw the inone ",

the.Thaines.- The. Chinaman, with the inborn 0: vatimn peculiar to, ancient nations, is arrogant eeite4. His institutions, social and religious, are, Ps estimation, as much: superior to anything Europe is ponible for light to be preferable to darkfless. much fm the Chinese question, and its bearing 011 emigration question. Bomething short of one huudred cyclist' volun- , rvs assembled at Crewe on Saturday evening to 'lto part in the projected manceuvres in Cheshire ever the week end and on Bank Holiday. The cy- , eiists.may be said to have come from all " arts and for they were there from London and Tyne, "Aoutli, Bristol and Bradford, Cornwall (Camborne), tuld Hereford, Bradford, Hastings, Croydon, Ashton- ' b-ncler-Lyne, Warwickshire, and Manchester. Some 1321 e has remarked that cyclist naancelivres and wet ..w.eather are always coupled together, and Saturday Ight certainly did not break the unpropitious Vltlitlion, for the downpour was steady and persistent U well into the morning of Sunday. ; The first part of the operations was to consist of midnight, march of about 28 miles to Warrington, 00 checkmate the tactics of an imaginary enemy— Atli° had landed at Southport, and was on the ,parch south —by carrying off the military stores that town, and blowing up the bridge over the Mersey. The men were accordingly paraded shortly lifter nine o'clock on the Alexandra ground, Crewe, lind promptly at ten o'clock a start was made, the ~tolumn ot militant wheelmen being headed by four eYclista of the 2nd Ch -shire (Crewe) Railway Engi- ?nlers, who acted as guides. The route lay through 44 lad' ewic h , Noithwich, Great Budworth, and lgtretton, the roads to Stretton being mostly on the nutiiig gradient, but from that village there was a elear run down into Warrington. All the conditions 'Were unfavourable to such a march, as the rain tell Continually and heavily till within a few miles of 'Warrington. The roads were soft, and, the night ex- tremely dark, but the cyclists kept pluckily to their 'work, and, with the exception of a few stragglers tic> came up later on, reached Warrington in a body about halt-past three on Sunday morning. A ce,uple of fast riders of the 2nd Manchester—Sergt. .7 alter Smith and Private Warden—who had been r.t'Patched from Crewe about five minutes before re main column with a message for the umpire, Leached Warrington about half-past one. supposed, either been removed or destroyed and the j bridge blown up—was executed in four sections. The first, under Captain Bell, Tynemouth Artillery Volunteers, with Captain Willis, Lieutenant Cole, and 20 men of the London Scottish, 2nd Warwick, 16th Lancashire, and by Shellon and Weaver- harn on Sandi Way (13 miles), whence they extende4l • pearly to North wick. The second, under Captain Hughes, 20th Lancashire, assisted by Lieutenant Bonsor and Lieutenant Smith, . had 10 men of the 20th Lancashire. Cinque Ports, and Corn- wall Regiments, and marched by Frodsham and Delamere Forest on the Abbey , Arms (16 miles). The third, under Captain Griffiths, with Lieutenants Hewlett, Bryan, and Hassan, and 18 men of the 4th Lancashire, Ist Surrey, 13th and 18th Middlesex, 7th ' Lancashire, Ist Gloucester, and•the 2nd Yeomanry, marched onlielsall Hill; and the 4th. under Captain Fletcher Vane, with Lieutenants Phillips and Dut- ton, occupied Tarviu with detachments of the 30th Middlesex, Ist Hereford, and 2nd Cheshire, number- ing 14 men. The departure of the cyclists was witnessed by great crowds of townspeople, who seemed to be deeply interested in the men and their maphines. The cycles were provided by the volunteers them- selves, and were of all "sorts and sizes." Colonel Savile himself rode a Humber tricycle, and there were also to be seen tandem tricycles, an omnicycle, carrying four, besides numerous ordinary and safety bicycles, the latter being the most numerous. Those wile rode tricycles and safety bicycles had their ' rifles attached to their machines, but the riders of " ordinaries " had their fire-arms strapped to their backs. The cyclists wore a great variety of uni- lorms, those of the Londoners perhaps being the most picturesque: During Sunday afternoon the riders were practised in piquet and outpost work on the Cheshire roads, and in the evening they all con- centrated at Chester. On Sunday the weather had been fine, though slightly windy, but on Monday the elements were again unfavourable, as rain fell most of the day. The day was spent in manceuvres in the country be- tween Chester and Crewe, and at this latter place a final parade was made about five in the afternoon, when Colonel Savile congratulated the men, one and all, on the success of the manceuvres. Within the next hour or two nearly all those who had taken part in these important operations were speeding their way homewards.

THE INTERCEPTING DEPOT IN HARDY-ST. Sir,—l think it is high time that something was done to suppress the nuisance caused to those who have to live in this locality by the abominable stench which comes from the depot in Hardy-st. A greater mistake 11.1103 never made than putting a place of that kind near any houses. There is something very strange about the working of it, too. On Wednesday the smell was sicken- ing nearly all day, but on Thursday there was not much smell. About noon we found out the cause of the im- provement. A carriage containing the Borough Sur- veyor and a number of gentlemen drove up ; they examined the place, and of course everything was as nice as it -could be. After they had gone, it was as bad as ever. Now this sort of thing has happened before; but is it fair to the strangers who come here to look at the place and are allowed to go away believing that there is no nuisance caused, and perhaps establish this sort of thing in other towns? I think it is about a.s glaring a "false pretence" as could well be made, and someone will reap curses and not blessings when the truth comes out. I knoW plenty of people who are ill through the stench; and have two children ill myself from this same thing. I don't want to leave my house, hut I can't stand it any longer. I shall give my notice next Monday, and clear ,nut and go to live in a locality where there is a chance to breathe— Warrington, Aug. 10th, 1888
PURE AIR.

THE COUNCIL AND THE GAS QUESTION. Bir,—At the last Council meeting Alderman Davies Made use of the following words :—" He was pleased to think that that Council was independent of any adverse influence from such people," and "there was a great •mmount of mischiet done by ignorant people [I suppose Yatepayers in public meeting assembled] to a class more Ignorant than themselves." This language is on a par with the conduct of a large number of gentlemen in the Council. They do not represent theeratepayers, the great boAy of whom, according to some of these enlightened (?) gentlemen, are ignorant, and consequently have no right to inure into anything. It is quite time the " arrangement " between the two political clubs WAS swept away, and the ratepayers had a direct control over those who profess to manage the affairs of the borough. It is acknowledged by everyone that a few "rule the roast " in the Council, and Alder- man Davies has once more displayed his usual ability by helping the Gas Committee out of their dilemma. But does he think the gas question is settled? No; he will hear much more on this subject yet. I would ask is it, or is it not, a fact that the Gas Committee were afraid to trust to Mr. Haddock's ability, and wanted to take the precaution of having Mr Paterson at hand in case of need. If so, why did they not say so? Councillor F. A. Ro- berts, who is a member of the Gas Committee, stated at this same meeting that in his opinion the town had lost £4OO or £5OO a year by the withdrawal of Mr. Paterson's services. What does this mean ? Is it a confession that Mr. Haddock is, after all, not fully competent, and that the town is going to lose this much money yearly in con- sequence of his not having Mr. Paterson's advice? Per- haps Alderman Davies will "lift the blind" on these points.

A DISGUSTED RATEPAYER. Warrington, August 10, 1838. I-We are always willing to permit of a free expression of opinion in our columns ; but would suggest to future correspondents that it would be as well to leave Mr. Haddock's name out of the discussion—until, at any rate, he has hada fair trial.—Ed. Ex.]

THE MUSIC IN THE PARK. Sir,—l am glad to see that the public are beginning to find out by means of your columns that there are mat- ters in connection with the music provided during the week in Bank Park which require looking into and im- proving. I quite agree with your last week's correspon- dent that it would be for the public good, as well as tor the convenience of the bandsmen, if the Park was pro- vided with a new bandstand. But are we to wait until it is presented by the good-natured "man with a for- tune," talked of by your correspondent? The hints thrown out in that direction by him remind one of the half-bricks recommended to be used in their stead by a certain collier who figured in "Punch" some time ago. I must, however, say that it speaks badly for the in- dependence of the people of Warrington if their prevail- ' ing spirit is representedby thebold spirit under a nona-de- plume who addressed you upon the subject last week. I sincerely hope that Pro Bono Publiao" does not ex- press the sentiment current in Warrington. If so, it is a bad thing for Warrington, and if my estimate of the character of Warrington people is correct,they will make themselves heard in the matter, and will, through the Town Council, pay for their luxuries themselves. I notice that for matters of minor importance that august body do not appear very anxious to count the cost, so that it will be rather too good a joke if they preach. economy on this matter. If, however, the matter doei come before the Council, there is one question which I think is certain to be asked, and that is whether the public appreciates the music. This, to any spectator on " music " night is apparent, but it may be depended upon that there will be some sceptical being who will point to the 21d and 4cl collections of last week, and the question will arise as to whether the best mode a paying for the music is by "voluntary contributions." I myself think that the Council ought to vote a sum of money for the purpose. It is the ratepayers' money that they use, and the Council have voted it for much less useful purposes. I hope that very soon this matter will receive their attention.—l am, sir, yours, atc.,
SPECTATOR.

div.head: Warrington, August 9th, 1838. THE MARRIAGE OF MISS POWYS, OF
div.p: Warrington, August 9th, 1838. THE MARRIAGE OF MISS POWYS, OF
WARRINGTON.

At St. Paul's, Onslow-square, London, on Thurs- day afternoon, the marriage of the eldest daughter of the Hon. Leopold W. IL Powys and Lady Mary Powys with Captain Charles Blood 3lulville. late of the Dragoon Guards, was solemnised by the Rev. the Hon. E. Powys. The bride wore a dress of white crepe, with a long train of poult de soie. The bridesmaids—the Misses Powys (2), Reeve, and Moore—were gowned in white nun's veiling, and wore moire sashes and Leghorn hats. Captain and Mrs. Mulville left later for the continent. The Powys family, it is needless to say, have been long and honourably connected with 14 arrington ; but although possessing an extensive estate at Bewsey, where the late Lord Lil ford built the new Bewsey Hall, ,no member of the family has permanently resided there for the last 25 years. Twice a year, however, in Sep- tember and November, the Hon. Leopold Powys (brother of the present Lord Lilferd), to whom the estate belongs., has left his residence, Milford- lodge, Godalmuag, to enjoy a week or two's sport at Bewsey. On such occasions he has generally been accompanied by Lady Mary and daughters, wha have evinced a genuine interest in the tenantry and in church and other movements being promoted in tbe neighbourhood. The marriage of Miss Powys was considered a fitting occasion for an expression on the part of the Bewsey tenantry of the esteem in which the family is helcf, and a magnificent sil- ver salver, elaborately engraved, supplied by Messrs Wood and Son, Sankey-st., together with an address bound in morocco, was forwarded to the bride. The address bore the names of 30 subscribers,who offered their hearty congratulations to the recipient, and re- ferred to the respect in which the family had been held for several generations in that neighbourhood.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
RUNCORN.

This week, the steam navvy which has been increasing the length of the cutting from Norton to the Old Quay has succeeded in working its way through to "Nor- man's Pottery." The line of rails which were a fortnight I or so ago laid from that spot along the Old Quay Docks has been joined to the line in the cutting, and as soon as the necessary permission is given by the Runcorn Im- provement Commissioners to Mr. Walker, this line will be continued along the foreshore and certain streets from the Quay Docks through Runcorn Bridge. At low tide one of the days this week advantage was taken of surveying the river at a spot between the Old Baths and the ship-building yard of the company. At Weston operations are still progressing. The village of huts in course of construction on the Marsh by Messrs. Thomas Kirkham and Co., for the accommodation of the work men, are rapidly approaching completion. THE EXPLOSIVE MAGAZINE AT MORRIS

div.head: BROOK.
div.p: BROOK.

Messrs. G. B. Dewhurst and C. Lister, of Lymm, paid a visit of examination to the new magazine for explo- sives now being erected near to Morris Brook farm, on the Ship Canal, on Wednesday morning, and expressed their satisfaction with the nature of the precautions taken. Application will be made at the Police Court on Monday morning for the necessary authority to store the explosives.

div.head: THELIVALL AND STATHAM.
div.p: THELIVALL AND STATHAM.

There is little new to record as to the section from Morris Brook to Statham. The neighbourhood of Morris Brook is one of the busiest on the whole length of the canal, as there are several powerful steam navvies in constant operation. The work here is carried on close to Thelwali-lane, and many passers by take advantage of this circumstance to have a peep into the deep " cut " which is to be the canal channel, and in which the steam navvies are almost hidden. Another busy scene is to be witnessed at the river diversion works opposite Thelwall village, and so much progress has been made here that it seems justifiable to surmise that within a brief period the Mersey Will begin to flow in its new bed in this locality. BARTON SECTION.

The French excavator at Stickings Island has beeni working again night and day during the past week, fill- ing an average of about 400 wagons in ten hours. A steam navvy has also been started in the Lock pit. At the river diversion, near Salt Eye Brook. a steam dredging machine is now working, and will soon have cleared the dams away from each end of the new channel. On the Salt Eye cutting the steam navvy con- tinues to do good work. The second girder of the ap- proach bridge to Trafford Park will shortly be placed in position, and when finished the bridge will undoubtedly form a feature of interest to the Barton people. The site of the old Corn Mill rock is now being quarried with the expectation of finding some fairly good stone. At Irwell Park the Whittaker's excavator and steam navvy continue to do good work, and the rock found on this part of the section is being steadily removed. In Traf- ford Hall cutting the wheelbarrow and the spade con- tinue to be used. In the Little Bolton cutting another Whittaker's excavator has been started, and like the steam navvy is doing well. Crossing from here is the' Mode Wheel cutting, where the building of the boundary wall to Sir H. De Trafford's Park has already been commenced.

div.head: TIMELY RESCUE.
div.p: A TIMELY RESCUE.

Betweenone andtwo on Thursday afternoon, as Mr. 0. Reilly, from the resident engineer's offica, was coming acro,s the footway under the aqueduct, he was consider- ably startled at hearing a loud splash. On looking round he discovered a man struggling in the river below. Hav- ing some poles with him he lost no time in rendering the man asssistance, and ultimately ga him out, not much the worse tor his immersion, just as the lock-keeper had run for the grapnels. TREAT TO SHIP CANAL CHILDREN.

On Monday about two hundred children who attend the Ship Canal Mission School in Irwell-lane, Runcorn, had a trip up the Old Quay Canal to Latchford. Through the kindness of Mr. Crregson, the agent, the party were accommodated on a large barge, which was drawn, by the steamer Ellen, and the sail proved a very pleaUnt one. Mr. Rhead, the material agent, had charge of the boat, while Mr. Watson, the mission- ary, exercised general supervision. On arriving at Latchford, the children engaged in a variety of games, and had the privilege of competing in races, &c., for prizes. Ample refreshments were provided for the children, who spent a most pleasant day. NAVVIES IN PERIL.

The other day a rather exciting incident happened at Eastham. Some timber had got adrift in the tide, and three men, without much thought as to whether they could steer in such a current, jumped into a boat that was moored at the Eastham landing stage on purpose to nye it. The current, however, was too strong for them, and the wind blowing a stiff breeze from the west they were soon drifting away towards Garston. Not know- ing much of boating, and having only one oar in the boat they were powerless, and were carried by the Oh tide down to Liverpool. When off the landing stage they managed to attract the attention of the steam tug "Mersey King," who took them on board and towed the boat to the landing stage at Liverpool, from whence they were taken to Eastham in one of the ferry boats, their arrival giving great relief to those in charge. THE LIABILITIES OF SHAREHOLDERS.

At the Manchester Court pf Record on Thursday, be- fore Mr. H. W. West, Q.C., an action was brought by, the Manchester Ship Canal Company to recover from Joseph Vaughan, of Rochdale-road, Manchester, the amount of the allotment and calls on three shares in the canal undertaking. Mr. Yates appeared for the plain- tiff company, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Sparrow. It was-stated that the defendant applied for three shares in the Ship Canal Company, and although that number had been allotted to turn, he had failed to pay the £2 per share required on allotment, and the sub- sequent calls amounting to £6.—For the defence Mr. Sparrow argued that under the Manchester Ship Canal Act. 1885, no share was to be issued, or was to vest, un- til at least one-fifth of its value had been paid. In that case not a single penny had been paid by the defendant either on application or on subsequent notice of allot- ment. He contended that the company acted vitro rites when they allotted the shares, and consequently ought not to succeed in an action against the defendant.—Mr. Yates, for the company, said that point had been dis- posed of by the case of the East Gloucestershire Railway Company v. Bartholomew. After some discussion the ' Recorder decided that the case cited by Mr. Yates ap- plied to the point of issue, and directed the jury to find a verdict for the amount claimed. The jury found for plaintiff for £l2, and judgment was made aclordingly. - FUSTIAN CUTTERS -AND CANAL EMPLOYMENT.

The deputation appointed last week to wait upon the Messrs. Dewhurst and other gentlemen, asking for their influence to enable the cutters to get work on the Ship Canal have met much success. On Tuesday Mr. John Dewhurst visited Mr. Walker's offices in Manchester, and an arrangement was made to meet oti the works in Stat- ham on Wednesday afternoon. Accordingly Messrs. G. B. Dewhurst, John Dewhurst, and R. Dutton, with the deputation, Messrs. J. Buckley and T. Gatley, met Mr. Price a; three o'clock, and explained how from the nature of the work to which they had been used it was impos- sible for the fustian cutters to work alongside the pre- sent experienced navvies, and asking that the fustian cutters might be found work by themselves at fair and reasonable remuneration until such time as they could work with the other men. Mr. Price at once admitted the reasonableness of the request, and offered to pay the same price for excavating to the cutters as to the other men. They should be allowed to work by themselves until they become inured to it, and inquired how many wished to start. The deputation stated about 40, and it was arranged that the deputation should meet Mr. Price on Thursday morning. This was done, and Mr. Price has set apart a piece of land between Laskey Brook and Statham for the experiment. The men are to ar- range themselves in gangs according to their age and strength, and work as they are able, as soon as the neces- sary plant can be got on the ground, and it is thought that His or Z 1 a week may be earued for a start. • MI3C EILANEOUS. The cutting from Warburton to Barton is making great progre-s, and extends nearly the whole length of the section. varying in depth from half-a-dozen to fifty feet. Considerably more men have been put on near to and at Irlam, where cuttings are now being made and tlie buildings rapidly rim up. Much progress has also been made during the week at Moore, Acton Grange, and Morley Common. As the last two or three days have witnessed a great improvement in the weather, there have been a considerable number of visitors 0 the works.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENTS ON THE SHIP CANAL
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENTS ON THE SHIP CANAL
WORKS.

Harry Pyke, aged 23 years, a married man, who lived in Robert-st., Runcorn. was injured on the Ship Canal works at Norton, on Monday morning, and died on Tuesday morning. It appears that he was employed as the rope runner to the tipping engine, and a link of the chain having been broken, he was standing in the four foot repairing it. About three feet six inches away was ' the end of a train of waggons, laden with clay, to which I was attached an engine, and this train was suddenly backed to the tipping ergine. Pyke, in trying to escape from his perilous position, was caught between the buf- fers of the last waggon, and the tipping engine, and was terribly crushed. He was conveyed to the temporary hospital at Halton, and Dr. McDougall and his assistant were quickly in attendance, and did everything Possible for the sufferer. Later in the day Dr. Jones, of Liver- pool, consulting surgeon to the Ship Canal works, was called in, and an operation was performed. The injuries were, however, of a terrible character, and Pyke never rallied, death occurring as stated. Me.: Gregson was very solicitous after the welfare and comfort of the suf- ferer, and spent many hours by his bedside. The inquest on the body was held at the Runcorn Burial Board Office, on . Wednesday morning, before Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner. Mr. C. A. F. Gregson, C.E., agent for the Runcorn section of the Ship Canal. watched the proceedings on behalf of Mr. Walker, the contractor. ,Oamuel Pyke, of saddle- worth, said he was the father of the deceased, who was employed as a rope runner or guard on the Ship Canal , works. John Free, of Halton-road, engine-driver on the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGVST ll, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGVST ll, 1888.

Ship Canal works, said the duties of the deceased were to hook and unhook wagons to the tipping engine. On Monday morning an S link of the chain of the engine became sprung, and the deceased commenced to repair it. Witness was leaning over the break of his engine watching. There was a train of loaded wagons on the line, the last wagon being about 31t. ein. away from the engine. Witness saw the wagons move, and he shouted to the deceased to get out of the way, at the same time starting his engine away. The deceased was, however, caught between the buffers of the wagon and the en- gine, at the loins, and was very badly hurt. He was carried to the hospital. An engine had started the wagons. William Smith, of Brick Kiln-houses, rope runner on the Ship Canal works, said he had charge of the train of filled wagons. He ordered the train tp come hack a bit, and did not perceive the deceased until he shouted out when he was hurt. Had he seen the de- ceased he should not have given the order. He was about sixty yards away from the deceased. He did not know whether the engine whistled or not. It was the driver's duty to whistle. Mr. Gregson said the men would never expect a man to be where the deceased was, and the deceased ought to have taken precautions. Joseph Atki-ison, of Suffolk-st., engine-driver on the canal works, said he had a train of 18 waggons, and as he had not to move them more than four or five feet, when he received the rope runner's signal to "hack," he did not whistle. It was his duty to whistle.—The Coroner: Why did not you whistle ?—Witness : I don't know what possessed me not to do so.—By Mr. Gregson : I was simply adjusting the train I had brought in. I backed the wagons up to the tipping engine in the usual way.—By the Coroner,: I have been an enginge driver 18 years.—Dr. McDougall gave evidence as to the extent of the injuries.—Mr. Gregson was sworn, and stated that the drivers had no instructions as to whistling': but in dangerous places there were placed boards with " Whistle" printed in large letters upon them. Having only to move these waggons a distance of four feet it was not the duty of the driver to whistle, and had he whistled he (Mr. Greg- son) did not think it would have saved the life of the deceased.—The Coroner said the driver had been an en- gine-driver for 18 years, and ought to know his business, and it was quite clear that it was his duty to have whis- tled. If the jury were of opinion that through the driver neglecting to whistle this man came to his death they must return a verdict of manslaughter against the driver. If they came to the conclusion that the man meant that it was his duty to whistle if he had seen the danger, or that if he had whistled the accident could not have been avoided, they must return a verdict of ac- cidental death.—The jury aecided that the man came to his death by a pure accident, and the Coroner recorded a verdict of "Accidental death." SECOND FATALITY. . A second fatal accident occurred in connection with the Ship Canal operations on Wednesday morning. Enoch Hall, 17 years of age, was employed in assisting to unload large beams from a flat at Old Quay Docks. He was standing on a stack of timber, when it toppled over and he was struck on the head by one of the falling beams, and his head nearly severed from his body. Death was instantaneous.—An inquest was held on the body the same morning; by Mr. J. E. Worsloy. Mr. W. Geo. • Rhead, the material agent to the Ship Canal Works, ap- peared on behalf of Mr. Walker, the contractor.—Thos. Hall, of 30, Perry-st, said the deceased was his stepson and was a labourer at the Old Quay for the Ship Canal Works. He was in the at at the tune, and did not se the accident.—Samuel Westwell, of 8, Irwell-st., la- bourer, said he was on the pile of logs with the decearel: The logs were wound from the flat by a crane, and were_ from 20 to 40 feet-long. They had been piled 9or 10 feet high. The width at the base would be twelve feet. He felt the logs slip and he ran to the side, but they knocked him off and left him just at the edge of the canal. His leg and side were hurt. The deceased was nearer the edge of the baulks than he was, and he was buried beneath them. The logs were stacked in the usual way—By Mr Rhead: He never noticed that the stack was unsafe. It would not be. practicable to put scotches across, because the, beams were not all of the same length and thickness. He felt the thing was perfectly safe.—John Letrnon, of Pennington House. Canal side, said he was a checker, or measurer of timber. He was on the top of the stack measuring each baulk as it name from the flat. He per- ceived the stack to move slightly just as they landed a log, and he shouted out and stepped on to another stack. He did not know what caused the stack to shift, Nit he had heard that it was through a subsidence at the edge of the wharf.—Mr. Rhead 7 I attribute it to the wet weather.—Witness: The logs wore very greasy. He had been accustomed to unloading timber nearly all his life, and in this instance it was properly' unloaded and properly stacked. The timber WM not of. one size, and it was impossible to sprag it.—The Coroner said eight or nine feet was not an unreasonable height, and the work seemed to have been well done, and he thought the jury would have no difficulty in returning a; verdict of "accidental death."—The foreman of the jury (Mr. Grice) : I think it is well known that Mr. Walker takes every care that he possibly- can do.—The Coroner : I believe so.—A verdict as suggested was re— turned.

RUGBY FOOTBALL CONTEST.—A seven a side football contest, under Rugby rules, for seven silver medals, received three entries, viz., Upholland F.C., Highfiehl F.C., and St. Helens Recreation (It. Langley's team.) The two last named were drawn together, and Uphol- land secured the bye. The play in the first tie was in favour of the St. Helens men, who led until near the I "finish, by a try (Pilkington, from a pass by Gerrard), and two minors to nil. Their opponents then pressed, and during a scrimmage near the St. Helens goal line, Highfield got over and scored a try, which Gee conver- ted into an easy goal amid cheers. No further points were scored, and the referee (Mr. E. Foreman) declared the result a draw as the three clear points to secure a victory had not been obtained by either side. Highfield, who were leading, by two points, claimed the tie, and re- fused to play any longer. The St. Helens men were then ordered to secure a try and kick a goal, and this having been done without opposition St. Helens were ayrarded the be. They afterwards net Upholland in the final. A pleasantly contested and hard fought game resulted in a victory for St. Helens, who thus secured the medals by two goals to one goal. ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CONTIOKT.—Seven silver medal's were also offered for a seven a side contest under Assetciation rules, and the teams entered were Rainford, Skel- mersclale United, and St. Mark's (St. Helens.) The lat- ter had the bye, and Rainford and Skelmersdale played off the first tie. Skelmerstiale soon showed their supei riority, and before half-time scored three goals. In the second period of play they added tvxot more, and as their opponents failed to notch a singily point Skehnersdale were declared the winners by five. gnats to none. Skel- mersdale and St. Mark's afterwardk, met in the final tie. Soon after starting Skehnersdale scored, and St. Mark's played hard to secure an equalising, point, but they were unable to do so. The second half was very exciting, and both goals were endangered. No finther scoring was witnessed, and Skelmersdale thus wore the medals by one goal to none. • The whole of the prizes were afterwards presented to the winners by Mrs W. Richardson, of Rhinford House.

She Irad not known for a long time. He tlid not believe his (the husband's) own], mother had known for a long time. _ Mary Ann Eaton, wife of Richard Eaton 41,. Orford- st., a wire-worker, deposed that the deceased had lodged with her for nearly ten weeks. Last Wednes lay she re- ported to Constable Monaghan the robbery of a peer of boots fro& her dwelling-house. She gave information as to who elm suspected of having stolen them, and at about one o'clock the same day she saw the deceased and the boots at the police station. She identified the boots as her property, and heard the Prisoner reply, "It is quite right,' to the charge. She remembered the (De- ceased corning home the worse for drink one night last week—Thursday or Friday. She said that she hoped "they would find her dead—either in hell or heaven in The morning." Impactor Spinks deposed that at about one o'clock on Wednesday the deceased was brought to the police sta- tion by Constable Monaghan, and he received the charge from the' constable. She was charged in the usual way with stea,ling the boots. She gave the name of Clara Ellen Kennedy. She was then removed to the women's day yard. There was no one else in the female. yard. Half an hour afterwards wit- new went upstairs to his dinner, and gave instruc- tions te.Mrsz. Spinks to see the prisoner about her dinner. Mrs. Sinks said "1 can't make her hear," and witness, looking from an ripper windof, saw the deceased lying inside the dao-leatee, face downwards. He obtained the assistance' of two constables and went in. Deceased was unconscious. There were two handkerchiefs tied tightly round'herthroat. She was carried to the open yard, and efferts.weremade to restore animation, a messenger in thermeantimebeing sent to the nearest doctor, Dr. Peaeockei whoewrived almost immediately. After an examination the- doctor pronounced that she was dead. There.vrere ntesigns c 4 drink on the deceased when she was apprehended.. Pelice.genstabltr rake spoke to the correctness of the evidence given by Inspector Spinks. He said that when deceased was fimml the handkerchief produced was round her neck,, and was tied with three knots very tightly: IThr arms were extended. A second handkerchief wastied in a bow on the top of the other one. Site was Nearer,. tut her tongue which was black, protraded.fromher mouth. From the position of the handkerchiefs,, deceased must have tied them herself. Brandy was'administetied to her, but she did not appear te swallowit. Dr. Peacocks deposed that on Wednesday he was calledtothwdeceased. Respiration was suspended, but witness thoughrhe could perceive a small pulsation of the heart. He f&und after a moment or two that life was extinct. Strangulation' was the cause of death. The face waslivid and thethroat was marked. The doctor added that cases of strangulation, otherwise than by sus- pension, were extremelY rare, and some people had doubted the possibility a such a thing being done. There had, however, been other ea_aes reported, bht he had never tomeacrossorrehimself.

The Coroner, im summin,, up, said that he would not enter into the private circumstances of the life of the de- ceased, but he menttisned, that the letter to her from the flrst'vritness was-couched'in affectionate terms. It was proved that the deceased had strangled herself, though they heard that that was al very uncommon thing. The jury returned a.verdict to the effect that the de- ceased committed suicide by strangulation in the woman's day yard'at the police station, she being then and there warrantably detained.

div.head: SHOCKING SUICIDE IN PRISON AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SHOCKING SUICIDE IN PRISON AT WARRINGTON.

Some sensation was caused in Warrington, on Wednesday evening, by the circulatian of a report, that a young woman, while in custody at the Borough police station on a charge of felony, had committed suicide by hanging herself.. On inquiry being made at tlie police station it was found to be only too true that a female prisoner had taken away her life. The mode she adopted was to strangle herself with a couple of pocket handkerchiefs. which she had wound round her neck and then tightened to an almost incredible degree. Deceased, who had given her name as Clara Ellen Kennedy, and was described as a singer, of 41, Orford-St., had been apprehended on a charge of stealing a pair of shoes from the house of Mrs. Heaton, 41, Otford-at., where she lodged. She had not been long on the Bridewell premises, and had only for a very, short time been by herself unobserved, when it was dis- covered that she had committed the rash deed. The police used their utmost endeavours to restore the unfortunate woman to consciousness, and Dr. Peacock. who lives near at hand, and was at home when his assistance was sent for, was on the spot a few minutes after the occurrence. Their efforts, unfortunately, were futile. Deceased was a Musical Hall artist, and had been engaged at different public-houses in Warrington, where there are singing rooms, and at one time she was engaged at the Theatre Royal in Scotland-road. Her hus- band is an actor. She was about thirty years of age. The following is the substance of a statement made by Mr. Hunt (the chief constable) in relation to the deplorable affair. Complaint was made to Constable Monoghan on Wednesday morning, at about eleven o'clock, by Mrs Heaton, of 41, Orford- st., that she had missed a pair of boots, her property under rather strange circumstances. Monoghan 'macro-inquiries, and found that the boots had been predged at Mr. Jackson's pawnshop for half-a- crown by a person who gave the name of Nellie Rice.. That person turned out to be the lodger of Mrs Heaton. About one o'clock in the afternoon • Cimstabln Monoghan found Clara Ellen Kennedy in the EU public-house, Buttermarket-st., and took her to the police station, where on being charged with having stolen the booth, she replied, "It is quite right." She, was not lOcked up in a cell; but was placed in, the women's day yard. About half an hour afterwards upon some- one 'going to see the prisoners about their dinners, -the feet' df a woman were seen on the greund pro- jecting-from the day-house. Inspector Spinks and Police-constable Pace were called, and they found Kennedy Tying on the ground, face downwards, with a silk pocket-handkerchief tied tightly round her throat; and another handkerchief tied round it. They instantly removed the handkerchiefs from the woman's neck, turned her on her back, and used every possible means to restore animation. While this was being done, Dr. Peacock was sent for, but on his arrival it was found that life was extinct. The police have evidence that some few days ago the deceased had used some rather strange expres- sions as to what might happen during the night. Deceased and her husband had been lodging for seven or-eight weeks in Orford-st., but the husband, who‘iS are actor. had occasion to leave to take an en- gagement at Wolverhampton. Deceased had since earned her living by singing in different public- houses. She had been engaged at two or three pla- ces, her Hist engagement being at the Hop Pole, Horsemarket-et. , At the sitting of the Borough magistrates on Thursday morning, the matter was mentioned to the magistrates in attendance—Major Litton and. Councillor John Greening. On the sheet used for that purpose waa a charge against "Clara Kenned.f.; singer, of 41, Orford-st., for having stolen from the dwelliiig-hoirse of Richard Heaton, 41, Orford-s, one pair of ladies' elastic side boots, of the value of Os, tile property of Ann Heaton." The Chief Con- stable; after. the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. B. White)died read over the charge, informed the Bench of the unfortunate occurrence tlpit had taken place,on the day previous, over which, he said, lie thought Oro-police had no control whatever. He then entered into lull particulars of 'the affair, after which the Magistrates Clerk mentioned that Mr. Stringer, .(the . Theatre Royal. Scotland-road, had informed tarn that the deceased was formerly a member-of a Company appearing at that theatre. The.engargement finished about the 15th of last June, and'since then the deceased had had no connection with thetheatre, haying taken temporary engage- ments.. The Chief Constable said that a person of resp,ctability bad been speaking to him on the question of whether anything could be done to stop singing. and dancing in public - houses in , Warrington. Something more would, perhaps, 'be said on Atria subject afterwarde, but the pollee had no control over these places.-,- The Magistrates' Clerk: Unless there is disorderly condixt.—Ma ior Litton : I suppose we cannot do' anything in the matter until there is an Inquest.— The Chief Constable : We can do nothing here, but there was a charge on the books which had to be explained. The next thing will be an inquest,— The. Magistrates' Clerk intimated that if the magis- trates desired to refer to anything objectionable at. public-houses in the respect mentioned they could db.so on the annual licensing day.—An entry was then made on the official record to, the effect that the prisoner had been found dead. THE INQUEST. Yesterday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy- coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry into. the circumstances of the death in the Parade-room at the. Police Station. Mr. Hunt (chief constable) was preAent. lon behalf of the police. The follbwing evidence was John Macouberv, an actor, professionally known. as John Aubrey, said that he had no, settled address, but, was at present living at -28, Towet,st., Wolverhampton. He had seen the body lying in the police cells, and it was that of Clara Ellen-Rice, known me Nelly Kennedy. Tier maiden name, to the best of his belief, was Clara Olen Kennedy. He believed that hee husband's name was

Robert Rice, but he could not swear to it. He dill not know where her husband was now. He (the deceased's husband), was professionally known as R. A. jtoberts, and ho was an actor—a comedian, witness %ought. From her own statement deceased was thirty-three years of age. Witness last saw her alive on a Sunday afternoon bekbre he left Warrington, at 41, Orford-st. He had been engaged in Warring,ton. He was afterwards out of an, engagement for seven weeks, while deceased was engaged at a smaLt amount. He was only engaged in Warrington for three•athts,.on the Sunday following which he last saw her. Deceased had recently been a singer and dancer, and was previ- ously an actress. Be and the deceased, had been hying , together for about ten months, as nearly as he could I say. The letter produced, addressedto Mrs J. Aubrey, was to her, and was in witness's handwriting. [The Letter was opened by the Coroner, but the contents were not made public.l The last engagement deceased had was at the Hop Pole Inn, and that had terminated.— The Chief Constable: They were simply casual engage- ments 2 Witness: Yes.—Tho Coroner: Was sha singing at publfo-houses ? Witness : Yes, owing entiAly to the dearth of engagements in the regular theatres.— Th.-1 Qe,roner ; Did she daock to publio-housoS

div.p: RAIN FORD ATHLETIC SPORTS..

I' In beautiful weather, the eleventh annual Rain- ford athletic festival was held on Tuesday after- noon, in a Reid kindly lent by Mrs. J. Birchen. There was a very large, attendance of spectators— about 2,000 lining the ropes-- and all the arrange- ments were carried out in a most satisfactory man- ner. The receipts amounted to about .£lOl more than the highest amount received on any previous occasion. The committee and officials, including the energetic secretary, Mr. J. Ball, and treasurer. Mr. B. MISCELLANEOUS.—TIie Royal' Assent was given by Commission to 11 public' and private ibillk—Lord Sams- /317FM moved the second reading of .the !Arndt Commis- sion Bill. He said the House of'Commonnaccepted the principle of the bill on its secondleading. The Govern- ment entered on the subject with ,retucttance, but they believed that, whater'er the issue of the Commission, it would put an end to controversies iaf a dangerous kind, and would dissipnte a cloud of scandlilous calumny. —Lord HERSCHEL opposed the biII.—EarI.CIRRAP.TON be- lieved the bill necessary, and that the Cbmmission of Judges was the best that could be appolntod.The LORD CnAxcinrort said the desire of the Chivert2nent was to clear the House of Comrnons,of a ,grave scandal attach- ing to certain hon. members:—Earl KIavIIEWLEY and Earl GRANVILLE believed a Select Committee 'would have been better.—Earl DEEM" supported the 'measure, and the bill was read a second timei—Several Lillis,. including the Expiring Laws Continuance were -read a third time.
The sitting was suspended during pleasure at eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COIViSIONS. The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock.

BRITISH WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. Established 1866. Incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862. CHIEF Orricr.s : BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending April 30th, 1888. Notwithstanding.the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke. who for udwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to All up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £1,009, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders.. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,928 lie 9,1. The total amount of payments was £163,018 14s id, leaving a balance Upon the year's accounts of £15,292 4s 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Od. The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, including £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid up to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 is 10d. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, showing a net increase of 39,070 Assurants, and £27,820 lie 0(1 in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director. D. A. BECKETT, Secretary. DISTRICT OFFICE: MARKET GATE CHAMBERS, WARRINGTON. S. GREEN, SUPERINTENDENT.

On Tuesday evening, at a meeting of the Directors of the Starr-Bowketnudding Society, of which Mr. Legge was chairman, reference was made to the loss which the society had sustalned, several of those present remarking On the pleasant relations:they had had with their late chairman, and the higliesteem in which he was held. A resolution of condolence with the family was unani- mously adopted. - IN MEMORIAM. I'S,TOAII LEGGE, DIED 2ND AI7GT:IST, 1888. A general tear is falling for the dead, II In every face the heavy gloom is read'; Hearts that were wont to sympathise with all That he hath thought, throb at this sudden call. So sudden! that we scarcely knew him laid . Upon his bed of sickness ere 'twas said His spirit hath gone forth—bath soared away To greet the light of the eternal day.. So sudden! that the partners of his home Nor thought, nor reason'd he was near the tomb; So sudden! dear ones absent from his side, . , Failed to embrace him, ere the parent died! , Heart pangs of solemn "thoughts too deep' for tears"; Heart loves, that clung around his love for yeals— All now must bend, and in submission yield To that dread Power that doth our pathivay shield! lirhim was virtue rife, his dearest aim To wear a useful and unsullied name; To cheer the poor, to give the needy aid, And cast a halo round the part he played. He's gone—and we must follow in his wake, We, pilgrims here, are sighing for his sake ; 'Tis warning all—let all regard the text— In church one Sunday—in his grave the next! Ah, gentle spirit, o'er thy sacred bier; • We thintrof thee and sped a farewell tear; And Many a day, with many a thought of thee, We shall proclaim how good a man can be! .T. 'M. —Warrington, August 4th, 1888.
